selected pixels form a pattern. 1.3 what is a pixel? black definition: a pixel (picture element) is the smallest addressable element of a raster image or display. pixel means picture element. every pixel has a position in the image. a pixel stores colour or intensity information. a collection of pixels forms a raster image. 1.4 2d graphics primitives black a graphics primitive is a basic geometric element used to construct more complex graphical objects. in 2d graphics, positions are described using two coordinate directions: x-axis (horizontal) and y-axis (vertical). primitive meaning example point a single position, usually represented by (x, y). (3, 4) line a straight path joining two endpoints. from (2, 2) to (8, 6). circle a closed curve whose points are at a fixed distance (radius) from its centre. centre (0, 0), radius 5. rectangle a four-sided polygon with four right angles. four connected line segments. ellipse an oval closed curve with major and minor axes. horizontal and vertical radii. polygon a closed shape made from three or more straight line segments. triangle, pentagon. 1.5 what are raster graphics algorithms? black raster graphics algorithms are procedures that determine which pixels should be selected to represent a graphical object on a raster display. converting a geometric description into pixels is called scan conversion or rasterization . mathematical line rasterize selected pixels conceptual illustration: a geometric line is represented by selected pixels. 1.6 important algorithms in this unit object / task algorithms or methods priority line drawing dda, bresenham's line algorithm red circle drawing midpoint circle, bresenham's circle algorithm red ellipse drawing midpoint ellipse algorithm yellow polygon filling scan-line polygon filling yellow area filling boundary-fill, flood-fill yellow 1.7 raster graphics vs vector graphics black read the comparison once and understand the difference. raster graphics vector graphics made from pixels. made from mathematical paths and shapes. resolution-dependent. scalable without pixelation of the paths. suitable for photographs. suitable for logos and illustrations. examples: jpeg, png, bmp. example: svg. 1.8 applications digital photography and image editing. computer games and animation. medical images and scans. digital painting and web images. 1.9 exam revision black introductory questions to read once: define raster graphics. what is a pixel? this is the foundation for understanding all line-generation algorithms. no matching standalone question was identified in the checked papers. how much depth is needed: 1-mark definition and a short 5-mark explanation. 2.1.1 what is a line in computer graphics? a line segment is a straight path joining two endpoints. in computer graphics, it is usually specified by two coordinates: starting point (x₁, y₁) and ending point (x₂, y₂) . 2.1.2 what is scan conversion? scan conversion is the process of converting a geometric description of an object into a set of discrete pixels that can be displayed on a raster screen. for a line, the algorithm chooses which pixels should be turned on so that the displayed result looks as close as possible to the ideal straight line. selected pixels (blue) ideal mathematical line (red dashed) figure: a continuous line is approximated using discrete screen pixels (illustrative grid). 2.1.3 why is scan conversion required? a raster display contains a finite grid of pixels, not infinitely many points. a mathematical line may pass between pixel centres. the algorithm must select suitable pixels to make the line appear straight and continuous. good algorithms should be accurate, consistent in brightness and fast. remember: scan conversion does not change the mathematical line. it decides how that line is represented on a discrete pixel grid. 2.2 line equation and direct method yellow why study this? it explains the mathematical foundation used by incremental line algorithms. the supplied older mca/bca material includes line-coordinate and line-generation questions; the direct method itself is supporting preparation. how much depth is needed: understand the equation and explain why incremental algorithms are preferred. 2.2.1 slope-intercept form a non-vertical straight line can be represented by: y = mx + c where m is the slope and c is the y-intercept. given two endpoints: m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁) = δy / δx then the equation can be used to calculate a y-coordinate for a selected x-coordinate. a vertical line has undefined slope and is handled separately. 2.2.2 direct line-generation method read the two endpoints. calculate the slope m . use the line equation to calculate intermediate coordinates. round each calculated coordinate to a pixel position and plot it. 2.2.3 limitation of the direct method repeated multiplication and division, floating-point calculations and rounding can make the method less efficient. it also needs special handling for vertical lines and steep slopes. incremental methods such as dda and bresenham calculate each next point from the previous one and are more suitable for raster line generation. important: the direct equation is a mathematical explanation, not the same algorithm as dda or bresenham. 2.3 dda line drawing algorithm yellow why study this? dda is one of the standard line-generation algorithms covered by the primary mca line-generation question and by related supplied question material. the available papers do not establish a reliable percentage threshold, so this is not labelled red by frequency. how much depth is needed: prepare definition, formulas, algorithm, pseudocode, a complete numerical example, advantages and disadvantages. practise a 5-mark answer and a long numerical answer. 2.3.1 definition dda (digital differential analyzer) is an incremental scan-conversion algorithm that generates a line by calculating small, equal increments in x and y and plotting the nearest pixel at each step. 2.3.2 formulae used in dda let the endpoints be (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) . δx = x₂ − x₁ change in x δy = y₂ − y₁ change in y steps = max(|δx|, |δy|) number of increments x_increment = δx / steps change in x per step y_increment = δy / steps change in y per step start with x = x₁ and y = y₁ . at every iteration, plot (round(x), round(y)) , then add the two increments. 2.3.3 why do we use maximum of |δx| and |δy|? at each step, the algorithm should move by no more than one pixel in either coordinate direction. choosing the larger absolute difference as the number of steps ensures the larger coordinate changes by one unit per step, while the smaller coordinate changes by a fraction of a unit. 2.3.4 dda algorithm — step by step input the two endpoints (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) . calculate δx = x₂ − x₁ and δy = y₂ − y₁ . calculate steps = max(|δx|, |δy|) . calculate x_increment = δx / steps and y_increment = δy / steps . set x = x₁ and y = y₁ . plot the pixel at (round(x), round(y)) . increase x and y by their respective increments. repeat through the final step. 2.3.5 pseudocode dda (x1, y1, x2, y2) dx = x2 - x1 dy = y2 - y1 steps = max(abs(dx), abs(dy)) x_inc = dx / steps y_inc = dy / steps x = x1 y = y1 for i = 0 to steps plot(round(x), round(y)) x = x + x_inc y = y + y_inc 2.3.6 solved numerical example — dda example: draw a line from (2, 3) to (10, 8) using dda. step 1 — find differences δx = 10 − 2 = 8 ; δy = 8 − 3 = 5 . step 2 — find number of steps steps = max(8, 5) = 8 . step 3 — find increments x_increment = 8/8 = 1 ; y_increment = 5/8 = 0.625 . step 4 — generate pixels step x (before rounding) y (before rounding) plotted pixel 0 2.000 3.000 (2, 3) 1 3.000 3.625 (3, 4) 2 4.000 4.250 (4, 4) 3 5.000 4.875 (5, 5) 4 6.000 5.500 (6, 6) 5 7.000 6.125 (7, 6) 6 8.000 6.750 (8, 7) 7 9.000 7.375 (9, 7) 8 10.000 8.000 (10, 8) final plotted pixels: (2,3), (3,4), (4,4), (5,5), (6,6), (7,6), (8,7), (9,7), (10,8). (2,3) (10,8) blue circles: rounded pixel positions figure: pixel sequence for the worked dda example. 2.3.7 advantages of dda simple and easy to understand and implement. works for positive, negative, steep and shallow slopes when signed increments are used. uses incremental calculations rather than solving the full line equation for every pixel. 2.3.8 disadvantages of dda uses floating-point arithmetic. requires rounding at each step. repeated rounding can introduce small cumulative errors. generally less efficient than integer-based bresenham for raster hardware. remember: in dda, use max(|δx|, |δy|) , not just δx . this is essential for steep lines and lines in different directions. 2.4 bresenham line drawing algorithm yellow why study this? bresenham is a major line-generation algorithm and is included in the supplied question material. its exact frequency percentage is not claimed because the mixed-paper denominator has not been verified. how much depth is needed: prepare the definition, decision parameter, two cases, algorithm, pseudocode, numerical example and comparison with dda. 2.4.1 definition bresenham's line drawing algorithm is an incremental raster line-generation algorithm that selects the next pixel using an integer decision parameter. in its basic form for a line with slope between 0 and 1, it chooses between the east (e) and north-east (ne) candidate pixels. 2.4.2 basic assumption and candidate pixels for the simple derivation below, assume the line moves left to right, 0 ≤ m ≤ 1 , x₂ > x₁ and y₂ ≥ y₁ . each step increases x by one. the next pixel is either e = (x+1, y) or ne = (x+1, y+1) . e ne at each x-step, select the candidate closest to the ideal line. figure: the two candidate pixels considered in the basic bresenham case. 2.4.3 decision parameter let δx = x₂ − x₁ and δy = y₂ − y₁ . for the basic case 0 ≤ m ≤ 1 , the initial decision parameter is: p₀ = 2δy − δx at each step: condition choose new decision parameter p < 0 e: (x+1, y) p(next) = p + 2δy p ≥ 0 ne: (x+1, y+1) p(next) = p + 2δy − 2δx the parameter tells the algorithm which candidate pixel is closer to the ideal line. the tie case p = 0 is handled here by choosing ne; a consistent tie rule should be used throughout. 2.4.4 algorithm steps — basic slope 0 to 1 input the two endpoints. calculate δx and δy . set p = 2δy − δx . start at (x₁, y₁) and plot it. for each next x-coordinate, if p < 0 , choose e and add 2δy to p. otherwise choose ne and add 2δy − 2δx to p. plot each selected pixel until the endpoint is reached. 2.4.5 pseudocode bresenham (x1, y1, x2, y2) dx = x2 - x1 dy = y2 - y1 p = 2 * dy - dx x = x1 y = y1 plot(x, y) while x < x2 x = x + 1 if p < 0 p = p + 2 * dy else y = y + 1 p = p + 2 * dy - 2 * dx plot(x, y) 2.4.6 solved numerical example — bresenham example: draw a line from (2, 3) to (10, 8) . step 1: δx = 10 − 2 = 8 , δy = 8 − 3 = 5 . step 2: initial decision parameter p₀ = 2(5) − 8 = 2 . step 3: apply the decision rule at each step. if p is negative choose e; otherwise choose ne. current pixel p before decision choice next pixel p after update (2,3) 2 ne (3,4) −4 (3,4) −4 e (4,4) 6 (4,4) 6 ne (5,5) 0 (5,5) 0 ne (tie rule) (6,6) −8 (6,6) −8 e (7,6) 2 (7,6) 2 ne (8,7) −6 (8,7) −6 e (9,7) 4 (9,7) 4 ne (10,8) −6 final plotted pixels: (2,3), (3,4), (4,4), (5,5), (6,6), (7,6), (8,7), (9,7), (10,8). numerical check: the table uses p ≥ 0 to choose ne. this tie convention is stated explicitly so that the worked steps are reproducible. 2.4.7 advantages uses integer arithmetic in the basic algorithm. avoids repeated floating-point multiplication and division. efficient and accurate for raster line generation. incremental decision updates are simple. 2.4.8 disadvantages / limitations the basic form above is derived for a line with slope between 0 and 1. other slopes and directions need a generalised version that handles steepness and signs. the decision rule must be adapted when x is not the major direction. 2.4.9 handling other slopes for a complete line-drawing implementation, first determine whether |δy| > |δx| . if so, interchange the roles of x and y (steep line). also determine the signs of δx and δy to select the direction of travel. the core idea remains the same: use an integer decision variable to choose the nearest candidate pixel. remember: do not apply the simple formula p₀ = 2δy − δx blindly to every possible slope. state the basic-case assumption in an exam answer, or explain that the generalised algorithm handles all octants. 2.5 dda vs bresenham — comparison yellow why study this? the comparison follows naturally from the two algorithms and is useful for a short-note or 5-mark answer. it is not labelled as a separate direct question unless an exact matching question is confirmed. basis dda bresenham full form / name digital differential analyzer bresenham line drawing algorithm calculation uses incremental floating-point values. uses an integer decision parameter in its basic form. pixel selection rounds calculated x and y values. chooses between candidate pixels using the decision parameter. arithmetic uses division and floating-point addition. mainly integer addition and subtraction. implementation simpler to understand and implement. requires decision logic and slope/direction handling. efficiency generally slower than integer bresenham. generally more efficient for raster hardware. rounding rounding is performed at every plotted step. no floating-point rounding is needed in the integer formulation. 2.5.1 important terms term meaning pixel smallest addressable picture element on a raster display. scan conversion converting a geometric description into pixels. slope (m) ratio of vertical change to horizontal change. incremental algorithm an algorithm that calculates the next result using the previous result. decision parameter a value used by bresenham to select the next pixel. rounding choosing the nearest integer pixel coordinate. octant one of eight directional regions used to classify line slopes and directions. 2.6 exam preparation and quick revision 2.6.1 previous-year question evidence red — direct primary mca evidence the supplied mca 2022–24 paper (ccmca403) asks for the major line-generation algorithms . this is direct evidence that line-generation algorithms as a group are important for the mca examination. yellow — related supplied paper evidence the older mca paper (cs-de-21) includes a question about coordinate systems used for drawing lines and circles. the supplied bca papers include questions on dda and bresenham line algorithms. these are different sources and paper levels. do not describe an older mca or bca question as a direct question from the 2022–24 primary mca paper. no percentage is stated because the complete denominator of comparable papers has not been reliably counted. 2.6.2 exam-ready answers 1-mark preparation what is scan conversion? it is the process of converting geometric objects into a set of pixels for display on a raster screen. what is dda? dda is an incremental line drawing algorithm that calculates successive pixel positions using x and y increments. what is bresenham's algorithm? it is an integer-based incremental line drawing algorithm that uses a decision parameter to choose the next pixel. what is the initial decision parameter for the basic bresenham case? p₀ = 2δy − δx , for 0 ≤ m ≤ 1 . 5-mark preparation — dda define dda. write the formulas for δx, δy, steps, x increment and y increment. explain the algorithm steps. write pseudocode. show a small numerical example and mention advantages/disadvantages. 5-mark preparation — bresenham define bresenham's line algorithm. state the basic slope assumption. write the initial decision parameter. explain the e and ne decision cases and updates. show a numerical example and list advantages. 15-mark preparation — line generation algorithms introduce scan conversion and the need for line-generation algorithms. explain the direct line equation briefly. explain dda with formulas, algorithm, pseudocode and a complete numerical table. explain bresenham with its decision parameter, cases, pseudocode and a complete numerical table. compare the two algorithms. conclude with the efficiency and integer-arithmetic advantage of bresenham. 2.6.3 quick revision raster screens represent images using pixels. scan conversion chooses pixels to approximate a geometric line. dda uses steps = max(|δx|, |δy|) . dda increments are δx/steps and δy/steps . dda rounds each calculated coordinate to the nearest pixel. basic bresenham starts with p₀ = 2δy − δx for 0 ≤ m ≤ 1 . if p is negative, choose e; otherwise choose ne under the stated tie rule. bresenham uses integer updates and is generally more efficient. generalised bresenham handles steep lines and all directions by swapping axes and using direction signs. 2.6.4 common mistakes to avoid using δx as the dda step count for every line instead of the maximum absolute difference. forgetting to round dda coordinates before plotting. confusing dda increments with bresenham's decision parameter. applying the basic bresenham formula to steep or negative-slope lines without adapting the algorithm. not writing the assumed slope range in a numerical answer. 2.6.5 topic 2 resources — youtube videos 1. dda line drawing drawing 2d primitives, subtopic “scan converting lines”. next in the syllabus: scan converting circles. next → scan converting circles · ↑ back to index 3 topic 3 of 7 scan converting circles red priority red — direct mca pyq evidence why this topic matters: the supplied mca 2022–24 paper (ccmca403) asks students to draw a circle using c++ or java. an older mca paper also includes circle-coordinate questions. the circle-generation algorithm is therefore a direct exam-preparation priority. how much depth is needed: learn the circle equation, eight-way symmetry, bresenham’s circle algorithm, decision parameter, both update cases, a complete numerical example, pseudocode and a c++-style implementation. 3.1 what is circle scan conversion? a mathematical circle is a continuous curve. a raster display, however, is made of discrete pixels. circle scan conversion means selecting a set of pixels that represent the circumference as closely as possible. a circle with centre (x c , y c ) and radius r is described by: (x − x c )² + (y − y c )² = r² for a circle centred at the origin, this becomes x² + y² = r² . centre (x₀,y₀) r selected pixels red dashed: ideal circle · blue dots: illustrative raster points figure 3.1: a continuous circle is represented by discrete pixels on a raster grid. 3.2 why do we calculate only one-eighth of the circle? a circle has eight-way symmetry . if one point (x, y) is on a circle centred at the origin, then the following seven reflected or swapped-coordinate points are also on the same circle: (x,y), (y,x), (−x,y), (−y,x), (−x,−y), (−y,−x), (x,−y), (y,−x) these eight positions lie in eight 45-degree regions called octants . so the algorithm calculates pixels only in the first octant, from (0,r) towards the diagonal x = y . each calculated point is reflected to obtain the other seven positions. start (0,r) first octant y x o 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 figure 3.2: eight-way symmetry. only the first octant is calculated; the rest are mirrored. why this saves work: without symmetry, we would calculate points around the entire circumference. with eight-way symmetry, we calculate approximately one-eighth and reflect each point. the axis and diagonal points overlap, so duplicate plotted pixels may occur and can be ignored. 3.3 bresenham’s circle drawing algorithm definition: bresenham’s circle drawing algorithm is an incremental raster algorithm that selects the next pixel on a circle by using an integer decision parameter. it uses additions and subtractions rather than repeatedly evaluating the circle equation with floating-point calculations. for the version used in these notes, the circle is initially assumed to be centred at the origin. we begin at the top point (0,r) and move through the first octant. 3.4 candidate pixels and decision parameter at each iteration, x increases by 1. the next pixel is chosen from two candidates: east (e): (x + 1, y) — x increases, y stays the same. south-east (se): (x + 1, y − 1) — x increases and y decreases. the decision parameter tells us which candidate is closer to the true circular boundary. for the integer form used here, the initial value is: p₀ = 3 − 2r e: (x+1,y) se: (x+1,y−1) the algorithm chooses one of these two candidate pixels. figure 3.3: candidate pixels considered at each step in the first octant. 3.5 decision rules and update formulas start with x = 0 , y = r and p = 3 − 2r . then apply the following rule. in the formulas below, x′ and y′ mean the new coordinates after the move. condition selected pixel coordinate update decision update p < 0 east (e) x′ = x + 1 y′ = y p′ = p + 4x′ + 6 p ≥ 0 south-east (se) x′ = x + 1 y′ = y − 1 p′ = p + 4(x′ − y′) + 10 important order: first decide which pixel is selected, calculate the new coordinates, then use those new coordinates in the corresponding update formula. finally, assign x = x′ , y = y′ , p = p′ . easy way to remember: if p is negative, choose e and keep y unchanged. if p is zero or positive, choose se and reduce y by one. 3.6 complete algorithm — step by step read the radius r and centre (x₀,y₀) . set x = 0 and y = r . set the initial decision parameter p = 3 − 2r . plot the eight symmetric points around the required centre. while x ≤ y , check the decision parameter. if p < 0 , choose e: increase x by 1 and keep y unchanged; update p = p + 4x + 6 using the new x. otherwise choose se: increase x by 1, decrease y by 1; update p = p + 4(x − y) + 10 using the new x and new y. plot the eight symmetric points for the new coordinate pair. stop when x > y . the first-octant calculation is complete. loop-condition note: the point where x = y belongs to the calculated octant and should be plotted once. therefore, a convenient implementation uses while (x ≤ y) and checks the condition again after updating the coordinates. 3.7 flowchart / working sequence start input r and centre (xc, yc) x = 0, y = r, p = 3 − 2r plot 8 symmetric pixels x ≤ y ? yes no p < 0 ? yes no e: x++, y same se: x++, y-- stop update p using the selected case, then plot and repeat. figure 3.4: simplified decision flow. both branches update p and return to the loop test. study tip: in an exam, a neat stepwise algorithm and a decision table are usually clearer than trying to reproduce a complicated flowchart. if you draw the flowchart, show both decision branches and the loop back. 3.8 solved numerical example — radius r = 6 question: use bresenham’s circle drawing algorithm to calculate the first-octant points for a circle of radius 6 centred at the origin. step 1 — initial values x = 0 , y = 6 p₀ = 3 − 2r = 3 − 2(6) = −9 the starting point is (0,6) . step 2 — apply the decision rule repeatedly current (x,y) p before decision choice new (x′,y′) calculation of new p p after update (0,6) −9 e (1,6) −9 + 4(1) + 6 −9 + 10 = 1 (1,6) 1 se (2,5) 1 + 4(2−5) + 10 1 − 12 + 10 = −1 (2,5) −1 e (3,5) −1 + 4(3) + 6 −1 + 18 = 17 (3,5) 17 se (4,4) 17 + 4(4−4) + 10 17 + 0 + 10 = 27 at (4,4) , x equals y, so this diagonal point is plotted. the next update would make x greater than y, so the first-octant loop ends. first-octant points: (0,6), (1,6), form. uses additions and subtractions instead of repeated multiplication, division and square roots. uses eight-way symmetry, so only one octant needs to be calculated. incremental updates make it efficient for raster displays. produces a consistent sequence of pixels around the circle. limitations the basic derivation assumes an integer radius and a circle aligned to the pixel coordinate system. it generates a raster approximation, not a mathematically continuous curve. duplicate pixels can occur on axes and on the 45-degree diagonal; these should be treated as one visible pixel. the as a stretched or compressed circle. it has a centre, a horizontal radius and a vertical radius. these two radii are usually written as r x and r y . horizontal radius (r x ): distance from the centre to the ellipse boundary along the x-axis. vertical radius (r y ): distance from the centre to the ellipse boundary along the y-axis. centre (x c , y c ): the point around which the ellipse is symmetric. major axis: the longer diameter of the ellipse. minor axis: the shorter diameter of the ellipse. (x₍c₎, y₍c₎) rₓ rᵧ x-axis y-axis the horizontal and vertical radii can have different lengths. figure 4.1: an ellipse has two radii measured from its centre. 4.2 mathematical equation of an ellipse for an ellipse centred at the origin with its axes parallel to the coordinate axes: x²/r x ² + y²/r y ² = 1 for an ellipse centred at (x c , y c ) : (x − x c )²/r x ² + (y − y c )²/r y ² = 1 to make the decision calculations easier, multiply the origin-centred equation by r x ²r y ² and define the implicit function: f(x,y) = r y ²x² + r x ²y² − r x ²r y ² how to read f(x,y): if f(x,y) = 0 , the point lies on the ideal ellipse. if f(x,y) < 0 , it is inside. if f(x,y) > 0 , it is outside. the midpoint algorithm evaluates this function at carefully selected midpoints to decide which pixel is closer to the curve. 4.3 why do we calculate only one quadrant? an axis-aligned ellipse is symmetric about both the x-axis and the y-axis. therefore, every point in the first quadrant has three matching points in the other quadrants. we calculate one quadrant and reflect each point to obtain the full ellipse. this is called four-way symmetry . (x,y) (-x,y) (-x,-y) (x,-y) quadrant i quadrant ii quadrant iii quadrant iv +y +x figure 4.2: one calculated point produces four symmetric ellipse points. for an ellipse centred at the origin, the four points are: (x,y), (−x,y), (x,−y), (−x,−y) for a centre at (x c , y c ) , add the centre coordinates: (x c +x, y c +y) , (x c −x, y c +y) , (x c +x, y c −y) , (x c −x, y c −y) 4.4 why are there two regions? the slope of the ellipse changes as we move around the first quadrant. near the top of the ellipse, the curve is relatively flat: x changes at each step while y may stay the same or decrease. near the right-hand side, the curve becomes steep: y decreases at each step while x may stay the same or increase. to handle these different behaviours efficiently, the first quadrant is divided into two regions at the point where the tangent slope is −1 . differentiate the ellipse equation: x²/r x ² + y²/r y ² = 1 2x/r x ² + (2y/r y ²)(dy/dx) = 0 dy/dx = −(r y ²x)/(r x ²y) at the region boundary, the slope is −1 . therefore: r y ²x = r x ²y equivalently, compare the doubled terms: 2r y ²x = 2r x ²y region 1 region 2 slope = −1 x y x increases → y decreases ↓ figure 4.3: region 1 is the flatter part; region 2 is the steeper part. region direction of progress candidate pixels decision idea region 1 x increases by 1 e: (x+1,y) or se: (x+1,y−1) choose whether y stays or decreases. region 2 y decreases by 1 s: (x,y−1) or se: (x+1,y−1) choose whether x stays or increases. region 1 condition: continue while 2r y ²x < 2r x ²y . switch to region 2 when this condition becomes false. 4.5 midpoint ellipse drawing algorithm — the central idea the midpoint ellipse drawing algorithm is an incremental raster algorithm. instead of calculating every point from the ellipse equation, it tests the midpoint between two candidate pixels. the sign of the decision parameter tells us which candidate is closer to the ideal ellipse boundary. start at the top of the first quadrant: (x,y) = (0,r y ) . then process region 1 and region 2. for each calculated point, plot its four symmetric points. important difference from circle drawing: a circle uses eight-way symmetry. an axis-aligned ellipse uses four-way symmetry. also, the ellipse algorithm needs two regions because its slope changes across the quadrant. 4.6 region 1 — initial decision parameter and updates initial point: x = 0,   y = r y the initial midpoint decision parameter for region 1 is: p 1,0 = r y ² − r x ²r y + ¼r x ² at every step, x increases by one. there are two cases: condition choose pixel coordinate update decision update p₁ < 0 east (e) x = x+1 ; y stays the same p₁ = p₁ + 2rᵧ²x + rᵧ² p₁ ≥ 0 south-east (se) x = x+1 ; y = y−1 p₁ = p₁ + 2rᵧ²x − 2rₓ²y + rᵧ² in the update formulas, use the new x and y values after choosing the next pixel. the algorithm continues until the region 1 condition 2r y ²x < 2r x ²y is no longer true. incremental terms: to avoid recalculating squares repeatedly, maintain: dx = 2rᵧ²x ; whenever x increases, add 2rᵧ² . dy = 2rₓ²y ; whenever y decreases, subtract 2rₓ² . 4.7 region 2 — initial decision parameter and updates region 2 begins at the last point calculated in region 1, say (x₀,y₀) . its initial decision parameter is: p 2,0 = r y ²(x₀+½)² + r x ²(y₀−1)² − r x ²r y ² at every region 2 step, y decreases by one. there are two cases: condition choose pixel coordinate update decision update p₂ > 0 south (s) y decreases by 1; x stays the same p₂ = p₂ − 2rₓ²y + rₓ² p₂ ≤ 0 south-east (se) x increases by 1; y decreases by 1 p₂ = p₂ + 2rᵧ²x − 2rₓ²y + rₓ² again, use the new coordinate values in the update. continue until y = 0 . the four-way symmetry points are plotted at every step in both regions. remember the sign rules: region 1: negative chooses e, otherwise se. region 2: positive chooses s, otherwise se. the inequality directions are different—do not mix them up. 4.8 complete solved numerical example — rₓ = 8, rᵧ = 6 question: use the midpoint ellipse algorithm to rasterize an ellipse centred at the origin with horizontal radius rₓ = 8 and vertical radius rᵧ = 6 . find the first-quadrant pixels and explain how to obtain the complete ellipse. step 1 — calculate the squares rₓ² = 8² = 64 and rᵧ² = 6² = 36 . step 2 — start at the top point (x₀,y₀) = (0,6) . step 3 — calculate the region 1 initial parameter p₁,₀ = rᵧ² − rₓ²rᵧ + ¼rₓ² = 36 − (64 × 6) + (64 ÷ 4) = 36 − 384 + 16 = −332 . step 4 — work through region 1 use p₁ < 0 → e ; ² − r x ²r y + ¼r x ² . in region 1, while 2r y ²x < 2r x ²y , choose e if p₁<0 ; otherwise choose se. update the decision parameter. at each point, plot the four symmetric pixels around the centre. at the last region 1 point, calculate p₂ using the region 2 initial formula. in region 2, while y≥0 , choose s if p₂>0 ; otherwise choose se. update the decision parameter. plot four symmetric pixels for each region 2 point. stop when y=0 . 4.10 pseudocode midpointellipse(xc, yc, rx, ry) rx2 = rx * rx ry2 = ry * ry x = 0 y = ry dx = 0 dy = 2 * rx2 * y p1 = ry2 - rx2 * ry + 0.25 * rx2 while dx < dy plotfourpoints(xc, yc, x, y) x = x + 1 dx = dx + 2 * ry2 if p1 < 0 p1 = p1 + dx + ry2 else y = y - 1 dy = dy - 2 * rx2 p1 = p1 + dx - dy + ry2 p2 = ry2 * (x + 0.5)^2 + rx2 * (y - 1)^2 - rx2 * ry2 while y >= 0 plotfourpoints(xc, yc, x, y) y = y - 1 dy = dy - 2 * rx2 if p2 > 0 p2 = p2 + rx2 - dy else x = x + 1 dx = dx + 2 * ry2 p2 = p2 + dx - dy + rx2 note: in this pseudocode, the update uses the new x and y values. the same convention is used in the numerical tables above. 4.11 c++ implementation #include <iostream> #include <cmath> using namespace std; void plotfourpoints(int xc, int yc, int x, int y) { cout << "(" << xc + x << "," << yc + y << ") "; cout << "(" << xc - x << "," << yc + y << ") "; cout << "(" << xc + x << "," << yc - y << ") "; cout << "(" << xc - x << "," << yc - y << ")\n"; } void midpointellipse(int xc, int yc, int rx, int ry) { double rx2 = rx * rx; double ry2 = ry * ry; int x = 0; int y = ry; double dx = 0; double dy = 2 * rx2 * y; double p1 = ry2 - rx2 * ry + 0.25 * rx2; // region 1 while (dx < dy) { plotfourpoints(xc, yc, x, y); x++; dx += 2 * ry2; if (p1 < 0) { p1 += dx + ry2; } else { y--; dy -= 2 * rx2; p1 += dx - dy + ry2; } } // region 2 double p2 = ry2 * (x + 0.5) * (x + 0.5) + rx2 * (y - 1) * (y - 1) - rx2 * ry2; while (y >= 0) { plotfourpoints(xc, yc, x, y); y--; dy -= 2 * rx2; if (p2 > 0) { p2 += rx2 - dy; } else { x++; dx += 2 * ry2; p2 += dx - dy + rx2; } } } int main() { midpointellipse(0, 0, 8, 6); return 0; } implementation note: this educational implementation prints the four symmetric coordinate positions. in a graphics program, algorithms scan-line approach move a horizontal scan line across the shape, calculate boundary intersections and fill the spans between intersection pairs. scan-line polygon fill; scan-line filling of rectangles and ellipses. seed-fill approach start from a known interior pixel (seed) and expand to neighbouring pixels while a colour or boundary condition permits. boundary-fill and flood-fill. easy memory trick: scan-line filling asks, “which horizontal spans are inside?” seed filling asks, “starting from this inside pixel, which neighbouring pixels can i reach?” 5.2 filling rectangles a rectangle is one of the simplest filled areas because its horizontal limits are constant on every scan line. suppose its opposite corners are \((x_{\min},y_{\min})\) and \((x_{\max},y_{\max})\). every pixel whose coordinates lie inside these limits belongs to the rectangle. for each y = y_min ... y_max: for each x = x_min ... x_max: setpixel(x, y, fillcolour) in an actual raster implementation, the right and top edges may be treated as exclusive to avoid drawing shared edges twice when adjacent rectangles are filled. the exact convention depends on the graphics api and coordinate system. one span rows are filled from left to right figure 5.2 — a rectangle can be filled by drawing a horizontal span on each row. algorithm: rectangle fill read the two opposite corners of the rectangle. ensure the minimum and maximum x and y values are correctly ordered. start at the first scan line, \(y=y_{\min}\). for every row, visit each x-coordinate from \(x_{\min}\) to \(x_{\max}\). write the fill colour to each pixel. move to the next row and repeat until the last row is processed. rectanglefill(x1, y1, x2, y2, colour): xmin = min(x1, x2) xmax = max(x1, x2) ymin = min(y1, y2) ymax = max(y1, y2) for y = ymin to ymax: for x = xmin to xmax: setpixel(x, y, colour) time complexity: \(o(w \times h)\), where \(w=x_{\max}-x_{\min}+1\) and \(h=y_{\max}-y_{\min}+1\). every pixel in the rectangle is written once. space complexity: \(o(1)\) extra space for the simple nested-loop method. 5.3 polygon filling a polygon is a closed 2d shape made from straight line segments called edges. a triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon and irregular closed shape are polygons. a polygon fill algorithm colours the pixels that lie inside its boundary. filling becomes more interesting when a polygon is concave (it has an inward dent). a horizontal scan line may enter and leave the polygon several times. therefore, the algorithm must find every intersection, sort them from left to right and fill the correct pairs. concave polygon scan line fill span 1 fill span 2 figure 5.3 — a concave polygon can produce more than one inside span on a scan line. 5.3.1 odd–even rule (even–odd rule) the odd–even rule is a way to decide whether a point is inside a polygon. imagine drawing a ray from the point toward infinity. count how many times the ray crosses the polygon boundary: odd number of crossings: the point is inside. even number of crossings: the point is outside. for scan-line filling, sort the intersections from left to right. the first crossing changes the state from outside to inside; the second changes it back to outside. so fill between intersection 1 and 2, 3 and 4, and so on. sorted intersections: x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄, ... fill: [x₁, x₂], [x₃, x₄], ... this is also called the parity rule because each boundary crossing toggles the inside/outside state. 5.3.2 scan-line polygon fill algorithm this is the main geometric polygon-filling method. a horizontal line called a scan line moves from the polygon’s lowest y-coordinate to its highest y-coordinate. at each row, the algorithm finds where that row intersects polygon edges and fills the pixels between successive pairs. step-by-step working find the minimum and maximum y-coordinate of the polygon. for the current scan line, find intersections with all relevant non-horizontal polygon edges. sort the intersection x-coordinates in increasing order. pair the intersections: first with second, third with fourth, and so on. fill pixels between each pair using the chosen pixel-rounding convention. move to the next scan line and repeat. interior span y = current row find crossings → sort → fill between pairs figure 5.4 — a scan line intersects polygon edges; the interior interval is filled. worked example — pairing intersections suppose one scan line crosses a polygon at x-coordinates 2, 5, 9 and 14. after sorting, there are four intersections. apply the odd–even rule: pair span action 1st and 2nd 2 to 5 fill the first inside interval. 3rd and 4th 9 to 14 fill the second inside interval. coordinates strictly between the endpoints are unambiguous. in an actual raster program, use a consistent rule such as a left-inclusive/right-exclusive span to prevent adjacent spans from drawing a shared boundary pixel twice. 5.3.3 edge table (et) and active edge table (aet) checking every polygon edge again for every scan line is wasteful. an efficient implementation uses two data structures: edge table (et): stores each non-horizontal edge in a bucket indexed by the edge’s lower y-coordinate, \(y_{\min}\). active edge table (aet): stores edges that intersect the current scan line. the aet is sorted by their current x-intersection. an edge record commonly stores: field meaning \(y_{\max}\) upper endpoint y-coordinate; the edge is no longer active at its upper limit under the common half-open convention. \(x\) current x-intersection with the scan line. \(1/m\) inverse slope, used to update x when the increment is zero. et/aet procedure ignore horizontal edges for intersection counting; they do not cross a scan line in the usual parity calculation. for each remaining edge, identify its lower from a selected pixel inside a closed region and spreads outward. the algorithm colours neighbouring pixels until it reaches pixels having the specified boundary colour. it assumes that the region is enclosed by a clearly defined boundary colour. for example, if a shape has a black outline and a white interior, choose an interior seed pixel and fill the white area with blue. the black boundary stops the process. seed black boundary fill expands neighbouring pixels are tested until the boundary is reached figure 5.6 — boundary-fill begins at an interior seed and stops at the boundary colour. 4-connected and 8-connected boundary-fill connectivity defines which neighbouring pixels the algorithm checks. 4-connected p 8-connected p figure 5.7 — 4-connected checks only the four sides; 8-connected also checks the four diagonals. connectivity neighbour pixels coordinates relative to (x,y) 4-connected top, bottom, left, right (x+1,y), (x−1,y), (x,y+1), (x,y−1) 8-connected all four sides plus four diagonals four side neighbours and (x±1,y±1) boundary-fill pseudocode — 4-connected boundaryfill4(x, y, fillcolour, boundarycolour): current = getpixel(x, y) if current != boundarycolour and current != fillcolour: setpixel(x, y, fillcolour) boundaryfill4(x + 1, y, fillcolour, boundarycolour) boundaryfill4(x - 1, y, fillcolour, boundarycolour) boundaryfill4(x, y + 1, fillcolour, boundarycolour) boundaryfill4(x, y - 1, fillcolour, boundarycolour) the 8-connected version makes the same test but also calls the function for the four diagonal neighbours. the fill-colour check prevents the algorithm from repeatedly processing pixels that have already been filled. limitations and precautions the boundary must be closed. a tiny gap can allow the fill to leak outside. the boundary colour must be distinguishable from the fill colour. recursive implementations can exceed the call-stack limit for large regions. an explicit stack or queue is safer in production software. 4-connected fill can leave diagonal gaps in some pixel arrangements. 8-connected fill reaches diagonal neighbours, but can leak through diagonal boundary gaps. connectivity must be chosen consistently with the boundary representation. 5.5 flood-fill algorithm flood-fill also begins from a seed pixel, but its stopping condition is different. instead of stopping when it encounters a specified boundary colour, it replaces a connected region of a specified old/interior colour with a new fill colour. think of the paint-bucket tool in an image editor. if you click on a white region, the tool changes the connected white pixels to blue. it does not need to know the colour of the outline; it checks whether each pixel still has the target old colour. before: target colour = white after: new colour figure 5.8 — flood-fill replaces all connected pixels matching the old colour. flood-fill pseudocode — 4-connected floodfill4(x, y, oldcolour, newcolour): current = getpixel(x, y) if current != oldcolour: return setpixel(x, y, newcolour) floodfill4(x + 1, y, oldcolour, newcolour) floodfill4(x - 1, y, oldcolour, newcolour) floodfill4(x, y + 1, oldcolour, newcolour) floodfill4(x, y - 1, oldcolour, newcolour) special case: if oldcolour equals newcolour, return immediately. otherwise, the algorithm may revisit pixels indefinitely or perform unnecessary work, depending on the implementation. iterative flood-fill using a stack for a large image, recursive flood-fill may create thousands or millions of nested function calls. an iterative version stores pending pixels in an explicit stack. this avoids relying on the programming language's call stack. floodfilliterative(seedx, seedy, oldcolour, newcolour): if oldcolour == newcolour: return stack = empty stack push(stack, (seedx, seedy)) while stack is not empty: (x, y) = pop(stack) if pixel(x, y) != oldcolour: continue setpixel(x, y, newcolour) push(stack, (x + 1, y)) push(stack, (x - 1, y)) push(stack, (x, y + 1)) push(stack, (x, y - 1)) in real code, check image boundaries before reading or pushing neighbours. a visited array can be used when pixels are not modified immediately or when colour. stopping condition stops at the specified boundary colour or at pixels already filled. stops when neighbouring pixels do not match the old colour. requirement needs a known boundary colour and a closed boundary. needs a known target colour in the connected region. typical use filling a closed shape with a known outline colour. replacing a connected colour region, like a paint-bucket tool. connectivity 4-connected or 8-connected. 4-connected or 8-connected. exam memory line: boundary-fill checks the boundary colour; flood-fill checks the old interior colour. 5.6 filling an ellipse an ellipse can be filled by processing one horizontal scan line at a time. for an axis-aligned ellipse centred at \((x_c,y_c)\), with horizontal radius \(r_x\) and vertical radius \(r_y\), its equation is: (x − x_c)² / rₓ² + (y − y_c)² / rᵧ² = 1 for a selected scan line y, rearrange the equation to calculate the horizontal distance from the centre: x = x_c ± rₓ √[1 − (y − y_c)² / rᵧ²] the two values give the left and right intersections of the scan line with the ellipse. fill the pixels between them. only scan lines satisfying \(|y-y_c| \le r_y\) intersect the ellipse. fill this horizontal span each scan line has its own left and right intersection figure 5.9 — ellipse filling calculates a left and right intersection for each valid row. algorithm: scan-line ellipse fill read the ellipse centre \((x_c,y_c)\) and radii \(r_x,r_y\). start at \(y=y_c-r_y\) and continue through \(y_c+r_y\). for the current y, calculate \(q=1-(y-y_c)^2/r_y^2\). calculate \(d=r_x\sqrt{q}\). find the left and right intersections: \(x_l=x_c-d\), \(x_r=x_c+d\). fill the integer pixels between the rounded left and right limits. repeat for the next scan line. fillellipse(xc, yc, rx, ry, colour): for y = yc - ry to yc + ry: q = 1 - ((y - yc) * (y - yc)) / (ry * ry) if q >= 0: dx = rx * sqrt(q) left = ceil(xc - dx) right = floor(xc + dx) for x = left to right: setpixel(x, y, colour) note: this direct equation-based method is easy to understand, but it uses square roots and floating-point arithmetic. faster raster implementations can reuse symmetry or incremental ellipse calculations from the midpoint ellipse method, then fill horizontal spans between symmetric boundary points. approximate time complexity: \(o(r_y+r_xr_y)\) for the simple loop, because it processes about \(2r_y+1\) rows and writes the interior pixels. the number of writes is proportional to the ellipse's raster area. 5.7 pattern filling pattern filling fills an area with a repeating design instead of one solid colour. a pattern may be a small bitmap tile containing stripes, dots, checks, bricks, texture or another repeated arrangement. the pattern is repeated across the interior of the shape. the polygon or other shape still determines which pixels are inside; the pattern determines the colour/value written to those inside pixels. repeating tile clipped to the polygon interior figure 5.10 — a repeating checker pattern is visible only inside the polygon. how pattern coordinates are calculated assume the pattern tile has width \(p_w\) and height \(p_h\). for a screen pixel \((x,y)\), calculate the corresponding tile coordinate: patternx = (x − originx) mod p_w patterny = (y − originy) mod p_h read the pattern pixel at \((patternx,patterny)\), then write that value to the screen pixel if \((x,y)\) is inside the filled shape. the modulo operation makes the pattern repeat. in languages where a negative remainder can be negative, use a positive-modulo function so the pattern index remains in the valid range. pattern-fill procedure define or load a small pattern tile. determine the interior pixels using a polygon scan-line method or another area-fill method. for every interior pixel, map its screen coordinate to a tile coordinate using modulo. read the corresponding pattern colour. write that colour to the screen pixel. if the pattern supports transparency, leave transparent tile pixels unchanged. patternfill(interiorpixels, pattern, patternwidth, patternheight): for each pixel (x, y) in interiorpixels: px = positivemodulo(x - originx, patternwidth) py = positivemodulo(y - originy, patternheight) colour = pattern[py][px] if colour is not transparent: setpixel(x, y, colour) applications: texture and material representation, map symbols, backgrounds, hatching in technical drawings, surface decoration and fills in paint or drawing software. 5.8 comparison of the main filling methods method basic idea best suited for main caution rectangle fill nested loops over x and y ranges. axis-aligned rectangles and rectangular regions. choose inclusive/exclusive edge rules consistently. scan-line polygon fill find and pair intersections on each horizontal row. polygon interiors, including concave polygons. handle horizontal edges and shared vertices correctly. boundary-fill expand from a seed until boundary colour is found. closed regions with a known boundary colour. leaks if boundary is open or connectivity is unsuitable. flood-fill replace connected pixels matching an old colour. connected colour regions and paint-bucket tools. large recursive fills may overflow the call stack. ellipse fill calculate left/right intersections for each row. axis-aligned ellipses. direct formula uses floating point and square root. pattern fill repeat a tile over interior pixels. textures, hatching and decorative regions. must map pattern coordinates consistently. 5.9 advantages and disadvantages scan-line polygon filling advantages: efficient for polygons; handles convex and concave shapes; et/aet avoids testing every edge from scratch on every row. disadvantages: vertex and horizontal-edge handling is subtle; self-intersecting polygons need a clearly selected fill rule; rounding can cause small raster gaps if inconsistent. seed-fill methods advantages: conceptually simple; useful when a seed point is available; works naturally for irregular connected regions. disadvantages: may use significant memory; recursive versions can overflow; boundary-fill depends on a closed boundary and correct colour tests. pattern filling advantages: produces textures and visual detail; reusable small tiles reduce the need to store a large image for a repeated design. disadvantages: pattern alignment can look inconsistent if the origin changes; transparency and tile boundaries need careful handling. 5.10 exam-ready answers 2-mark answer — what is area filling? area filling is the process of assigning a colour or pattern to all raster pixels lying inside a closed graphical object. common methods include scan-line filling, boundary-fill, flood-fill and pattern filling. 5-mark answer — explain scan-line polygon filling. scan-line polygon filling fills a polygon row by row. a horizontal scan line is moved through the polygon. for each row, its intersections with polygon edges are calculated and sorted by increasing x-coordinate. the pixels between the first and second intersections, third and fourth intersections, and so on are filled according to the odd–even rule. for efficiency, an edge table stores edges by their minimum y-coordinate and an active edge table stores edges intersecting the current scan line. the x-intersection is updated for the next row using the inverse slope \(1/m\). horizontal edges and shared vertices must be handled consistently to avoid counting a vertex twice. 5-mark answer — differentiate between boundary-fill and flood-fill. boundary-fill begins from an interior seed pixel and spreads until it encounters a specified boundary colour. flood-fill begins from a seed pixel and replaces all connected pixels having a specified old colour. boundary-fill therefore checks the boundary colour, whereas flood-fill checks the interior colour. both can use 4-connected or 8-connected neighbourhoods. boundary-fill is suitable for a closed outline of known colour, while flood-fill is commonly used by paint-bucket tools to replace a connected colour region. 5-mark answer — explain 4-connected and 8-connected filling. in 4-connected filling, each pixel checks its four direct neighbours: top, bottom, left and right. in 8-connected filling, it checks these four neighbours plus the four diagonal neighbours. thus, 8-connected filling can reach diagonal pixels that 4-connected filling cannot. however, connectivity must be selected carefully because diagonal gaps in a boundary may allow a fill to leak. 15-mark answer — explain polygon area-filling methods. polygon area filling assigns colour or a pattern to the interior pixels of a polygon. the main approaches are scan-line filling and seed filling. scan-line polygon fill: a horizontal scan line intersects polygon edges. the intersection x-coordinates are sorted, and pixels between successive pairs are filled using the odd–even rule. the edge table (et) stores edges by their lower y-coordinate, while the active edge table (aet) maintains edges intersecting the current scan line. each edge stores its upper y-coordinate, current x-intersection and inverse slope. as the scan line moves, edges are inserted or removed and x is incremented by \(1/m\). boundary-fill: it starts from an interior seed pixel and fills neighbouring pixels until the specified boundary colour is encountered. it can be 4-connected or 8-connected. flood-fill: it starts from a seed and replaces connected pixels matching a specified old colour with a new colour. it is used in paint-bucket operations. pattern filling: instead of a solid colour, a repeating bitmap or tile is mapped over the interior. modulo arithmetic maps each screen pixel to a coordinate in the repeating tile. scan-line filling is well suited to polygon geometry, while seed-fill methods are useful when an interior seed and a pixel-colour condition are available. all methods require consistent pixel and boundary handling. 5.11 quick revision area filling: colour or pattern the interior pixels of a closed shape. rectangle: nested loops over x and y. scan-line polygon fill: find intersections, sort them, fill alternate pairs. et: edge table, bucketed by \(y_{\min}\). aet: active edge table, edges crossing the current scan line. inverse slope: \(1/m=\delta x/\delta y\), used to update x for the next row. boundary-fill: stops at boundary colour. flood-fill: replaces connected old-colour pixels. 4-connected: four side neighbours. 8-connected: four side plus four diagonal neighbours. ellipse fill: calculate left/right x-intersections for each y-row. pattern fill: map screen coordinates to repeating tile coordinates using modulo. 5.12 common mistakes to avoid do not confuse drawing a polygon boundary with filling its interior. do not fill every alternate pixel. scan-line filling fills intervals between paired intersections. do not forget to sort intersections from left to right before pairing them. do not count horizontal edges as ordinary scan-line crossings. do not count a shared vertex twice accidentally. use a consistent endpoint convention. do not reverse the stopping conditions: boundary-fill checks boundary colour; flood-fill checks old colour. do not assume 8-connected is always safer. it can leak through diagonal boundary gaps. do not use recursive seed-fill blindly for a huge image; prefer an explicit stack/queue or span-based implementation. do not use a negative modulo result directly as an array index in languages where remainder can be negative. 5.13 previous-year question evidence evidence you will learn in this topic first understand what clipping means. then learn point clipping, line clipping, polygon clipping, and finally how the same idea applies to circles and ellipses. the three algorithm names to keep separate are cohen–sutherland (line) , liang–barsky (line) , and sutherland–hodgman (polygon) . 6.1 meaning of clipping — start with a simple example clipping is the process of removing the part of a drawing that lies outside a selected region and keeping the part that lies inside it. the selected region is called the clipping window . imagine that a large picture is placed behind a small rectangular window. you can see only the portion of the picture visible through the window. computer graphics clipping works in the same way. clipping window outside part: removed inside part: retained only the green segment is displayed. why is clipping needed? to show only the required part of a scene. to prevent objects outside the viewing area from appearing. to remove invisible portions of lines and shapes. to make window-based viewing and drawing more efficient. 6.2 clipping window and its coordinates for a rectangular clipping window, we specify four boundaries: left: x min    right: x max bottom: y min    top: y max a point (x, y) is inside or on the window when both conditions are true: x min ≤ x ≤ x max and y min ≤ y ≤ y max . inside / visible region x min x max y max y min x y 6.3 point clipping — the simplest case point clipping checks one point at a time. if the point satisfies both coordinate conditions, it is accepted. otherwise, it is rejected. accept (x, y) when: x min ≤ x ≤ x max and y min ≤ y ≤ y max example: let the window be x = 10 to 50 and y = 10 to 40. point reason decision (20, 25) both coordinates are within the limits. accept (55, 25) x = 55 is greater than x max = 50. reject (30, 5) y = 5 is less than y min = 10. reject (10, 40) the point lies on the window boundaries. accept 6.4 line clipping — what are the possible results? a line segment has two endpoints. when we compare the line with a rectangular window, there are three basic possibilities: 1. fully inside 2. fully outside 3. crossing: keep green part completely inside: keep the complete line. completely outside: reject the complete line if it cannot cross the window. partially inside: calculate the boundary intersections and keep only the segment inside. 6.5 cohen–sutherland line clipping algorithm cohen–sutherland is a line-clipping algorithm used with a rectangular window. its main idea is to give each line endpoint a 4-bit region code (outcode) . this code tells us where the endpoint is located in relation to the window. step 1: divide the area into nine regions the clipping window is the centre region. around it are eight outside regions: top, bottom, left, right and four corners. 1001 1000 1010 0001 0000 0010 0101 0100 0110 top bottom left right bit order used in this diagram: top, bottom, right, left. a bit becomes 1 when the point is outside in that direction. the centre region has code 0000 . region outcode condition inside 0000 point is inside all four boundaries. top 1000 y > y max bottom 0100 y < y min right 0010 x > x max left 0001 x < x min top-left corner 1001 above the top and left of the window. for example, a point above and left of the window has both top and left bits set. its code is 1001 . step 2: remember the three decisions decision 1 — trivial accept: if both endpoint codes are 0000 , both endpoints are inside. accept the complete line. decision 2 — trivial reject: if the bitwise and of the two endpoint codes is not zero, both endpoints are outside on at least one same side. reject the line. decision 3 — partial clipping: otherwise, the line may cross the window. find an intersection with a boundary, replace the outside endpoint with that intersection, calculate its new outcode and repeat the tests. very important memory rule: or = 0 means accept. and ≠ 0 means reject. if neither condition is true, calculate an intersection. step 3: boundary intersection formulas let the endpoints be p 1 (x 1 , y 1 ) and p 2 (x 2 , y 2 ). boundary crossed coordinate fixed calculate the other coordinate top y = y max x = x 1 + (x 2 − x 1 )(y max − y 1 )/(y 2 − y 1 ) bottom y = y min x = x 1 + (x 2 − x 1 )(y min − y 1 )/(y 2 − y 1 ) right x = x max y = y 1 + (y 2 − y 1 )(x max − x 1 )/(x 2 − x 1 ) left x = x min y = y 1 + (y 2 − y 1 )(x min − x 1 )/(x 2 − x 1 ) worked numerical: cohen–sutherland question: clip the line from p 1 (5, 20) to p 2 (60, 30) against the rectangular window x min = 10, x max = 50, y min = 10, y max = 40. step 1 — find the endpoint codes. p 1 (5, 20) is left of the window. code = 0001 . p 2 (60, 30) is right of the window. code = 0010 . step 2 — test the codes. both codes are not zero, so we cannot trivially accept. 0001 and 0010 = 0000 , so we cannot trivially reject. therefore, the line is a possible crossing line. find its intersections. step 3 — find the left intersection (x = 10). y = 20 + (30 − 20)(10 − 5)/(60 − 5) y = 20 + 10 × 5/55 = 20.91 left intersection = (10, 20.91) step 4 — find the right intersection (x = 50). y = 20 + (30 − 20)(50 − 5)/(60 − 5) y = 20 + 10 × 45/55 = 28.18 right intersection = (50, 28.18) final result the visible line segment is approximately (10, 20.91) to (50, 28.18). the portions outside the window are discarded. (10, 20.91) (50, 28.18) clipping window green = retained segment; dashed red = removed part cohen–sutherland pseudocode 1. calculate the 4-bit outcode for each endpoint. 2. repeat: a. if (code1 or code2) == 0000: accept the line. stop. b. else if (code1 and code2) != 0000: reject the line. stop. c. otherwise: select an endpoint outside the window. find its intersection with the relevant boundary. replace that endpoint with the intersection. recalculate its outcode. 3. repeat until the line is accepted or rejected. 6.6 liang–barsky line clipping algorithm liang–barsky also clips a line against a rectangular window, but it uses a different method. instead of assigning region codes and repeatedly replacing endpoints, it writes the line using a parameter u and finds the part of the parameter range that lies inside the window. do not mix the two algorithms: cohen–sutherland uses outcodes; liang–barsky uses a parametric equation. step 1: write the parametric line equation x = x 1 + u(x 2 − x 1 ) y = y 1 + u(y 2 − y 1 ) 0 ≤ u ≤ 1 when u = 0, we are at the first endpoint. when u = 1, we are at the second endpoint. values between 0 and 1 represent points along the line. step 2: calculate p and q values δx = x 2 − x 1    δy = y 2 − y 1 p 1 = −δx,   q 1 = x 1 − x min p 2 = δx,   q 2 = x max − x 1 p 3 = −δy,   q 3 = y 1 − y min p 4 = δy,   q 4 = y max − y 1 step 3: understand entering and leaving values start with u enter = 0 and u leave = 1. for p < 0, the line is potentially entering. update u enter using the larger value. for p > 0, the line is potentially leaving. update u leave using the smaller value. if p = 0 and q < 0, the line is parallel to that boundary and outside, so reject it. after all four boundaries, if u enter > u leave , reject. otherwise, calculate the clipped endpoints. worked numerical: liang–barsky using the same line window: x = 10 to 50 and y = 10 to 40. line: (5, 20) to (60, 30). first, δx = 60 − 5 = 55 and δy = 30 − 20 = 10. boundary p q q/p update left −55 −5 0.0909 entering: u enter = 0.0909 right 55 45 0.8182 leaving: u leave = 0.8182 bottom −10 10 −1 entering: keep larger value, 0.0909 top 10 20 2 leaving: keep smaller value, 0.8182 since u enter = 0.0909 is smaller than u leave = 0.8182, the line has a visible part. find the first clipped endpoint: x = 5 + 55(0.0909) ≈ 10 y = 20 + 10(0.0909) ≈ 20.91 first endpoint ≈ (10, 20.91) find the second clipped endpoint: x = 5 + 55(0.8182) ≈ 50 y = 20 + 10(0.8182) ≈ 28.18 second endpoint ≈ (50, 28.18) final result the clipped line is approximately (10, 20.91) to (50, 28.18), the same visible segment found using cohen–sutherland. 6.7 polygon clipping — sutherland–hodgman algorithm a polygon is a closed shape made from connected straight edges. polygon clipping removes the parts outside the clipping window and keeps the part inside. sutherland–hodgman clips a polygon one window boundary at a time. for a rectangular window, process the left, right, bottom and top boundaries in sequence. the output from one boundary becomes the input for the next boundary. clipping window original polygon retained region the four cases — learn this table carefully for each polygon edge, let s be the starting vertex and p be the ending vertex. check whether each is inside or outside the current clipping boundary. case start s end p what is added to output? 1 inside inside end point p. 2 inside outside intersection point only. 3 outside inside intersection point, then p. 4 outside outside nothing. easy memory line: in → in: keep the end. in → out: keep the crossing point. out → in: keep the crossing point and the end. out → out: keep nothing. small example against the left boundary suppose the left boundary is x = 10. a point is inside this boundary when x ≥ 10. s(15, 20) → p(25, 30): inside to inside, so output p(25, 30). s(15, 20) → p(5, 30): inside to outside, so output the intersection with x = 10. s(5, 20) → p(25, 30): outside to inside, so output the intersection and p(25, 30). s(5, 20) → p(8, 30): outside to outside, so output nothing. repeat this for every polygon edge and then for the remaining window boundaries. the final list of output vertices forms the clipped polygon. 6.8 clipping circles and ellipses the syllabus also includes circles and ellipses. the same basic rule applies: keep the curve portion inside the clipping window and remove the portion outside. the curve may cross one or more window boundaries, so the intersection points are important. circle clipping a circle with centre (h, k) and radius r has the equation: (x − h) 2 + (y − k) 2 = r 2 if the circle is fully inside the window, retain the complete circle. if it is fully outside and does not overlap the window, reject it. if it crosses the window, find the intersection points and retain only the arcs inside. ellipse clipping an axis-aligned ellipse with centre (h, k), horizontal radius a and vertical radius b has the equation: (x − h) 2 /a 2 + (y − k) 2 /b 2 = 1 if the ellipse is fully inside, retain it completely. if it does not overlap the window, reject it. if it crosses the window, calculate the boundary intersections and keep the visible arcs. do not mix the algorithm names: cohen–sutherland and liang–barsky are line-clipping algorithms. sutherland–hodgman is a polygon-clipping algorithm. circle and ellipse clipping use their curve equations and boundary intersections. 6.9 comparison of the three named algorithms algorithm object clipped main idea cohen–sutherland line 4-bit region codes and bitwise or/and tests. liang–barsky line parametric line equation; calculates entering and leaving values. sutherland–hodgman polygon clips one polygon boundary at a time using four cases. 6.10 advantages and limitations algorithm advantages limitations / points to remember cohen–sutherland easy to understand; quickly accepts or rejects many lines using bitwise tests. may calculate intersections repeatedly for a line that crosses the window. liang–barsky uses a compact parametric calculation and can avoid some unnecessary intersection work. requires careful calculation of p, q and entering/leaving parameter values. sutherland–hodgman systematic method for clipping a polygon against a convex clipping window. the basic form is intended for convex clipping regions; complex concave cases need more care. 6.11 exam preparation 6.11.1 previous-year question evidence yellow — related bca evidence the exam plan lists cohen–sutherland line clipping among the related bca questions. no direct clipping question was identified in the supplied mca papers. clipping is part of the official unit i syllabus and should be studied. the priority colour reflects only the supplied paper collection. it does not mean the topic cannot appear in an examination. 6.11.2 exam-ready answers 2 marks — define clipping. clipping is the process of removing the portions of a graphical object that lie outside a specified clipping window and retaining the portions inside it. it is used to display only the required part of an object. 5 marks — explain cohen–sutherland line clipping. cohen–sutherland is a line-clipping algorithm used with a rectangular clipping window. it divides the plane into nine regions and assigns a 4-bit outcode to each endpoint. the code indicates whether the endpoint is above, below, right or left of the window. if both endpoint codes are 0000, accept the line. if the bitwise and of the two codes is non-zero, reject the line. otherwise, calculate the intersection with the appropriate window boundary. replace the outside endpoint with the intersection and calculate its new outcode. repeat until the line is accepted or rejected. 5 marks — explain sutherland–hodgman polygon clipping. sutherland–hodgman is a polygon-clipping algorithm. it clips a polygon against each boundary of the clipping window one by one. for each polygon edge, it checks whether the starting and ending vertices are inside or outside. the four cases are inside-to-inside, inside-to-outside, outside-to-inside and outside-to-outside. depending on the case, it outputs the ending vertex, an intersection, both an intersection and the ending vertex, or nothing. the output is passed to the next clipping boundary. 15 marks — explain line and polygon clipping techniques. introduction: clipping retains only the part of a graphical object that lies inside a selected clipping window. line clipping: cohen–sutherland assigns a 4-bit outcode to each endpoint. it accepts a line when both codes are zero, rejects it when the bitwise and is non-zero, and otherwise calculates boundary intersections until the visible segment is obtained. liang–barsky represents a line parametrically and calculates the entering and leaving values of parameter u. polygon clipping: sutherland–hodgman clips a polygon against each window boundary in sequence. it checks each polygon edge using four inside/outside cases and builds a new list of vertices. curves: circle and ellipse clipping retain the arcs that lie inside the window and remove the outside arcs, using the curve equations and their intersections with the window boundary. conclusion: cohen–sutherland and liang–barsky are used for line clipping, while sutherland–hodgman is used for polygon clipping. clipping helps display only the required visible portions of graphical objects. 6.12 quick revision clipping: keep inside, remove outside. window: x min , x max , y min , y max . point clipping: check both coordinate limits. cohen–sutherland: 4-bit codes; or = 0 accepts; and ≠ 0 rejects. liang–barsky: parametric equation; find u enter and u leave . sutherland–hodgman: polygon clipping; four inside/outside cases. circle and ellipse: retain only the visible arcs inside the window. 6.13 common mistakes in examinations clipping is not filling. filling colours the inside of a shape; clipping removes the outside portion relative to a window. cohen–sutherland is for line clipping, not polygon clipping. remember the cohen–sutherland tests correctly: or = 0 accepts; and non-zero rejects. liang–barsky uses parameter values, not the cohen–sutherland outcode method. remember the direction of all four sutherland–hodgman cases. when a circle or ellipse crosses the window, retain its inside arcs; do not automatically discard the complete curve. 6.14 learning resources video lessons youtube search · hindi gate smashers — computer graphics clipping search for clipping-window basics and the cohen–sutherland algorithm. youtube search · hindi 5 minutes engineering — clipping alternative explanation of line and polygon clipping. youtube search · hindi sutherland–hodgman polygon clipping focus on the four inside/outside cases.
