to index ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ 6 topic 6 of 6 coordinate systems black priority why black? no direct or clearly related standalone pyq for this subtopic is confirmed in the available exam evidence. 6.1 meaning of coordinate systems a coordinate system is a reference framework used to describe the position of points in space. in 3d computer graphics, a point is commonly represented by three coordinates: (x, y, z). different coordinate systems are used at different stages of graphics processing. they help describe an object's own position, place it in a scene, define the camera view, perform projection and finally display the image on a screen. 6.2 main coordinate systems in 3d graphics 1. object (model) coordinate system this is the local coordinate system in which an individual object is created. the object's vertices are defined relative to its own origin. for example, a cube may be modelled around the point (0, 0, 0), before being placed in a larger scene. 2. world coordinate system the world coordinate system is the common reference system for the complete 3d scene. objects are positioned, rotated and scaled within this shared space. it allows several objects to be arranged in relation to one another. 3. viewing (camera) coordinate system this coordinate system is defined with respect to the camera or viewer. the camera position and orientation determine how the world is seen. the scene is transformed from world coordinates into viewing coordinates before projection. 4. projection coordinates projection converts the 3d view into a representation suitable for a 2d projection plane. the mathematical operation depends on whether parallel or perspective projection is selected. 5. normalized device coordinates after projection and the required homogeneous-coordinate conversion, the visible image can be mapped into a standard normalized viewing region. this gives a device-independent representation before mapping to a particular display. 6. device (screen) coordinate system device coordinates identify positions on the actual output device, such as a monitor. the normalized image is mapped to screen or viewport coordinates, commonly measured in pixels. 6.3 coordinate transformation pipeline a 3d graphics system converts object coordinates through a sequence of coordinate systems before displaying the final image. general 3d viewing pipeline object / model coordinates ↓ model transformation world coordinates ↓ viewing (camera) transformation viewing coordinates ↓ projection transformation projected / normalized device coordinates ↓ viewport transformation device / screen coordinates each transformation changes the reference frame or representation of the points. the object itself does not need to be physically moved; its coordinates are mathematically converted. 6.4 homogeneous coordinates homogeneous coordinates are used to represent 3d points in a form that makes translation, rotation, scaling and other transformations convenient to combine using matrices. 3d point in homogeneous form cartesian point: p = (x, y, z) homogeneous point: p = (x, y, z, 1) for a homogeneous point (x, y, z, w): x = x/w, y = y/w, z = z/w for ordinary 3d points, w is commonly 1 before projective transformations. after perspective projection, w may have another value and the coordinates are converted back by dividing by w, provided w is not zero. 6.5 example — moving a point from object to world coordinates question: an object's point is p = (2, 1, 3). the object is translated by (5, 2, 1). find the point in world coordinates, assuming no rotation or scaling. solution: add the translation values to the corresponding coordinates. calculation xw = 2 + 5 = 7 yw = 1 + 2 = 3 zw = 3 + 1 = 4 world coordinate point = (7, 3, 4) 6.6 importance of coordinate systems they provide a consistent way to represent positions in a 3d scene. they allow objects to be modelled independently and then placed in a common world. they define the camera's position and orientation for viewing. they make projection and conversion to screen coordinates possible. they help graphics systems support different output devices and viewport sizes. exam answer (5 marks) coordinate systems are reference frameworks used to specify the position of points in 3d space. in computer graphics, object coordinates describe an object's local geometry, world coordinates locate objects in the complete scene, and viewing coordinates describe the scene relative to the camera. projection coordinates are produced when the 3d view is projected onto a 2d plane. normalized device coordinates provide a standard representation, which is finally converted into device or screen coordinates for display. transformations are used to convert points from one coordinate system to another. 6.7 previous-year question (pyq) evidence the available exam-plan evidence identifies unit vi as an important unit, but it does not confirm an standalone pyq. 1.1 meaning of achromatic light achromatic light is light that has no hue (no colour such as red, green or blue). its appearance is described by its intensity, producing shades from black through grey to white. in computer graphics, an image represented only by these shades is called a grayscale image . 1.2 intensity of achromatic light intensity describes the amount or strength of light. in a grayscale image, the intensity value of each pixel determines how dark or light that pixel appears. a lower value appears darker, while a higher value appears brighter. 8-bit grayscale intensity range 0 = black 1–254 = shades of grey 255 = white since 2⁸ = 256, an 8-bit grayscale pixel can represent 256 different intensity levels. 1.3 characteristics of achromatic light no hue: it does not represent a distinct colour. intensity-based: its appearance depends on the amount of light. grayscale shades: it ranges from black to white through intermediate grey levels. single intensity channel: a grayscale pixel normally stores one intensity value rather than separate red, green and blue values. 1.4 intensity, luminance and brightness intensity: the amount or strength of light represented at a point. luminance: a measurable quantity describing light emitted or reflected in a particular direction, weighted according to human visual sensitivity. brightness: the subjective sensation of how light or dark something appears to a viewer. these terms are related, but they are not identical. intensity and luminance are measurable quantities, whereas brightness describes human perception. 1.5 applications black-and-white photographs and images. scanned documents and printed text images. medical images such as x-rays. image-processing operations where intensity differences are important. exam answer achromatic light is light that has no hue or colour information. it is represented by different intensity levels, ranging from black through shades of grey to white. in computer graphics, an image containing only these shades is called a grayscale image. each pixel stores an intensity value that determines its appearance. in an 8-bit grayscale image, the values range from 0 to 255: 0 represents black, 255 represents white and the intermediate values represent different shades of grey. achromatic representation is used in black-and-white photography, document scanning, medical imaging and image processing. 1.6 previous-year question status pyq clarification: the mca 2022–24 paper (ccmca403) included the unit vii topic “chromatic colour and colour models”. as red, green, blue or yellow. it is associated with coloured light and is described using properties such as hue, saturation and intensity or brightness. unlike achromatic light, which contains only shades of black, grey and white, chromatic colour carries colour information. 2.2 main characteristics of chromatic colour hue: the attribute that identifies the basic colour, such as red, green, blue or yellow. it is commonly associated with the dominant wavelength of the light. saturation: the purity or vividness of a colour. a highly saturated colour looks strong and vivid, while a less saturated colour looks dull or washed out because it contains a greater neutral component. intensity / brightness: describes the amount or perceived strength of light. increasing light intensity generally makes the colour appear brighter. 2.3 hue hue tells us which colour we are seeing. for example, red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet are different hues. in many digital colour interfaces, hue is represented as an angle around a colour wheel, usually from 0° to 360°. illustrative hue positions in a common colour wheel 0° — red 60° — yellow 120° — green 180° — cyan 240° — blue 300° — magenta 360° — red again these are conventional positions used in a hue-wheel representation; they are not a direct measurement of wavelength. 2.4 saturation saturation describes how pure or vivid a colour appears. high saturation: the colour appears strong, vivid and pure. low saturation: the colour appears dull, pale or washed out. zero saturation: the colour has no chromatic component and appears as a shade of grey. for example, bright red is more saturated than a pale, pinkish red. 2.5 intensity and brightness intensity is related to the amount of light. brightness is the human perception of how light or dark the colour appears. a colour can keep the same hue while its brightness changes. for example, dark blue and light blue have a similar hue, but differ in their perceived lightness or brightness. 2.6 chromaticity chromaticity describes the colour quality independently of its overall brightness. in a common description, hue and saturation together specify the chromatic character of a colour, while intensity or luminance describes its light level. the cie chromaticity diagram is one method used to represent colour qualities and compare colours. 2.7 difference between achromatic and chromatic colour achromatic chromatic no hue or colour information has a distinct hue black, grey and white shades red, green, blue, yellow, etc. described mainly by intensity described by hue, saturation and intensity/brightness example: grayscale image example: full-colour photograph exam answer chromatic colour refers to coloured light that has a distinct hue, such as red, green or blue. it is commonly described by three characteristics: hue, saturation and intensity or brightness. hue identifies the basic colour and is associated with its dominant wavelength. saturation indicates the purity or vividness of the colour; a highly saturated colour appears vivid, while a low-saturation colour appears dull or washed out. intensity refers to the amount of light, while brightness is the perceived lightness or darkness. hue and saturation together describe the chromatic quality of a colour. chromatic colour is used in computer graphics to represent coloured images and visual information. 2.8 previous-year question status actual mca pyq — unit vii: the mca 2022–24 paper (ccmca403) included the topic “chromatic colour and colour models”. colour model is a method of representing colours using numerical components. in raster graphics, each pixel is assigned a colour value, and a colour model defines how that value is described. different models serve different purposes, such as displaying images, printing and selecting colours. 3.2 rgb colour model rgb stands for red, green and blue . it is an additive colour model mainly used by monitors, televisions and other devices that produce light. a colour is created by combining different intensities of red, green and blue light. red + green = yellow green + blue = cyan blue + red = magenta full red + green + blue = white no light from any channel = black rgb pixel representation colour = (r, g, b) 8-bit channel: 0 to 255 example: (255, 0, 0) is red; (0, 0, 0) is black; (255, 255, 255) is white. with 8 bits for each channel, an rgb pixel uses 24 bits and can represent 256 × 256 × 256 = 16,777,216 possible channel combinations. 3.3 cmy colour model cmy stands for cyan, magenta and yellow . it is a subtractive colour model , mainly associated with colour printing. it starts with white paper. the inks absorb (subtract) parts of the incident white light, and the remaining reflected light is seen as colour. cyan absorbs red light. magenta absorbs green light. yellow absorbs blue light. ideal conversion from normalized rgb to cmy c = 1 − r m = 1 − g y = 1 − b r, g and b are normalized to the range 0 to 1. in theory, combining cyan, magenta and yellow at maximum amounts produces black. in real printing, the result is often not a deep, neutral black. 3.4 cmyk colour model cmyk stands for cyan, magenta, yellow and key (black) . it extends cmy by adding a separate black channel. it is widely used in printing because dedicated black ink produces clearer text and deeper black areas, while reducing the need to combine large amounts of the other inks. 3.5 hsv colour model hsv stands for hue, saturation and value . it represents colour in terms that are easier for people to understand and select than raw rgb channel values. it is commonly illustrated using a hexagonal cone or cylinder-like colour solid. hue (h): the basic colour, represented as an angle from 0° to 360°. saturation (s): the purity or vividness. zero represents a neutral grey; higher values are more vivid. value (v): the brightness level in this model. zero represents black; 1 (or 100%) represents the maximum value. hsv is useful in colour pickers and image-editing applications where users choose a colour by its appearance. 3.6 hls / hsl colour model hls (also commonly written hsl) stands for hue, lightness and saturation . it describes colour using hue, saturation and lightness rather than rgb channel amounts. hue: identifies the colour and is represented by an angle. lightness: describes how light or dark the colour is. zero represents black, 1 represents white, and 0.5 is the middle level. saturation: describes colour purity. at zero saturation, the colour is a shade of grey. hls is often represented by a double cone and is useful for colour selection and adjustment. 3.7 yiq / yuv colour models yiq and yuv are colour representations that separate a brightness-related component from colour information. they are associated with television and video systems. y: represents luminance or a brightness-related signal. i and q: in yiq, represent two colour-difference components. u and v: in yuv, represent colour-difference components. this separation allows systems to handle brightness and colour information separately. related representations such as ycbcr are also widely used in digital video and image compression. 3.8 comparison of important colour models colour model components type / main use rgb red, green, blue additive; monitors and digital displays cmy cyan, magenta, yellow subtractive; colour printing cmyk cyan, magenta, yellow, black printing with a separate black channel hsv hue, saturation, value human-friendly colour selection hls / hsl hue, lightness, saturation colour selection and adjustment yiq / yuv brightness-related and colour-difference components television and video systems exam answer a colour model is a method of representing colours using numerical components. in raster graphics, it specifies how the colour of each pixel is stored or described. important colour models include rgb, cmy, cmyk, hsv, hls and yiq/yuv. rgb is an additive model that combines red, green and blue light and is used in display devices. cmy is a subtractive model used in printing, while cmyk adds a separate black channel. hsv represents colour through hue, saturation and value, and hls uses hue, lightness and saturation. yiq and yuv separate brightness-related information from colour information and are associated with television and video systems. each model is selected according to the application for which colour is being represented or reproduced. 3.9 previous-year question status actual mca pyq — unit vii: the image or scene. in computer graphics, colour must be reproduced by output devices such as monitors, televisions and printers. the goal is to make the reproduced colours look as close as possible to the intended colours. exact matching can be difficult because different devices use different methods and have different colour capabilities. 4.2 additive colour reproduction — rgb display devices such as monitors and televisions generally use the rgb additive colour model . they produce colour by emitting red, green and blue light in different intensities. red, green and blue light combine to create other colours. when all three are at maximum intensity, the result is white. when all three are absent, the result is black. example: a computer monitor creates a yellow region by combining red and green light. 4.3 subtractive colour reproduction — cmy / cmyk printers generally use the cmyk colour model . it is subtractive because coloured inks absorb some parts of the white light falling on the paper and reflect the remaining light. cyan, magenta and yellow inks absorb different portions of light. black ink (k) is added to produce deeper blacks and sharper dark details. the final colour depends on the combination and amount of inks applied to the paper. example: a colour photograph printed on paper is reproduced by placing different amounts of cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink. 4.4 difference between display and printing display device printer uses emitted light uses reflected light from paper usually uses rgb usually uses cmyk additive colour mixing subtractive colour mixing full rgb light produces white combination of cmy inks ideally absorbs most light; black ink is added for practical printing 4.5 factors affecting colour reproduction device characteristics: different monitors and printers may reproduce the same numerical colour values differently. colour range (gamut): each device can reproduce only a limited range of colours. a colour outside that range cannot be reproduced exactly by that device. lighting conditions: the light under which a printed image is viewed can change how its colours appear. media and materials: paper type, ink and display technology affect the final appearance of colour. calibration: adjusting a device to a known reference helps make its colour output more consistent. 4.6 colour matching and colour management colour matching is the process of making colours appear consistent across different devices. a colour-management system helps achieve this by describing device colour behaviour and converting colour values when an image moves from one device or colour space to another. for example, when an image is transferred from a monitor to a printer, colour management helps convert the display colour values into values that the printer can reproduce more accurately. exam answer colour reproduction is the process of producing colours that resemble the colours of an original object, image or scene. in computer graphics, colour is reproduced mainly through display devices and printers. monitors and televisions generally use the additive rgb model, in which red, green and blue light are combined to produce different colours. printers generally use the subtractive cmyk model, in which cyan, magenta, yellow and black inks absorb parts of the incident light and produce the required colour on paper. colour reproduction may variables a function of two variables takes two independent input values, usually x and y, and produces one output value, usually z. in computer graphics, this form is useful for describing a 3d surface over the x-y plane. explicit surface representation z = f(x, y) for every pair (x, y), the function gives the corresponding height or depth value z. 1.2 example of a surface function consider the function: z = 2x + 3y if x = 1 and y = 2, then: z = 2(1) + 3(2) = 8 therefore, the point on the surface is (1, 2, 8) . by calculating z for many pairs of x and y, we can obtain points that form a 3d surface. 1.3 common ways to represent a surface explicit form: the dependent coordinate is written directly as a function of two independent coordinates, for example z = f(x, y). implicit form: the surface is described by an equation involving x, y and z, for example f(x, y, z) = 0. example of an implicit surface: x² + y² + z² − 25 = 0 this equation represents a sphere of radius 5 centred at the origin. 1.4 domain and range domain: the set of allowed input pairs (x, y) for which the function is defined. range: the set of output values z produced by the function. for example, if z = x + y and both x and y are restricted to values from 0 to 2, the domain is the selected square region in the x-y plane, and the output z ranges from 0 to 4. 1.5 connection with visible-surface determination when a 3d scene is projected onto a 2d viewing plane, different surfaces may overlap at the same screen position. a surface function can provide the z value at a particular (x, y) position. this value helps determine the relative depth of the surface at that position. for a given projected position (x, y), calculate or obtain the depth of each surface covering that position. compare the depth values using the viewing system's depth convention. the surface nearest to the viewer is the visible one at that position; the other surface is hidden there. important: whether the nearest surface has the smaller or larger numerical z value depends on the coordinate and depth convention being used. do not assume that the smallest z is always closest in every system. 1.6 why this concept is useful it provides a mathematical way to describe 3d surfaces. it helps calculate the depth of a surface at a given projected position. it provides a foundation for understanding depth comparison in visible-surface algorithms. exam answer a function of two variables is a mathematical function in which two independent variables, usually x and y, determine a third value z. in computer graphics, a 3d surface can be represented in explicit form as z = f(x, y), where each pair (x, y) gives a point on the surface. a surface may also be represented implicitly by an equation such as f(x, y, z) = 0. these functions are useful in visible-surface determination because they can provide the depth value of a surface at a projected position. when multiple surfaces overlap at the same screen position, their depth values are compared according to the viewing coordinate convention to identify the surface nearest to the viewer. 1.7 previous-year question status pyq status: the available exam plan depth-sort, which are examples of visible-surface techniques. it does not confirm a separate question specifically worded as “efficient visible-surface algorithms”. do not treat this topic title as an exact previous-year question. 2.1 meaning and need visible-surface determination (also called hidden-surface removal) identifies the surfaces or parts of objects that can be seen from a given viewing position. surfaces hidden behind nearer opaque surfaces are not displayed. in a complex 3d scene, checking every surface repeatedly can take considerable processing time. efficient algorithms reduce unnecessary calculations and avoid drawing hidden parts wherever possible. 2.2 main approaches object-space methods: compare objects or surfaces with one another in the 3d scene to decide which parts are visible. these methods work with the geometric objects themselves. image-space methods: decide visibility at positions on the projected image, usually pixel by pixel. the algorithm determines which surface is nearest at each image position. mixed methods: combine object-space and image-space operations, for example by arranging surfaces using depth and then resolving visibility in the image. remember: object-space methods reason about the scene geometry; image-space methods reason about the projected image pixels. 2.3 sorting sorting means arranging surfaces according to their depth or distance from the viewer. it helps the algorithm compare overlapping surfaces in a useful order. for example, in a painter-style approach, farther surfaces are drawn first and nearer surfaces are drawn later, so nearer surfaces cover the farther ones. depth sorting is useful, but intersecting or cyclically overlapping polygons may require additional tests or splitting. 2.4 coherence coherence is the tendency for nearby parts of a scene or image to have similar properties. efficient algorithms use already calculated information when it is likely to remain valid for nearby positions, instead of repeating the same work. object coherence: parts belonging to the same object often share useful properties. face coherence: nearby points on one face generally belong to that same face. edge coherence: the visibility relationship along a polygon edge usually changes gradually. scan-line coherence: adjacent scan lines often have similar visibility patterns. area coherence: nearby pixels in a small screen region are often covered by the same surface. depth coherence: depth values at nearby points on a surface usually change smoothly. frame coherence: consecutive animation frames usually differ only where objects or the viewpoint have changed. 2.5 examples of techniques back-face detection: removes polygon faces that point away from the viewer, avoiding further visibility work for those faces. z-buffer method: stores depth for each pixel and keeps the nearest surface found at that pixel. scan-line method: processes the image one horizontal scan line at a time and uses similarities between spans and adjacent lines. depth-sort / painter’s method: orders surfaces by depth before drawing them. area-subdivision method: divides the viewing area into smaller regions until visibility in each region can be determined. these techniques exploit different combinations of object-space processing, image-space processing, sorting and coherence. the later topics in this unit explain several of them separately. 2.6 choosing an efficient method the suitable method depends on factors such as: number and complexity of objects in the scene. whether the objects are polygons or other surface types. available memory and processing capability. whether the scene is static or animated. required image quality and handling of overlapping or transparent surfaces. 2.7 exam-oriented answer efficient visible-surface algorithms determine which parts of a 3d scene are visible from a specified viewpoint while reducing unnecessary calculations. they are commonly classified into object-space, image-space and mixed methods. their efficiency is improved using sorting , which orders surfaces according to depth, and coherence , which reuses information about nearby objects, faces, edges, scan lines, areas, depths or frames. examples include back-face detection, z-buffer, scan-line, depth-sort and area-subdivision methods. 2.8 previous-year question scan-line determination black priority why black? the available exam-plan evidence does not confirm a separate direct mca question specifically on the scan-line determination algorithm. the topic is part of the official unit viii syllabus and is a standard visible-surface detection method. 3.1 meaning the scan-line method is an image-space visible-surface detection method. it determines the visible surface one horizontal scan line at a time, moving across the screen from left to right and then proceeding to the next scan line. instead of keeping depth information for the entire image, the method needs depth information for the current scan line. all polygons intersecting that scan line are considered together. 3.2 data structures used edge table (et): stores polygon edge information, such as edge endpoints, the inverse slope and a reference to the polygon to which the edge belongs. it helps identify where edges intersect scan lines. polygon table (pt): stores polygon information, such as plane coefficients, surface properties and references to related edges. active edge list (ael): contains only the edges that intersect the current scan line. the edges are maintained in increasing order of their x-coordinate. inside/outside flag: each polygon has a flag indicating whether the current position along the scan line lies inside or outside that polygon. 3.3 working of the scan-line method start with the first scan line at the top of the viewing area. use the edge table to find all polygon edges intersecting the current scan line. build the active edge list and arrange its edges in increasing x-coordinate order. move from left to right across the scan line. when a polygon's left boundary is reached, turn its inside flag on. when its right boundary is reached, turn its inside flag off. if no polygon is active, the position belongs to the background. if exactly one polygon is active, that polygon is visible there. if two or more polygons overlap at a position, compare their depth values and select the nearest surface according to the viewing convention. store the selected surface's intensity or colour in the frame buffer for the corresponding pixels. update the active edges for the next scan line and repeat until the entire viewing area has been processed. 3.4 why depth comparison is needed when only one polygon covers a part of the scan line, its surface is visible without comparing it against another polygon. when multiple polygons cover the same position, the algorithm calculates or updates their depth values and chooses the nearest one. important: the numerical meaning of “nearer” depends on the chosen depth-coordinate convention. the algorithm compares depths consistently using that convention. 3.5 scan-line coherence scan-line coherence means that neighbouring scan lines often have similar edge intersections and visibility relationships. the algorithm can use information from the previous scan line to update the active edge list instead of rebuilding everything from the beginning. this reduces repeated work when adjacent scan lines pass through the same polygons. 3.6 advantages and limitations advantages: processes only one scan line of depth information at a time; considers all polygons crossing that line together; can exploit scan-line coherence to reduce repeated calculations. limitations: requires management of edge and polygon tables; overlapping polygons require depth comparisons; the active edge list must be updated as each scan line is processed. 3.7 exam-oriented answer the scan-line method is an image-space algorithm for visible-surface determination. it processes the image one horizontal scan line at a time. it uses an edge table, polygon table and an active edge list. the active edges are sorted by increasing x-coordinate. as the algorithm moves from left to right, a polygon's inside flag is switched on at its left boundary and off at its right boundary. if several polygons overlap, their depth values are compared and the nearest surface is written to the frame buffer. scan-line coherence helps reuse information from neighbouring scan lines and reduces repeated work. 3.8 previous-year question status pyq status: the available exam-plan evidence does not confirm a separate direct mca question specifically on the scan-line determination algorithm. the topic is part of the official unit viii syllabus and is a standard visible-surface detection method. the yellow index colour indicates related hidden-surface topic evidence, not a confirmed scan-line question. z-buffer algorithms red priority why red? the available exam-plan evidence records a z-buffer question in the older mca paper (mca-2/d-12, code cs-de-21). the exact original wording is not preserved in the available notes, so this is topic-level pyq evidence rather than a verbatim question. 4.1 meaning of the z-buffer the z-buffer algorithm , also called the depth-buffer algorithm , is an image-space method used to determine which surface is visible at each pixel. it stores the depth of the currently visible surface for every pixel in a special memory area called the z-buffer. the frame buffer stores the pixel's colour or intensity, while the z-buffer stores its depth value. 4.2 buffers used frame buffer: stores the colour or intensity value that will appear at each screen pixel. z-buffer: stores the depth value of the surface currently selected as visible at each pixel. both buffers have corresponding entries for the pixels in the image. 4.3 working principle initialize every z-buffer entry to a depth value representing the farthest possible depth (or the appropriate initial value for the chosen depth convention). initialize the frame buffer with the background colour. process each polygon or surface in the scene. for every pixel covered by the current surface, calculate or obtain its depth value. compare this depth with the value already stored at that pixel in the z-buffer. if the new surface is nearer, update the z-buffer entry with the new depth and update the corresponding frame-buffer pixel with the surface colour. if the new surface is farther, leave both buffer entries unchanged. after all surfaces have been processed, the frame buffer contains the visible image. depth comparison (concept) if new depth is nearer → update z-buffer and frame buffer otherwise → keep the existing values the comparison operator depends on the depth-coordinate convention. in one convention smaller depth means nearer; in another, larger depth may mean nearer. 4.4 simple example suppose two opaque surfaces cover the same pixel. surface a has depth 8 and surface b has depth 3. if smaller depth represents a nearer surface, surface b is selected. the z-buffer stores depth 3, and the frame buffer stores the colour of surface b at that pixel. if the depth convention is reversed, the comparison must also be reversed. 4.5 advantages simple and widely used method for visible-surface detection. surfaces can generally be processed in any order because each pixel keeps the nearest depth found so far. suitable for scenes containing many overlapping polygons. visibility decisions are made independently for each pixel. 4.6 limitations requires additional memory for the z-buffer. depth precision is limited by the number of bits used to store each depth value. insufficient depth precision can cause z-fighting , where nearly coplanar surfaces compete and the displayed result may flicker or appear irregular. basic z-buffering handles opaque surfaces directly; transparency generally requires additional handling and correct blending order. 4.7 exam-oriented answer the z-buffer or depth-buffer algorithm is an image-space visible-surface detection technique. it uses two buffers: the frame buffer, which stores pixel colours, and the z-buffer, which stores pixel depths. initially, the z-buffer is filled with the farthest depth and the frame buffer with the background colour. each polygon is processed, and its depth is compared with the stored depth at every covered pixel. if the new surface is nearer, both the z-buffer and frame-buffer entries are updated. otherwise, the old values are retained. after all polygons are processed, the frame buffer represents the visible scene. 4.8 previous-year question status pyq status: the available exam-plan evidence records a z-buffer question in the older mca paper (mca-2/d-12, code cs-de-21). the exact original wording is not preserved in the available notes, so this is topic-level pyq evidence rather than a verbatim question. 4.9 sources geeksforgeeks — z-buffer / depth-buffer algorithm tutorialspoint — visible surface detection ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ next → list-priority algorithms · ↑ back to index ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ 5 topic 5 of 7 list-priority algorithms red priority why red? the available exam-plan evidence records a depth-sort question in the older mca paper (mca-2/d-12, code cs-de-21). the exact original wording is not preserved in the available notes, so this is topic-level pyq evidence rather than a verbatim question. the red index colour indicates this older mca depth-sort evidence. 5.1 meaning list-priority algorithms determine a visibility order for the surfaces in a scene. the surfaces are arranged in a list according to their depth priority, and then drawn in that order so that nearer surfaces cover farther surfaces. the best-known example is the painter’s algorithm , also called the depth-sort algorithm or priority algorithm . 5.2 painter’s algorithm — basic idea the method works like an artist painting a picture. the artist first paints the background and distant objects, then paints nearer objects over them. in the same way, the algorithm draws polygons from back to front: farther polygons are drawn first. nearer polygons are drawn later. when a nearer polygon covers a farther polygon, its pixels overwrite the earlier pixels in the frame buffer. 5.3 working steps find the depth range of each polygon, commonly represented by its minimum and maximum depth values. sort the polygons according to depth priority, arranging them from farthest to nearest. initialize the frame buffer with the background colour. scan-convert and draw the farthest polygon first. continue drawing the remaining polygons in back-to-front order. later, nearer polygons overwrite pixels belonging to farther polygons wherever they overlap. check ambiguous overlapping polygons. if their depth order cannot be established safely, perform additional tests and split polygons when necessary. 5.4 handling overlapping polygons sorting only by one depth value may not be sufficient when polygon depth ranges overlap. the algorithm uses additional tests to decide whether the assumed order is valid. screen extent test: check whether the projected x- or y-ranges of two polygons are separate. if they do not overlap in either direction, one cannot cover the other in the image. depth-range test: compare the minimum and maximum depth ranges. if one polygon is entirely behind the other, their order can be established. plane test: check whether the polygons lie on opposite sides of the other polygon’s plane, where applicable. splitting: if no reliable order can be established, divide one or both polygons into smaller parts so that the pieces can be placed in a consistent back-to-front order. 5.5 cyclic overlap problem a difficult case occurs when polygons overlap in a cycle: polygon a appears in front of b in one region, b appears in front of c, and c appears in front of a. no single global drawing order can satisfy all these relationships. in such cases, the algorithm may need to split polygons into smaller pieces. after splitting, the pieces can often be sorted and drawn in a valid order. 5.6 advantages the basic idea is simple and easy to understand. it can be efficient when the polygons have a clear, consistent depth order. it does not require a separate depth value to be stored for every screen pixel in the way a z-buffer does. 5.7 limitations sorting and checking overlapping polygons can be expensive. intersecting or cyclically overlapping polygons may not have a simple global order. polygon splitting may be required, increasing processing complexity. farther polygons may be drawn even in areas that are later covered by nearer polygons, causing unnecessary drawing work. 5.8 difference between z-buffer and list-priority method basis z-buffer list-priority / painter’s basic approach compares depth at each pixel. sorts surfaces into a drawing order. visibility decision pixel by pixel. primarily surface or polygon order. drawing order surfaces can generally be processed in any order. far-to-near order is required. extra handling needs depth-buffer memory and adequate depth precision. may need overlap tests and polygon splitting. 5.9 exam-oriented answer list-priority algorithms determine the visibility order of surfaces by arranging them in a list according to depth. the painter’s algorithm, also called the depth-sort or priority algorithm, is a common example. it draws polygons from farthest to nearest. the frame buffer is first filled with the background colour. far polygons are drawn first, and nearer polygons are drawn later, overwriting the pixels of distant polygons wherever they overlap. if overlapping polygons cannot be placed in a correct order, additional overlap tests are performed and polygons may be split. the method is simple, but sorting, intersecting surfaces and cyclic overlap can make it expensive. 5.10 previous-year question status pyq status: the available exam-plan evidence records a depth-sort question in the older mca paper (mca-2/d-12, code cs-de-21). the exact original wording is not preserved in the available notes, so this is topic-level pyq evidence rather than a verbatim question. the red index colour indicates this older mca depth-sort evidence. 5.11 sources geeksforgeeks — painter’s algorithm in computer graphics geeksforgeeks — painter’s algorithm video tutorialspoint — visible surface detection ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ next → area-subdivision algorithms · ↑ back to index ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ 6 topic 6 of 7 area-subdivision algorithms yellow priority why yellow? the available exam-plan evidence does not confirm a separate direct mca question specifically on the area-subdivision algorithm. related hidden-surface questions appear in the available bca-paper evidence, but that is not the same as a confirmed mca question on this algorithm. 6.1 meaning the area-subdivision algorithm is an image-space visible-surface detection method. it divides the viewing screen into smaller areas and determines which surface is visible in each area. if visibility cannot be decided for an area, that area is subdivided again into smaller regions. the process continues until the visible surface can be identified or the region becomes small enough to be treated as a pixel. 6.2 basic principle the algorithm uses the idea that a region may be classified easily when the surfaces covering it have a simple relationship. it checks the polygons that overlap a region and decides whether one polygon is definitely visible throughout that region. if a region is clearly covered by one visible surface, display that surface. if the region contains no polygon, display the background. if visibility is ambiguous because multiple surfaces overlap, divide the region into smaller parts and test each part again. 6.3 working steps start with the entire viewing area as one region. identify the polygons that overlap the current region. test whether the region can be assigned to a single visible surface using coverage and depth information. if no polygon covers the region, fill it with the background colour. if one polygon is definitely visible throughout the region, fill the region with that polygon's colour or shading. if the visibility test is ambiguous, divide the region into four smaller subregions. apply the same tests recursively to each subregion. stop subdividing when visibility is resolved or the region reaches the chosen minimum size, commonly a pixel. 6.4 the four subregions a common implementation divides a rectangular region into four equal quadrants: quadtree-style subdivision top-left · top-right bottom-left · bottom-right each quadrant is tested independently. only ambiguous quadrants need further subdivision. this repeated four-way division creates a hierarchical structure similar to a quadtree , where each parent region can have four child regions. 6.5 tests for determining visibility the algorithm examines the polygons overlapping a region. a region can be classified when the coverage and depth relationships show that a particular polygon is in front throughout that region. if the polygons overlap in a way that prevents a safe decision, subdivision is used to make the problem smaller. coverage: check whether a polygon completely covers the region. depth: compare the depth of candidate surfaces over the region. ambiguity: if the available tests cannot determine one visible surface for the entire region, subdivide it. 6.6 advantages large areas can be classified together instead of testing every pixel separately. only ambiguous regions need further subdivision. it can be efficient when large parts of the screen are covered by one surface or by the background. the hierarchical subdivision structure makes the process systematic. 6.7 limitations repeated subdivision can create many small regions in complex scenes. intersecting or closely overlapping surfaces may cause extensive subdivision. additional work is needed to test polygon coverage and depth within each region. in the worst case, subdivision may continue down to individual pixels, reducing the advantage of processing large areas together. 6.8 exam-oriented answer the area-subdivision algorithm is an image-space hidden-surface removal method. it starts with the complete viewing area and tests the polygons overlapping it. if the area is uncovered, the background is displayed. if one surface is definitely visible throughout the area, that surface is displayed. if visibility is ambiguous because multiple surfaces overlap, the area is divided into four smaller regions. the same procedure is repeated for each subregion until visibility is resolved or the region becomes a pixel. this method is efficient when large regions can be classified together, but complex scenes may require repeated subdivision. 6.9 previous-year question status pyq status: the available exam-plan evidence does not confirm a separate direct mca question specifically on the area-subdivision algorithm. related hidden-surface questions appear in the available bca-paper evidence, but that is not the same as a confirmed mca question on this algorithm. the yellow index colour indicates related hidden-surface evidence only. 6.10 sources geeksforgeeks — area subdivision algorithm in 3d (hidden surface removal) tutorialspoint — visible surface detection ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ next → octree algorithms · ↑ back to index ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ ❀ ✿ 7 topic 7 of 7 octree algorithms yellow priority why yellow? the available exam-plan evidence does not confirm a separate direct mca question specifically on octree algorithms. related hidden-surface questions appear in the available bca-paper evidence, but that does not establish a direct mca octree question. the yellow index colour indicates related hidden-surface evidence only. 7.1 meaning of an octree an octree is a hierarchical tree structure used to represent and organize objects or data in three-dimensional space. each internal node can be divided into at most eight child regions, called octants . in visible-surface determination, the viewing volume is represented using octree nodes. the nodes are projected onto the viewing plane in a suitable front-to-back order so that nearer surfaces are processed before farther surfaces. 7.2 how 3d space is divided begin with a cube or a 3d bounding region containing the scene. divide the region into eight smaller 3d regions by splitting it along the x, y and z directions. each smaller region is an octant and is represented by a child node. if a region still needs more detail, subdivide it again into eight smaller regions. continue until the required level of detail or voxel size is reached. a smallest represented volume element is commonly called a voxel (volume element). an octree therefore stores a hierarchical description of the 3d volume rather than treating every location as an unrelated element. 7.3 octree for visible-surface determination for hidden-surface removal, the octree nodes are visited in an order that processes the regions nearest to the viewer before the regions behind them. for a particular viewing direction, the four front octants are processed before the four rear octants. the same front-to-back ordering is applied recursively inside each subdivided octant. when a node contains a surface colour, its projected area is written to the corresponding frame-buffer area only if that area has not already received a colour from a nearer node. thus, a farther node does not overwrite a pixel already assigned by a nearer surface. 7.4 working steps represent the 3d viewing volume using an octree. identify the order of the octants according to the viewing direction, from front to back. traverse the octree recursively in that order, processing nearer child regions before farther child regions. project each relevant node or voxel onto its corresponding area on the viewing plane. check the corresponding frame-buffer area. if it has not yet been assigned a surface colour, write the current node's colour. if the projected area already contains a colour from a nearer node, do not overwrite it with the farther node's colour. skip a node and its descendants when the node is completely obscured and cannot contribute visible pixels. continue until all potentially visible nodes have been processed. 7.5 example of front-to-back processing suppose a viewing direction makes octants 0, 1, 2 and 3 the front group, while octants 4, 5, 6 and 7 are behind them. the algorithm processes the front group first. if a front octant paints a particular pixel area, a later rear octant cannot replace that colour. visibility rule first visible colour written → keep it later farther colour → do not overwrite the exact octant order depends on the viewing direction and the octree's numbering convention. 7.6 difference between quadtree and octree basis quadtree octree space represented two-dimensional area three-dimensional volume subdivision four smaller regions eight smaller regions basic unit area or image region voxel or volume region typical use here organizing subdivisions on the viewing plane organizing the 3d viewing volume for visibility processing 7.7 advantages organizes 3d space hierarchically. front-to-back traversal helps process nearer surfaces first. completely hidden regions can be skipped, avoiding unnecessary processing of their descendants. supports different levels of spatial detail through recursive subdivision. 7.8 limitations building and maintaining the tree requires additional memory and processing. complex or unevenly distributed scenes may require many subdivisions. the traversal order must be selected correctly for the viewing direction. projection and visibility checks are still required for nodes that may contribute to the final image. 7.9 exam-oriented answer an octree is a hierarchical structure used to represent a three-dimensional viewing volume. each node can be divided into eight smaller regions called octants. in visible-surface determination, octree nodes are projected onto the viewing plane in front-to-back order. the front octants are processed before the rear octants, and the same order is followed recursively. when a node's colour is projected onto the frame buffer, it is written only if the corresponding area has not already been filled by a nearer node. completely obscured nodes can be skipped. this removes hidden surfaces and avoids processing regions that cannot affect the visible image. 7.10 previous-year question status pyq status: the available exam-plan evidence does not confirm a separate direct mca question specifically on octree algorithms. related hidden-surface questions appear in the available bca-paper evidence, but that does not establish a direct mca octree question. the yellow index colour indicates related hidden-surface evidence only. 7.11 sources geeksforgeeks — octree: insertion and searching it was not directly asked in the previous papers, but it is the foundation for the rest of unit i. understand the basic meaning, how cloud computing works and what resources it provides. how much depth is needed? 1 mark: define cloud computing; explain the term cloud. 5 marks: explain cloud computing with basic working and examples; know its basic types. 15 marks: not a confirmed direct 15-mark question. cover the fundamentals, then study benefits, need and characteristics separately. 1.1 meaning of cloud computing cloud: the word cloud generally refers to resources and services available through a network, usually the internet. they are hosted at remote locations, not only on your personal computer. computing: using computer resources to process data, store files, run applications and manage databases. definition cloud computing is a technology that provides computing resources such as servers, storage, databases, networking and software over the internet whenever users need them. these resources are generally managed by a cloud service provider. users access them remotely without buying and maintaining all the hardware themselves. real-life example: google drive you open google drive on your mobile phone. you upload a photo using the internet. google stores the photo on its remote infrastructure. later, you open google drive on your laptop. you access the same photo without transferring it manually. important the cloud does not mean data is stored somewhere in the sky. data and computing resources are hosted on remote computers, usually inside large data centres. 1.2 what does cloud computing provide? resource meaning example computing power processing capacity to run applications virtual cpu storage space to save files and data google drive database system to store and manage data cloud-hosted database networking connectivity between computers and services virtual network software ready-to-use applications over the internet gmail development tools tools to build applications cloud development platform mobile phone 1. upload photo google cloud (remote data centre) photo stored here laptop 2. open same photo internet internet data lives on remote servers, so any device can reach it figure: google drive as a cloud example cloud resources computing power (virtual cpu) storage (google drive) database (cloud-hosted) networking (virtual network) software (gmail) development tools figure: what cloud computing provides 1.3 how does cloud computing work? traditional local computing: the user installs software and stores files on their own computer or the organization’s own servers. cloud computing: the user connects to a cloud provider over a network and uses resources hosted by that provider. basic working steps user request: a user opens a cloud application or requests a resource. internet connection: the request travels through the internet to the provider. cloud infrastructure: the provider’s servers process the request or retrieve the data. response: the result is sent back to the user’s device. resource management: the provider manages the infrastructure; the user’s responsibilities depend on the service used. example: when you open gmail, your browser sends a request to google’s systems, which process it and return your emails. 1.4 basic components client or front end: the device or interface used to access cloud services (mobile, laptop, web browser). internet or network: connects the user’s device to the cloud infrastructure. cloud infrastructure or back end: remote servers, storage, databases and software that provide the services. example with google drive: your laptop is the client, your internet connection carries the request, and google’s cloud infrastructure stores and retrieves your files. [ client ] <----- internet -----> [ cloud infrastructure ] laptop / mobile servers, storage, database client (front end) laptop, mobile, browser internet (network) cloud infrastructure (back end) servers storage database request response figure: basic components of cloud computing 1.5 important terms term simple meaning cloud service provider (csp) company providing cloud services: aws, google cloud, microsoft azure data centre facility containing servers, storage and networking equipment remote server server accessed through a network, not used directly on your own machine on-premises it infrastructure installed and managed at the organization’s own location pay-as-you-go paying according to the resources or services used 1.6 three main service models (basic introduction) studied in detail in unit ii. remember only the basic meanings now. model full form what it provides example iaas infrastructure as a service virtual servers, storage, networking amazon ec2 paas platform as a service platform to develop and deploy applications google app engine saas software as a service ready-to-use software over the internet gmail saas software as a service ready-to-use software gmail paas platform as a service build and deploy applications google app engine iaas infrastructure as a service servers, storage, networking amazon ec2 figure: iaas, paas and saas with examples 1.7 exam preparation 1-mark answer q. define cloud computing. cloud computing is a technology that provides computing resources such as servers, storage, databases and software over the internet on demand. 5-mark answer q. what is cloud computing? explain its basic working. cloud computing is a technology that provides computing resources such as servers, storage, databases, networking and software over the internet. it lets users access resources hosted on remote servers without buying and maintaining all the physical infrastructure themselves. working: the user sends a request through a device. the request travels through the internet. the cloud provider’s infrastructure processes the request. the required data or service is returned to the user. the provider manages the underlying infrastructure. example: google drive lets users store files on remote servers and access them through the internet. 1.8 quick revision cloud generally refers to remote computing resources accessible through a network. cloud computing provides computing resources over the internet. resources include servers, storage, databases, networking and software. a cloud service provider manages the underlying infrastructure. google drive and gmail are familiar examples. iaas, paas and saas are the three main service models. topic 2. benefits and need for cloud computing red red priority : directly asked in the mca semester iv previous paper (5 marks) why this topic? it deserves more detail than topic 1. prepare it so you can answer a 5-mark question confidently and also expand it into a longer answer. 2.1 why do we need cloud computing? before cloud computing, organizations generally bought and maintained their own it infrastructure. a company launching an online shop needs physical servers, storage devices, networking equipment, software and databases, plus it professionals to install, manage and maintain everything. problems with traditional computing high initial investment: servers, storage, networking equipment and software must be purchased before starting. maintenance responsibility: it staff must maintain hardware, install updates, monitor systems and solve problems. difficulty handling changing demand: a website with 1,000 visitors a day may get 100,000 during a festival sale, and existing servers may not cope. resource wastage: extra hardware bought for peak demand is wasted if unused. limited accessibility: local infrastructure makes remote access need extra arrangements. slow infrastructure setup: buying, installing and configuring servers takes time. how cloud computing solves these problems organizations rent computing resources from providers instead of buying and maintaining all the hardware. start with the resources you need. increase or decrease resources when demand changes. pay according to the selected pricing model and usage. the provider manages the physical infrastructure. applications and data are accessed remotely through a network. traditional problems 1. high initial cost 2. maintenance burden 3. changing demand 4. resource wastage 5. limited access 6. slow setup cloud computing cloud solutions rent resources scale up and down pay by usage provider runs hardware access over internet figure: problems of traditional computing and how cloud solves them 2.2 benefits of cloud computing yellow important for 5 and 15 marks cloud benefits cost savings scalability flexibility high accessibility reliability faster deployment easy collaboration backup and recovery reduced maintenance global reach figure: ten benefits of cloud computing 1. cost savings reduces the need to buy expensive servers, storage and networking equipment. rent resources and pay by usage instead of a large initial investment. example: a startup rents a virtual server from aws instead of buying a physical one. remember: cloud is not always free or cheaper. poor resource management can also increase costs. 2. scalability the ability to increase or decrease computing resources according to requirements. example: during a festival sale an e-commerce site adds server capacity, then reduces it after the sale. 3. flexibility the ability to use and adjust resources according to changing requirements, without buying new physical infrastructure each time. example: a software company uses extra cloud storage or computing power for a new project. 4. high accessibility services can be accessed from different locations and devices through the internet. example: upload a document to google drive from your phone, open it on your laptop. 5. reliability providers generally use backup systems, redundant infrastructure and data replication to reduce the impact of hardware failures. example: if one storage device fails, a properly configured system retrieves the data from another copy. important: reliability depends on the provider’s design and the customer’s configuration. cloud does not guarantee zero downtime. 6. faster deployment and speed cloud resources can be created much faster than buying and installing hardware. example: a developer creates a virtual machine within minutes. 7. easy collaboration multiple users can work on shared files and applications from different locations. example: several students edit the same google docs document. 8. data backup and disaster recovery backup and recovery services help restore information if hardware is damaged or data is deleted. example: a company keeps cloud backups of its business database to recover after a server failure. 9. automatic updates and reduced maintenance providers handle many infrastructure tasks such as hardware maintenance and certain software updates, reducing the it team’s workload. example: a managed cloud database. customers may still update their own applications and manage their data. 10. global reach providers have infrastructure in multiple regions, so applications can be deployed closer to users, improving accessibility and reducing delay. example: an indian company deploys its application in an aws region closer to european customers. demand / resources time traditional: fixed capacity festival sale peak cloud capacity scales up, then back down blue = demand figure: traditional fixed capacity (dashed) vs cloud scaling (red line follows the blue demand line) 2.3 business and it reasons for adopting cloud computing business perspective it perspective reduce infrastructure expenses reduce physical hardware requirements start business operations faster provision servers quickly support business growth scale computing resources improve employee collaboration provide shared applications and storage expand into new markets deploy services in different regions reduce infrastructure management workload use managed cloud services 2.4 traditional computing vs cloud computing basis traditional computing cloud computing infrastructure bought and maintained by the organization provided by a cloud provider initial investment generally high can be lower maintenance organization manages it provider manages physical infrastructure scalability needs extra hardware resources increased or decreased more easily accessibility depends on local infrastructure or network arrangements accessible through the internet payment hardware purchase and maintenance costs usage-based or subscription pricing deployment hardware setup takes time resources provisioned quickly traditional cloud buy servers, storage (capex) rent resources (opex, pay as you go) install and maintain by own it team provider manages physical infrastructure fixed capacity needs new hardware scale up or down on demand slow setup resources in minutes figure: traditional computing vs cloud computing 2.5 important terms term meaning capital expenditure (capex) money spent buying long-term assets such as physical servers operational expenditure (opex) regular expenses of running business operations scalability ability to increase or decrease resources reliability ability to provide services consistently resource provisioning making resources available when required disaster recovery restoring systems and data after a failure pay-as-you-go paying according to resources consumed capex vs opex: traditional computing needs more upfront investment in physical infrastructure (capex). cloud computing can shift some of this spending to ongoing operational expenses (opex), depending on the pricing arrangement. 2.6 exam-ready answers 1-mark question q. write any two benefits of cloud computing. cost savings. scalability. other acceptable answers: flexibility, accessibility, reliability. 5-mark question (previous paper) q. explain the benefits and need for cloud computing. cloud computing provides computing resources such as servers, storage, databases and software over the internet. organizations need it because traditional it infrastructure requires high initial investment, regular maintenance and extra hardware for increasing workloads. the major benefits are: cost savings: reduces the need to buy expensive hardware. scalability: resources increase or decrease according to demand. flexibility: different resources according to business requirements. accessibility: access applications and data from different locations. reliability: backup and redundant systems reduce service interruptions. faster deployment: resources provisioned quickly. easy collaboration: multiple users work on shared applications and data. disaster recovery: important data recovered through backups. thus, cloud computing helps organizations reduce infrastructure management effort, improve flexibility and use resources according to their requirements. 15-mark preparation expand using this structure: introduction and definition of cloud computing. need for cloud computing. problems with traditional computing. ten benefits explained with examples. traditional vs cloud computing comparison. conclusion. 2.7 quick revision cloud reduces the need for large upfront hardware investment. scalability: resources increase or decrease with demand. flexibility: adjust resources to changing requirements. accessibility: use services remotely. reliability improves through redundancy and backup. faster deployment helps start projects quickly. cloud backup supports disaster recovery. cloud can reduce maintenance responsibilities. youtube videos great learning: cloud computing tutorial for beginners in hindi. covers fundamentals, models and why cloud is used. open course high scalability. topic 4. cloud and virtualization yellow yellow priority : related to previous-paper questions, understand properly why important? virtualization is one of the technologies that makes cloud computing possible. it helps providers use physical hardware efficiently and give virtual resources to multiple users. covered here: meaning of virtualization, meaning of cloud, relationship between them, how virtualization works, role of the hypervisor, difference, advantages and limitations. 4.1 what is virtualization? virtualization is a technology that creates virtual versions of computing resources, such as computers, servers, operating systems, storage and networks, using software. it lets multiple virtual environments run on a single physical machine. instead of buying separate computers for different tasks, one powerful computer creates multiple virtual computers. example a company has one powerful server and wants to run application a (linux), application b (windows server) and application c (another linux environment). without virtualization it may need three physical servers. with virtualization it creates three virtual machines on one server. each vm behaves like an independent computer with its own operating system and applications. physical server (cpu, ram, storage) hypervisor (creates and manages vms) vm 1 linux application a vm 2 windows server application b vm 3 linux application c figure: virtualization: three vms on one physical server 4.2 what is a virtual machine (vm)? a virtual machine is a software-based computer that behaves like a physical computer. it has virtual cpu, ram, storage, network interface and an operating system. example: on a windows laptop you create a vm to run ubuntu linux. host machine = the actual physical computer. guest machine = the virtual computer running on the host. host machine: physical windows laptop (cpu, ram, storage) hypervisor (virtualbox) guest virtual machine ubuntu linux virtual cpu, ram, disk host = actual physical computer guest = virtual computer running on the host figure: host machine and guest virtual machine 4.3 what is a hypervisor? a hypervisor is software (or a software layer supported by hardware) that creates and manages virtual machines. it allocates physical cpu, ram and storage to different vms. example: a server with 16 cpu cores, 64 gb ram and 1 tb storage. the hypervisor allocates different portions to multiple vms, manages the allocation and keeps vms isolated from one another. type 1 and type 2 hypervisors are studied in detail in unit v. examples: vmware esxi, microsoft hyper-v, oracle virtualbox. physical server 16 cpu cores 64 gb ram 1 tb storage hypervisor allocates resources vm 1: 4 cores, 16 gb, 250 gb vm 2: 8 cores, 32 gb, 500 gb vm 3: 4 cores, 16 gb, 250 gb (example split of one physical server) figure: hypervisor dividing server resources among vms 4.4 what is cloud computing? cloud computing provides computing resources such as servers, storage, databases and networking over the internet whenever users need them. instead of buying and maintaining physical infrastructure, users access resources provided by a cloud service provider. example: amazon ec2 lets users create and use virtual servers through aws. 4.5 relationship between cloud computing and virtualization red most important part of this topic they are related but not the same. virtualization is a technology, whereas cloud computing is a way of delivering computing resources as services. virtualization creates multiple virtual resources from physical hardware. cloud computing uses virtualization, resource pooling, automation and network access to deliver those resources on demand. how are they connected? (aws example) aws has physical servers in its data centres. virtualization divides their resources into virtual computing environments. the cloud platform manages and allocates these resources. users request virtual servers when required. users access them through the internet and pay according to the pricing model. users: laptop, mobile, browser cloud platform (allocation, automation, billing) virtualization layer (hypervisor, virtual resources) physical servers in data centres figure: how virtualization supports cloud computing 4.6 difference between cloud computing and virtualization basis virtualization cloud computing meaning creates virtual versions of computing resources delivers computing resources as services nature technology service delivery model main purpose uses physical hardware efficiently provides resources on demand access can work within a local network commonly accessed over the internet resource management virtualization software cloud platforms and automation example running ubuntu in virtualbox creating a virtual server on aws ec2 important: virtualization can exist without cloud computing. virtualbox on your own laptop uses no cloud service. virtualization a technology creates virtual versions of resources cloud computing a service model delivers resources on demand enables cloud virtualization can exist without cloud (virtualbox on your laptop) figure: virtualization and cloud computing overlap 4.7 benefits of virtualization better hardware utilization: multiple vms share one physical server. cost reduction: fewer physical servers needed. isolation: each vm operates in a separate environment. flexibility: different operating systems on the same machine. easy management: vms created, configured and managed through software. scalability: virtual resources adjusted within available hardware capacity. testing and development: test applications on different operating systems without extra computers. virtualization benefits better hardware utilization cost reduction isolation flexibility (many os) easy management scalability testing and development figure: benefits of virtualization 4.8 limitations of virtualization performance overhead: vms may be slower than running directly on hardware. resource competition: vms may compete for cpu, ram and storage. management complexity: managing many vms can become complicated. host failure: if the physical host fails, its vms may become unavailable unless recovery arrangements exist. security risks: a hypervisor vulnerability can potentially affect multiple vms. 4.9 exam-ready answers 1-mark question q. what is virtualization? virtualization is a technology that creates virtual versions of computing resources, such as servers, operating systems and storage, using software. 5-mark question q. explain the relationship between cloud computing and virtualization. virtualization creates multiple virtual computing environments from a single physical machine, allowing multiple virtual machines to share its resources. cloud computing provides computing resources such as servers, storage and databases over the internet on demand. virtualization supports cloud computing as follows: it lets multiple virtual machines run on one physical server. it improves hardware utilization. it helps cloud providers create virtual computing resources. it supports resource sharing and allocation. it helps provide resources quickly according to user requirements. for example, aws uses virtualization technologies to provide virtual servers through ec2. thus, virtualization is an important enabling technology for cloud computing, while cloud computing delivers resources as services to users. 15-mark preparation introduction to virtualization. notes, one-time reading why study this topic? before choosing a cloud service, an organization must identify what it expects from it. a banking application, for example, needs strong security, high availability and reliable performance. these expectations are the cloud services requirements. 5.1 meaning cloud services requirements are the technical and operational conditions a cloud service must satisfy to meet the needs of its users or organizations. in simple words: what a cloud service must provide to work properly, securely and reliably. 5.2 major requirements 1. security protect data and applications from unauthorized access, theft and cyberattacks. example: a cloud database uses authentication and encryption to protect customer information. 2. availability the service should be accessible whenever users need it. example: an online banking application remains accessible throughout the day. 3. reliability the service should work consistently and correctly without frequent failures. example: cloud storage stores and retrieves files without unexpected data loss. 4. scalability resources should increase or decrease with changing workloads. example: an online shop handles extra visitors during festival sales. 5. performance acceptable response time, processing speed and network performance. example: a cloud application responds without unnecessary delays. 6. network connectivity reliable network connectivity so users can communicate with cloud servers and access applications. 7. backup and disaster recovery support data backup and recovery so important information can be restored after failures or disasters. 8. interoperability and portability interoperability: different systems and cloud services can communicate and work together. portability: data and applications can move between compatible environments with minimum difficulty. cloud service + sla security availability reliability scalability performance connectivity backup and recovery interoperability and portability figure: major requirements of cloud services 5.3 service level agreement (sla) an sla is an agreement between a cloud service provider and a customer that defines the expected service level. it may include: service availability. response time and performance. security responsibilities. support and maintenance. backup and recovery arrangements. compensation or service credits if agreed targets are not achieved. example: a provider promises a particular monthly availability percentage. an sla helps both parties understand their responsibilities and expected service quality. cloud service provider customer sla availability response time, performance security responsibilities support and maintenance backup and recovery service credits agrees agrees figure: service level agreement between provider and customer 5.4 quick revision table requirement meaning security protect data and applications availability keep services accessible reliability ensure consistent operation scalability adjust resources according to demand performance good response time and speed connectivity maintain network access backup and recovery restore data after failures interoperability different systems work together portability data and applications can move 5.5 exam-ready answer q. what are cloud services requirements? explain the major requirements. cloud services requirements are the technical and operational conditions that a cloud service must satisfy to meet the needs of its users. the major requirements are: security: protects data and applications from unauthorized access. availability: services are accessible when required. reliability: consistent and correct operation. scalability: resources increase or decrease according to demand. performance: acceptable response time and processing speed. connectivity: reliable network access. backup and recovery: restore data after failures. interoperability: different systems communicate with each other. an sla defines the expected service quality and the responsibilities of the provider and customer. thus, cloud service requirements help ensure that services are secure,
