evolution of erp yellow priority ★ what to prepare from this topic ★ the step-by-step growth: inventory control → mrp → mrp ii → erp → erp ii / cloud erp. what each stage added and which limitation of the earlier stage pushed the next one. approximate time line (decade-wise) and the key technology of each stage. how erp "contains" earlier systems (mrp and mrp ii are parts of the erp idea). comparison of mrp, mrp ii and erp. study approach: learn the chain in one line first — inventory control → mrp → mrp ii → erp → erp ii → cloud / intelligent erp — and then attach "focus + limitation" to every link. priority reason: "evolution of erp" is the first official topic of unit i, so a theory question such as "explain the evolution of erp" is a natural prediction. it is marked yellow (predicted from the syllabus and the usual erp question pattern); it is not claimed as a confirmed ranchi university pyq. the central idea erp did not appear suddenly. it grew out of simple stock-control methods, which became material planning (mrp), then planning of all manufacturing resources (mrp ii), and finally planning of the whole enterprise on one common database (erp). every stage fixed a weakness of the earlier stage. 1.1 meaning of "evolution of erp" yellow evolution of erp means the gradual development of business information systems from departmental inventory control to enterprise-wide integrated systems . at each stage the scope of the system became wider: first only stock, then materials needed for production, then all manufacturing resources, and finally every function of the organization — finance, hr, sales, purchase, production and more. note: years given below are the commonly cited approximate decades. different textbooks may shift a date by a few years, so write "approximately / around" in the exam. 1.2 before computers — manual and reorder-point control before computers were used in business, stock was controlled with paper registers, bin cards and simple rules. the popular technique was statistical inventory control : when stock of an item fell to a fixed re-order point (rop) , a fixed quantity (for example, the economic order quantity — eoq ) was ordered. black weakness: rop / eoq treats every item independently . it does not know that a bicycle needs a frame, two wheels and a chain at a particular time, so it cannot plan dependent demand (parts needed because a final product is planned). 1.3 evolution time line 1960s inventory control reorder point · eoq stock records 1970s mrp material requirement planning · bom 1980s mrp ii manufacturing resource planning · capacity · finance 1990s erp whole enterprise · common database 2000s → erp ii / cloud web · partners · saas mobile · analytics · ai scope keeps widening: stock → materials → manufacturing → enterprise → extended enterprise approximate decades — each stage includes and extends the previous one time line of erp evolution (approximate decades). 1.4 stage-wise explanation stage 1 — inventory control systems (1960s) mainframe computers were first used by large manufacturers to keep stock records and to apply re-order-point rules. focus: "how much stock do we have and when should we re-order?" limitation: handled each item separately; no planning of components for a finished product; no link with production schedule. stage 2 — material requirement planning, mrp (1970s) researchers and practitioners (joseph orlicky of ibm is the name usually associated with it) showed that component demand should be calculated from the plan for the finished product, not forecast item by item. inputs: master production schedule (mps) , bill of materials (bom) and inventory records . outputs: planned purchase orders and production orders with correct quantities and dates. focus: "what materials do we need, how many, and when?" limitation: assumed unlimited capacity (machines and labour) and had no feedback if the plan could not actually be executed; it covered materials only. stage 3 — closed-loop mrp and mrp ii (1980s) closed-loop mrp added capacity planning and shop-floor control with feedback — if the plan is not feasible, it is corrected. mrp ii (manufacturing resource planning) extended this to all manufacturing resources — materials, machines, labour and money — and linked sales & operations planning, purchasing, costing and finance . oliver wight is widely credited with promoting the name. focus: "can we make it with the resources we have, and what will it cost?" limitation: still centred on manufacturing ; hr, distribution, project work, quality and service functions stayed in separate programs and separate databases. stage 4 — enterprise resource planning, erp (1990s) the term erp was coined by the gartner group around 1990 to describe systems that go beyond mrp ii and cover the whole business. erp integrates finance, hr, sales & distribution, purchasing, inventory, production, quality, plant maintenance on a common database using client–server technology and relational databases. leading packages of the period: sap (r/3), oracle, baan, peoplesoft, jd edwards . focus: "one integrated view of the entire enterprise in real time." limitation: mostly inward-looking — good inside the organization, weak in connecting with customers, suppliers and partners; costly and heavy to implement. stage 5 — erp ii / extended erp (2000s) gartner used the term erp ii (around 2000) for erp that opens to the outside world through the internet . adds or connects crm (customer relationship management), scm (supply chain management), e-business, supplier / customer portals and collaborative commerce. focus: "collaborate with customers, suppliers and partners, not only run internal operations." stage 6 — cloud, mobile and intelligent erp (2010s onwards) erp is delivered as cloud / saas (subscription, no big server room), with mobile access and in-memory databases for fast reports. modern systems use analytics, automation, machine learning and iot data for forecasting, predictive maintenance and quicker decisions. benefit: lower start-up cost, faster upgrades, anywhere access, stronger analytics. challenges: data security, dependence on the vendor and internet, integration with existing systems, subscription cost over time. 1.5 summary table of the evolution stage period main focus what it added limitation that led to the next stage inventory control 1960s stock levels computerised stock records, rop / eoq rules item-by-item; no dependent-demand planning mrp 1970s materials mps, bom, time-phased planned orders no capacity check, no feedback, materials only mrp ii 1980s manufacturing resources capacity planning, shop-floor control, costing, finance link limited to manufacturing; separate systems for other functions erp 1990s whole enterprise finance, hr, sales, purchase, quality, maintenance on one database weak external collaboration; heavy and costly erp ii 2000s extended enterprise web, crm, scm, partner portals infrastructure cost; slow upgrades cloud / intelligent erp 2010s → anywhere, data-driven saas, mobile, analytics, ai / ml, iot security, vendor dependence, integration issues 1.6 how the systems fit inside each other each new system includes the earlier one and then widens the scope. mrp is a part of mrp ii, and mrp ii is a part of erp. erp ii / cloud erp — extended enterprise, partners, internet erp — whole enterprise on one common database mrp ii — all manufacturing resources mrp — material planning inventory control rop · eoq · stock records nested view — every outer system contains the inner systems. 1.7 factors that drove the evolution factor how it pushed erp forward advances in hardware mainframes → minicomputers → pcs and servers made computing cheaper and available to every department. better software and databases relational databases and client–server architecture allowed one shared database for many modules. global competition companies needed shorter lead time, lower cost and better customer service, which needed integrated information. limits of legacy / siloed systems separate departmental programs caused duplicate data, mismatched records and slow reports. business growth and complexity multi-plant, multi-location and multi-currency operations needed one consistent system. year-2000 (y2k) problem many firms replaced old date-limited systems with erp in the late 1990s. internet and cloud technology made collaboration with partners, remote access and subscription-based erp possible. 1.8 mrp vs mrp ii vs erp basis mrp mrp ii erp full form material requirement planning manufacturing resource planning enterprise resource planning scope materials only all manufacturing resources entire enterprise main question what, how many, when to buy / make? can we make it with available resources? how do all functions work together? functions covered inventory, purchasing, production orders mrp + capacity, shop floor, costing, finance link mrp ii + hr, sales & distribution, quality, maintenance, projects feedback none (open loop) closed loop with feedback real-time integrated feedback database separate material files manufacturing database single common enterprise database typical period 1970s 1980s 1990s 1.9 simple example — a growing bicycle company small shop: uses a stock register and re-orders tyres when only 20 are left (inventory control). growing factory: to build 500 bicycles next month, it calculates the exact number of frames, wheels and chains and their order dates from the bom (mrp). more machines: checks if the assembly line has enough hours and workers, and links the plan to cost and budget (mrp ii). many departments: finance, hr payroll, sales, purchase and stores all share one database, so a sale updates stock, billing and accounts together (erp). online business: dealers and suppliers log in through a portal and the company uses cloud erp with mobile dashboards (erp ii / cloud erp). 1.10 previous-year question / question-pattern evidence evidence status: yellow — predicted from the syllabus. the syllabus priority list that each question appeared in a ranchi university examination. the central idea erp brings the important business functions of an organization into an integrated information system. instead of each department keeping disconnected records, departments can work with connected processes and shared business information. 2.1 meaning and full form of erp yellow erp stands for enterprise resource planning . it is an integrated software system used by an organization to manage and coordinate its major business functions—such as finance, human resources, purchasing, inventory, production and sales—through connected applications and shared information. word meaning in simple language business example enterprise the whole organization or business. a manufacturing company with finance, hr, sales and production departments. resource anything the organization uses to run its work. money, employees, raw materials, machines, stock and information. planning organizing and using resources according to business requirements. planning how much material, labour and money are needed for an order. 2.2 formal definition for examination important definition enterprise resource planning (erp) is an integrated, real-time, cross-functional information system that supports the major internal business processes of an organization by connecting different functional departments and enabling the flow and sharing of information. in simple words: erp is one connected business system through which different departments can work with the same updated organizational information. 2.3 why does an organization need erp? consider a company that sells and manufactures laptops. it has separate departments for sales, inventory, production and finance. when these departments use unrelated software, the same information may have to be entered repeatedly. a sales employee may not know the latest stock position, and the finance team may receive order details late. before erp — disconnected systems sales sales software inventory stock software production production software finance accounting software separate records · manual communication · possible duplication and delay information is not automatically shared departments may work with different versions of business data. conceptual illustration of siloed departmental applications. erp addresses this problem by connecting the departments through a common system. after erp — integrated system erp system connected business processes sales orders inventory stock production manufacturing finance accounts shared / integrated business data conceptual erp integration: departments exchange information through connected modules. 2.4 how erp works — a simple business example suppose a customer places an order for 100 laptops. the order triggers connected activities in different departments. sales: records the customer's order in the erp system. inventory: checks the available laptop stock. production / procurement: if stock is insufficient, the organization can plan production or purchase the required materials. finance: uses order and delivery information for billing and accounting. management: can review updated order, stock and financial information through reports. important point the data is entered once where appropriate and then made available to other authorized functions through integrated processes. erp does not mean every employee can see every record; access is controlled by roles and permissions. 2.5 major characteristics of erp characteristic explanation example 1. integration connects different business functions and processes. a sales order can update inventory and provide information to finance. 2. common database uses a shared or logically integrated data repository for business information. sales and inventory use the same product and order records. 3. real-time information updates can become available to other connected processes without waiting for separate periodic data entry. after a goods issue is posted, stock information is updated. 4. modular structure erp is organized into modules for different business functions. finance, hr, inventory and sales modules. 5. process automation automates repeatable steps and workflows. purchase requisition approval or payroll calculation. 6. standardized processes encourages consistent procedures across the organization. different branches follow the same purchase approval workflow. 7. reporting and analysis combines information from business functions for reports and decisions. a manager reviews sales, stock and cost reports together. 8. security and access control controls access according to user roles and responsibilities. an hr user can access employee records while a sales user accesses order data. 2.6 functional modules of erp an erp package is generally divided into modules. each module supports a particular functional area, but the modules are connected to the overall erp system. module work performed typical information finance and accounting manages financial transactions and accounts. general ledger, accounts payable, receivable, budgets. human resources (hr) manages employee-related activities. employee records, attendance, payroll, recruitment. sales and distribution manages customer orders and delivery activities. customer orders, pricing, invoices, dispatch. production / manufacturing plans and monitors manufacturing. production schedules, bills of materials, work orders. inventory / materials management controls materials and stock movement. stock levels, goods receipt, goods issue, reorder data. supply chain management (scm) coordinates sourcing, suppliers, logistics and movement of goods. procurement, supplier, transportation and delivery information. note: module names and boundaries vary between erp products. crm and scm may be included as modules or connected applications, depending on the erp package. 2.7 basic erp architecture at a conceptual level, an erp system can be understood through three major layers. the exact technical architecture differs by product, but this model helps explain how users, business processing and data work together. presentation layer screens · web interface · dashboards application / business logic layer rules · workflows · validation · erp modules database layer shared / integrated business data simplified three-layer view of erp architecture. presentation layer: the interface through which employees enter information and view reports. application layer: processes business rules, validations and workflows, such as order approval or stock updates. database layer: stores and manages business data used by the connected modules. example: a sales employee enters an order using the presentation layer. the application layer validates the order and coordinates the workflow. the database layer stores the order and related information. 2.8 erp vs traditional / legacy / siloed systems a legacy system is an older information system that an organization continues to use. a siloed system is an application or database that works separately from other departments' systems. a legacy system can be integrated, but many older departmental systems are isolated. basis traditional / siloed systems integrated erp system structure separate applications for separate departments. connected modules within an integrated system. data storage may use separate departmental databases. uses a common or integrated data repository. data sharing may require manual transfer or custom interfaces. information flows through connected processes. data duplication greater risk of duplicate entry and inconsistent records. reduces unnecessary duplication through shared records. reporting reports may be limited to one department. can combine information from multiple functions. coordination departments may coordinate through email, files or manual updates. connected workflows support cross-department coordination. exam point: do not write that every legacy system is necessarily disconnected or bad. the important distinction is between isolated departmental applications and an integrated erp environment. 2.9 advantages and limitations — brief overview the official syllabus has a separate topic on advantages of erp, so the benefits are only introduced here. benefits: better coordination, reduced duplicate data entry, improved visibility, more consistent information and faster reporting. limitations: high implementation cost, complexity, training requirements, change resistance and dependence on data quality. 2.10 previous-year question / question-pattern evidence evidence status: yellow — important conceptual preparation. the question pattern provided for this approved study references and the topic-specific lesson identified below. no exact ranchi university pyq is claimed unless its wording is confirmed in the supplied examination papers. 3.1 introduction the erp market grew because organizations needed a better way to manage their expanding and interconnected business activities. separate applications and outdated systems often made it difficult to share accurate information, coordinate departments, respond quickly to customers and control costs. core idea organizations adopted erp to integrate business processes, improve operational performance, obtain reliable information for decisions, modernize old systems and support business growth. 3.2 major reasons for the growth of erp important 1. improved business performance erp connects activities such as purchasing, inventory, production, sales and finance. better coordination reduces unnecessary work and helps the organization complete business processes more efficiently. example: when a sales order is entered, inventory information can be checked without separately calling the store department. important 2. reduction in lead time and cycle time lead time is the total time between starting a request or order and completing it. cycle time is the time required to complete a particular process or activity. erp can reduce delays by connecting departments and automating information flow. example: a purchase request can move to approval and purchasing without repeatedly entering the same details. important 3. better customer service and satisfaction erp makes relevant information about orders, stock, delivery and customer accounts easier to access. employees can respond to customer questions more accurately and help avoid unnecessary delays. example: a customer asks when an item will be delivered. staff can check order and inventory status from connected information. important 4. support for business growth and expansion as a business adds new products, customers, branches or locations, its processes become more complex. erp provides an integrated system that can help coordinate these activities across the organization. example: a company opening a new branch can use common processes and shared reporting rather than maintaining completely separate records. important 5. elimination of limitations in legacy systems legacy systems are older applications that may be difficult to maintain, modify or connect with modern software. erp adoption helps organizations replace disconnected or outdated applications with an integrated platform. example: if finance and inventory use incompatible software, employees may need to enter the same transaction twice. integrated erp reduces this duplication. important 6. better information accuracy and availability when connected departments use shared business data, duplicate records and inconsistent information can be reduced. managers can access more up-to-date information for monitoring and planning. example: sales and inventory teams can refer to the same stock information instead of maintaining different spreadsheets. important 7. improved planning and decision-making erp brings information from different functions together. managers can analyze sales, costs, inventory and production information to make better-informed decisions. example: a manager can compare sales demand with available stock and production capacity before planning the next production cycle. important 8. better utilization of resources erp helps organizations plan and monitor the use of materials, employees, machines, money and time. better visibility can reduce waste and improve coordination. example: production planning can use inventory information to avoid ordering materials that are already available in the warehouse. important 9. flexibility and ability to respond to change organizations face changing customer requirements, competition, products and business processes. integrated information and coordinated workflows make it easier to understand the impact of changes and respond across departments. example: when demand for a product increases, sales, inventory and production teams can coordinate their response using connected information. important 10. advances in information technology developments such as client-server computing, relational databases, web-based applications, cloud computing and mobile access have made integrated enterprise systems more practical and accessible to organizations. example: cloud-based erp can allow authorized employees in different locations to access the same system through the internet. important 11. better coordination with suppliers and business partners erp can improve the flow of information between purchasing, inventory, production and supplier-related activities. this supports more coordinated ordering and supply planning. example: purchasing staff can use stock and production requirements to plan when raw materials should be ordered. important 12. competitive advantage organizations use erp to improve speed, coordination, service and the quality of management information. these improvements can help a business compete more effectively. example: a business that can process orders accurately and respond quickly may provide a better customer experience than a competitor using disconnected manual processes. 3.3 tangible and intangible reasons reasons supporting erp adoption can also be grouped into tangible and intangible benefits. tangible benefits are easier to measure in numbers, while intangible benefits are valuable but harder to measure directly. type meaning examples tangible benefits that can usually be measured using time, cost, quantity or financial figures. reduced lead time, lower operating cost, fewer repeated entries, improved inventory control, faster order processing. intangible benefits that are difficult to measure directly but improve organizational capability. customer satisfaction, better flexibility, improved decision-making, stronger coordination and information quality. why organizations adopt erp erp adoption tangible benefits less time · lower cost faster processing · better control intangible benefits customer satisfaction · flexibility better decisions · coordination the two groups describe different kinds of value that encourage organizations to invest in erp. 3.4 diagram — overall drivers of erp market growth major drivers behind erp market growth business drivers growth · competition customer satisfaction operational drivers time · cost · resources planning · coordination technology drivers legacy replacement modern it · cloud access increasing erp adoption integrated processes · better information · stronger performance business needs, operational improvement and technology changes collectively increase demand for erp solutions. 3.5 practical example example: a growing manufacturing company a manufacturer initially manages sales, inventory, purchasing and accounts through separate spreadsheets and applications. as orders increase, staff face duplicate entries, delayed stock updates and difficulty preparing reports. the company needs to process orders faster and reduce delays. it wants accurate stock information and better production planning. it needs managers to see current sales, cost and inventory information. it plans to open another branch and needs common processes. it replaces disconnected applications with an erp system. result: erp can connect the departments and support coordinated work. the actual improvement depends on correct implementation, reliable data and employee adoption. 3.6 short summary for revision reason what erp helps achieve syllabus. the main advantage names below follow the tutorialspoint erp lesson, with explanations supported by geeksforgeeks. this is not a claim that every heading is a confirmed direct pyq. 4.1 introduction enterprise resource planning (erp) integrates important business functions such as finance, sales, purchasing, inventory, production and human resources. because departments can work with connected processes and shared information, an organization can improve coordination, control and decision-making. core idea the main advantage of erp is that it connects business processes and information in one integrated system. this can reduce delays and duplication, improve visibility and help the organization use its resources more effectively. 4.2 major advantages of erp important 1. reduction of lead time lead time is the total time between placing or initiating an order/request and completing or delivering it. erp connects activities such as order processing, stock checking, purchasing and production planning. this can reduce waiting and communication delays. example: when a customer order is entered, the sales team can check stock information directly instead of waiting for a separate inventory report. important 2. reduction of cycle time cycle time is the time required to complete a particular process or activity. erp can streamline workflows and reduce repeated data entry, manual hand-offs and unnecessary approvals. example: a purchase request can move through a defined approval workflow, reducing the time spent sending forms between departments. important 3. on-time shipment erp connects order details with inventory, production and distribution information. this helps an organization plan material availability and delivery activities more effectively, increasing the possibility of shipping products on the promised date. example: the dispatch team can use order and stock status to plan which customer orders are ready to ship. important 4. improved resource utilization erp helps managers monitor and plan the use of resources such as materials, machines, employees, money and time. better visibility can reduce idle resources, unnecessary purchases and waste. example: production planning can check available raw materials before creating a new purchase order. important 5. better customer satisfaction erp can provide employees with updated information about customer orders, product availability, delivery and accounts. this supports more accurate responses and better service. example: customer support can check order progress and provide a more reliable delivery update. important 6. improved supplier performance erp connects purchasing, inventory and production requirements. this helps an organization plan purchases, track supplier-related transactions and evaluate whether materials arrive as required. example: purchase records can help the company review supplier delivery dates and identify repeated delays. important 7. increased flexibility integrated information and standardized workflows help an organization respond to changes in demand, products, processes and business conditions. modular erp systems may also allow organizations to add functions as needs grow. example: when demand increases, managers can review sales, inventory and production information together before adjusting the production plan. important 8. reduced quality costs erp can support quality management by connecting production records, inspection results, materials and supplier information. this helps organizations identify defects and trace where quality problems may have occurred. it can reduce costs related to rework, scrap and avoidable defects when quality processes are properly managed. example: if a batch fails inspection, the organization can trace its production and material records to investigate the cause. important 9. improved information accuracy when departments use shared data, the same transaction does not need to be entered into multiple disconnected systems. this reduces duplicate records and conflicting information. accuracy still depends on correct data entry and proper controls. example: a stock update recorded in the inventory module can be reflected in information used by sales and purchasing teams. important 10. better decision-making capability erp brings information from different departments together and provides reports, dashboards and analysis. managers can use this information to plan operations, monitor performance and make informed decisions. example: a manager can compare sales, expenses and inventory levels before deciding whether to increase production. important 11. better integration and coordination erp links business functions and supports the flow of information between them. this reduces departmental information silos and helps employees coordinate work. example: a sales order can trigger inventory checking and provide information needed by production and finance. important 12. reduced duplication and manual work erp automates repetitive workflows and allows multiple departments to use shared records. this can reduce repeated data entry, paperwork and errors caused by maintaining separate records. example: employee details maintained in the hr module can be used by payroll instead of entering the same details again. important 13. improved reporting and transparency erp can produce reports from connected operational and financial data. managers can get a clearer view of organizational activities, compare performance and identify issues more quickly. example: a finance manager can review sales and expense information from a common reporting system. important 14. better cost control by streamlining processes, reducing repeated work and improving resource planning, erp can help an organization control operating costs. the actual savings depend on the quality of implementation and how the system is used. example: improved stock visibility can help prevent unnecessary over-ordering and excess inventory. 4.3 summary table — advantages at a glance advantage meaning in simple words reduction of lead time complete orders and requests faster. reduction of cycle time complete individual processes in less time. on-time shipment improve planning for promised deliveries. resource utilization use materials, people and machines effectively. customer satisfaction provide better and more reliable service. supplier performance coordinate purchasing and monitor suppliers. flexibility respond to business changes more easily. reduced quality costs help identify defects and avoid rework. information accuracy reduce duplicate and conflicting records. decision-making use connected information for better decisions. 4.4 diagram — how erp creates advantages how erp creates business advantages integrated erp system operations less delay · less duplication better resource use customers better order visibility improved service management accurate reports better decisions improved overall organizational performance erp's shared information and connected workflows can create operational, customer-service and managerial benefits. 4.5 practical example example: an online electronics store an online store receives a customer's order for a laptop. sales: the order is recorded in erp. inventory: the system checks available stock. finance: payment and invoice information is recorded. warehouse: staff receive the information needed to prepare dispatch. customer service: staff can check order status and answer customer questions. advantages shown: less repeated entry, better coordination, more accurate information, improved order visibility and support for on-time shipment. 4.6 tangible and intangible advantages type meaning examples tangible benefits that can be measured using time, cost or quantity. reduced processing time, lower inventory cost, fewer data-entry errors, improved productivity. intangible benefits that are valuable but harder to measure directly. customer satisfaction, better communication, flexibility, improved decision-making. 4.7 important note — erp advantages are not automatic erp software does not guarantee that every organization will immediately reduce costs or improve service. benefits depend on: accurate and consistent data. suitable business processes and configuration. employee training and user acceptance. management support and proper implementation. ongoing maintenance and system improvement. this distinction is useful in exams: describe advantages as benefits erp can provide , not guaranteed results. 4.8 previous-year question / question-pattern evidence evidence status: yellow — important syllabus topic. “advantages support and commitment. poor planning, project management and unrealistic schedules. insufficient user involvement, training and resistance to change. inaccurate data and data migration problems. implementation failure factors. research findings are supporting context, not university exam questions. 5.1 introduction erp implementation is a complex process because it affects many departments, employees, business processes and information systems. an erp project may fail when the organization cannot implement the system properly, employees do not adopt it, or the final system does not meet the expected business requirements. core idea erp failure can happen because of poor management, weak planning, lack of user support, insufficient training, inaccurate data, excessive customization, poor testing or inadequate technical support. 5.2 what does erp failure mean? erp failure does not always mean that the software completely stops working. a project may also be considered unsuccessful when it: exceeds the approved budget by a large amount. takes much longer than the planned implementation time. does not provide the required business functions. creates serious disruption to normal business operations. is not accepted or properly used by employees. fails to deliver the expected benefits or is eventually abandoned. different studies use different definitions of “failure”. therefore, avoid memorizing a single failure percentage unless a specific source and definition are given. 5.3 major reasons for erp failure important 1. lack of top management support erp implementation requires decisions, funding, coordination and organizational changes. if senior management does not actively support the project, departments may not cooperate and important issues may remain unresolved. example: department managers refuse to provide staff for erp testing because senior management has not made the project a priority. important 2. poor planning and project management an erp project needs a clear plan, defined responsibilities, milestones, risk management and regular monitoring. poor project management can cause delays, confusion, budget overruns and incomplete implementation. example: the company starts installing erp without deciding which departments and processes will be included in the first phase. important 3. unrealistic time and cost estimates erp implementation may require software configuration, data migration, integration, testing and employee training. if the organization sets an unrealistic deadline or budget, teams may skip important activities to meet the target. example: management insists on launching the entire erp system in a few weeks even though data migration and user testing are incomplete. important 4. lack of user involvement employees who actually use erp understand many day-to-day business requirements. if they are not involved in requirement gathering, design and testing, the system may not match their real work needs. example: the warehouse team is not consulted, so the inventory module does not support its actual stock-handling process. important 5. resistance to change erp often changes existing workflows and responsibilities. employees may resist the new system because they are comfortable with old methods, fear losing control or do not understand the benefits of the change. example: employees continue maintaining separate spreadsheets instead of entering transactions into erp. important 6. inadequate training and education erp contains multiple modules and workflows. without sufficient training, employees may enter incorrect data, avoid using the system or make operational mistakes. example: a purchase employee does not know how to create a purchase order and enters the transaction incorrectly. important 7. inaccurate data and data migration problems data migration means transferring data from old systems into the new erp system. if old records are incomplete, duplicated, inconsistent or incorrectly mapped, the new system may produce unreliable results. example: the old inventory system contains incorrect product codes. these codes are transferred without cleaning, causing stock reports to become inaccurate. important 8. excessive customization customization means modifying standard erp software to match an organization's special requirements. too much customization increases cost and complexity, makes upgrades harder and can create maintenance problems. example: the company modifies many standard erp functions to copy every detail of its old system instead of reviewing whether the old process should change. important 9. wrong erp package or vendor selection if the selected erp product does not match the organization's size, industry, business processes or technical requirements, the organization may face expensive modifications and functionality gaps. weak vendor support can make these problems harder to resolve. example: a manufacturing company selects a system that lacks important production-planning functions. important 10. failure to redesign business processes business process reengineering (bpr) means examining and redesigning business processes to improve performance. if an organization simply copies inefficient old processes into the erp system, it may automate existing problems instead of improving the business. example: a company keeps unnecessary approval steps in its new erp workflow, so purchase requests remain slow. important 11. poor communication and coordination erp affects many departments. if information is not communicated properly between management, users, consultants and technical teams, requirements may be misunderstood and decisions may conflict. example: finance and sales teams follow different definitions for order status, leading to inconsistent reports. important 12. inadequate testing testing checks whether erp functions correctly and supports real business scenarios. if testing is incomplete, errors may appear after go-live and disrupt normal operations. example: the company tests normal sales orders but does not test returns, cancellations or peak-volume transactions. important 13. insufficient resources and skills erp implementation needs suitable project members, business analysts, technical experts, time and budget. if the team lacks the required skills or members are not available, implementation quality may suffer. example: the organization assigns erp implementation as an extra duty to already busy employees who cannot give enough time to the project. important 14. poor integration with existing systems erp may need to exchange information with older applications, external platforms, machines or third-party services. weak integration can create duplicate data, broken workflows and inconsistent information. example: the erp system does not correctly exchange order information with the organization's online store. important 15. inadequate post-implementation support erp work does not end at go-live. the organization needs monitoring, issue resolution, maintenance, user support and continuous improvement. without these activities, problems may continue and employees may lose confidence in the system. example: after launch, employees report errors but there is no support team to resolve them quickly. 5.4 erp failure factors by category category common failure factors management lack of leadership support, poor project governance, unrealistic expectations. people user resistance, poor involvement, insufficient training, lack of skills. planning unclear scope, poor project plan, unrealistic timeline and budget. process failure to redesign business processes, poor requirements definition. data incorrect legacy data, poor data cleansing and migration problems. technology wrong erp selection, excessive customization, weak integration and testing. support poor vendor assistance, weak communication and inadequate post-go-live support. 5.5 diagram — main causes of erp failure causes that can lead to erp implementation failure erp project failure management weak leadership poor project control people resistance · low involvement insufficient training planning unclear scope unrealistic schedule process poor process redesign data poor data quality technology wrong fit · weak integration erp failure usually results from a combination of management, people, planning, process, data and technology problems. 5.6 failure can occur at different stages stage examples of failure factors before implementation poor requirement definition, weak management support, wrong erp selection, unrealistic budget. during implementation insufficient resources, poor training, resistance to change, data migration problems, excessive customization, inadequate testing. after go-live insufficient user support, unresolved system issues, poor monitoring, weak maintenance and failure to review expected benefits. 5.7 practical example example: a manufacturing company's failed erp project a manufacturing company decides to implement erp to connect purchasing, inventory, production, sales and finance. management selects a very short implementation deadline. warehouse and production employees are not involved in requirement gathering. old stock records contain duplicate product codes, but the data is migrated without cleaning. employees receive very little training and continue using spreadsheets. the company skips realistic testing to meet the launch date. after go-live, orders and stock reports do not match, causing operational delays. why did it fail? the project had poor planning, weak user involvement, inaccurate data, insufficient training and inadequate testing. the example shows how several small failures can combine into a major erp problem. 5.8 how to reduce the risk of erp failure risk / cause preventive action lack of management support assign an executive sponsor and keep leadership involved. poor planning define scope, milestones, responsibilities and risks clearly. user resistance involve employees early and communicate the reason for change. insufficient training provide role-based training and practical exercises. bad data migration clean, validate and test data before migration. excessive customization prefer standard erp functionality where it meets business needs. inadequate testing test end-to-end workflows with real users before go-live. poor post-launch support monitor performance and provide a support team after go-live. 5.9 what is data? data means raw facts that have not yet been organized or interpreted. examples include customer id 1042, product quantity 20, invoice amount ₹15,000 and employee attendance of 8 days. what is information? information is data that has been processed, organized or interpreted so that it becomes meaningful and useful for a particular purpose. for example, “product a has only 5 units left, while average daily sales are 10 units” is information that can help a manager decide to reorder stock. raw data orders, sales, stock, employee records → processing sort, calculate, organize, compare → information useful reports for decisions figure 1 — the basic data-to-information process. what is an information system? an information system is an organized combination of people, procedures, data and technology that collects, processes, stores and distributes information to support the activities and decisions of an organization. element meaning erp example people users who enter, manage or use information salesperson, accountant, hr manager procedures rules and steps for handling work order approval and invoice process data facts used by the system customer, product, price and stock data hardware physical computing equipment servers, computers, scanners software programs that process data erp application and database software network connects users and systems office lan or secure internet connection remember: data is the raw input; information is the meaningful output. an information system uses people, procedures and technology to turn data into useful information. 2. why integrated management information is needed in an organization, departments are connected through business activities. a sales order can affect inventory, production, purchasing, delivery and finance. if each department keeps information separately, the organization may not have one consistent view of what is happening. integrated management information means that information generated or updated in one functional area can be shared with other relevant areas through a coordinated information system. in erp, this is commonly supported by connected modules and a shared database. problems created by isolated information data duplication: the same customer or product details may be entered in several departments. inconsistent records: sales may show one address while accounts or delivery records show another. delayed information: departments wait for emails, phone calls or manual reports. limited visibility: a manager cannot easily see the complete status of an order. repeated work: employees enter the same information more than once. slow decisions: reports must be collected and combined from separate systems. core idea: an enterprise needs information to move across departmental boundaries, not remain trapped inside individual departments. 3. traditional departmental information systems in a traditional arrangement, departments may use separate applications and databases designed for their own tasks. such systems can work locally, but sharing information across the organization becomes difficult. before erp — isolated departmental systems sales sales database finance accounts database inventory stock database hr employee database production production database purchasing supplier database separate records and applications can lead to duplicate entry and difficult reconciliation. example of the problem a customer places an order with the sales department. sales records the order in its own system. the inventory team may not see it immediately, so it cannot reserve stock. the finance team may need to enter customer and order details again before preparing an invoice. each department has only part of the picture. issue what may happen separate databases multiple versions of the same customer or product record manual transfer delay and possible typing errors different formats difficulty combining reports departmental focus managers cannot easily view the complete business process 4. integrated management information through erp erp brings major business functions together through integrated modules. the modules support different activities, but they exchange information and commonly work with a shared central database or coordinated data repository. after erp — integrated enterprise information erp system connected modules + shared information sales & distribution finance inventory human resources production purchasing figure 2 — departments use connected erp modules to share relevant information. how integration works a user enters or updates business data in the appropriate erp module. the system validates and records the transaction. relevant information becomes available to authorized connected modules. other departments use the updated information for their own activities. managers can generate reports using information from multiple functions. important clarification: integration does not mean every employee can see every record. access is controlled by roles and permissions. it means authorized users and modules can access the information required for their work. 5. how information flows across departments example: customer order to payment 1. sales enter customer order ↓ 2. inventory check and reserve stock ↓ 3. production / purchasing make or procure missing items ↓ 4. delivery pick, pack and ship order ↓ 5. finance create invoice and record payment figure 3 — a single order creates connected activities across the enterprise. when the order is entered, inventory can check availability. if stock is insufficient, production or purchasing can receive the required information. after dispatch, delivery details can be used by sales and finance. finance can prepare the invoice using the order and delivery records rather than re-entering all details from the beginning. exam tip: in a long answer, explain integration through one end-to-end example. it makes the relationship between departments easy to understand. 6. characteristics and components key characteristics common data source: departments rely on coordinated, shared business records. data entered once where practical: the same transaction details need not be repeatedly re-entered by every department. cross-functional integration: connected modules support processes that cross departmental boundaries. timely information: authorized users can access updated information without waiting for separate manual reports. consistent definitions: common codes and formats help reduce conflicting records. management reporting: information from multiple functions can be combined for analysis. controlled access: roles and permissions help protect sensitive information. common functional modules module information handled who uses it? sales customers, quotations, orders and deliveries sales team finance invoices, payments, expenses and accounts accountants and finance managers inventory stock quantity, location and movement store and warehouse team purchasing purchase requests, suppliers and purchase orders procurement team production production plans, material needs and output production managers human resources employee records, attendance and payroll hr team 7. benefits and limitations benefits better coordination: departments work with connected information. reduced duplicate entry: common data can be reused across modules. improved accuracy: fewer repeated manual transfers can reduce inconsistency. faster reporting: managers can combine information from different functions. better visibility: order, stock and payment status can be viewed across the process. improved decisions: timely and consistent information supports planning and control. process efficiency: connected workflows reduce unnecessary hand-offs. limitations and challenges implementation cost: software, infrastructure, migration and training require investment. data quality dependency: incorrect input can spread errors to connected processes. change management: employees need training and may resist new procedures. security responsibility: centralized information requires strong access control and protection. integration complexity: connecting older or external systems may require additional work. dependence on system availability: outages can affect several departments at once. therefore, integrated management information is valuable, but the benefits depend on correct implementation, reliable data, suitable controls and employee adoption. 8. practical business example imagine an electronics company that sells laptops through its website and physical stores. a customer orders a laptop online. the sales module records the order. the inventory module checks stock in the nearest warehouse. if the item is available, stock is reserved for that order. the delivery team receives the dispatch details. the finance module creates the invoice and records payment status. management can view sales, stock, pending deliveries and revenue through reports. without integrated information, each team might maintain a separate record and manually communicate updates. with erp, relevant information is shared across connected modules, making the order process easier to coordinate. 9. traditional vs integrated management information basis traditional isolated systems integrated erp information data storage separate departmental databases shared or coordinated enterprise data data entry may be repeated in many systems entered once and reused where possible information flow manual or limited between departments flows through connected modules consistency conflicting versions may occur common records improve consistency reporting requires collecting separate reports cross-functional reporting is easier visibility limited to departmental view broader enterprise-wide view 10. exam preparation important practice question — 5 marks what is integrated business model business processes and workflows how a business model is represented business modeling and erp implementation worked example: order-to-cash benefits and limitations business model vs data model exam preparation learning resources 1. meaning of business modeling business modeling is the process of creating a structured representation of how an organization works. it describes the organization as one integrated system and shows its major business functions, processes, people, resources, information flows, and the relationships among them. in simple words, business modeling is like drawing a map of a company. the map explains what the company does, who performs each activity, what information is needed, and how one activity affects another. a business model represents the organization as one connected system people processes resources information ↕ interconnections and dependencies ↕ purchasing production sales finance important: a business model in this erp context is not merely a way to earn revenue (such as b2b or b2c). it is a representation of the actual business structure and the way its functions and processes work together. simple example consider an electronics company. a customer places an order. sales checks product availability, inventory confirms stock, the warehouse dispatches the item, and finance generates an invoice and records payment. these are not isolated activities; together they form a connected business process. business modeling makes these connections visible. 2. why is business modeling needed? before implementing erp, an organization must understand how its business actually operates. installing software without understanding the existing processes can automate confusion rather than improve the business. understand the complete organization: provides a broad picture of departments, functions, and activities. identify relationships: shows how one department depends on another. find process gaps: exposes duplicate work, delays, unnecessary approvals, and missing information. support erp selection and configuration: helps determine which erp modules and workflows are required. improve coordination: clarifies the information each department must provide to others. support process improvement: helps redesign inefficient activities before or during erp implementation. provide a basis for the data model: the business processes and information requirements guide the design of the underlying data structure. remember: business modeling generally comes before configuring the erp system. first understand and represent the business; then decide how the erp system should support it. 3. main elements of a business model element meaning example people employees and other participants who perform or control activities. sales executive, store manager, accountant. processes related activities performed to achieve a business result. purchase-to-pay, order-to-cash. resources things used to perform business activities. raw materials, machines, money, facilities. information data required to plan, perform, monitor, and control activities. customer order, stock quantity, invoice. relationships connections and dependencies between functions and processes. production depends on inventory and demand information. goals business outcomes the organization wants to achieve. deliver orders on time and control cost. business processes are central a business process is a sequence or group of related activities that uses people, information, and other resources to produce a defined result. a process may cross several departments. 4. business processes and workflows a workflow describes the sequence in which tasks are performed, including the order of activities, the people responsible, and the decisions or conditions that move work forward. common enterprise processes procure-to-pay: identify a need → request purchase → approve → order from supplier → receive goods → verify invoice → pay supplier. order-to-cash: receive customer order → check stock → pick and dispatch → issue invoice → receive payment. plan-to-produce: forecast demand → plan production → check materials → manufacture → inspect finished goods. record-to-report: record transactions → post accounts → reconcile → prepare financial reports. these processes connect departments. for example, a sales order can affect inventory, warehouse operations, delivery planning, and accounting. 5. how is a business model represented? business models are often represented graphically so that people can understand the structure and flow of work. representation what it shows typical use flowchart steps, sequence, decisions, and direction of work. explaining an approval or order process. process flow diagram activities and how work moves between them. mapping purchasing or manufacturing. data flow diagram (dfd) how information moves between processes, data stores, and external entities. understanding information movement. system/context diagram the overall system and its interaction with external parties or subsystems. showing the enterprise boundary and major connections. example flowchart: simple purchase process need identified → purchase request → approval ↓ purchase order → receive goods → verify invoice → pay supplier the diagram is a simplified illustration. real organizations may include additional approvals, quality checks, supplier selection, and exception handling. 6. relationship between business modeling and erp erp software is designed to support and integrate business processes. business modeling helps an organization explain those processes before deciding how to configure the erp system. how business modeling supports erp implementation understand business goals → map current processes ↓ identify gaps and requirements → design / improve processes ↓ create business and data requirements → configure erp modules ↓ test and refine → operate and monitor current-state model (as-is): documents how work is performed today. future-state model (to-be): describes how work should operate after improvement and erp implementation. comparing as-is and to-be helps identify what must change in processes, roles, controls, and systems. erp should support the agreed business process; it should not be configured blindly. standardization and customization during erp implementation, an organization may adapt its process to standard erp practices or customize the software to preserve a special process. excessive customization can increase cost and complexity, so the business model helps the organization decide which differences are genuinely necessary. 7. worked example: order-to-cash in an electronics company suppose a customer orders a laptop from an electronics company. business modeling traces the whole process, not just the work of the sales department. step department activity information / result 1 sales register customer order. customer id, product, quantity, price. 2 inventory check available stock. available quantity and reservation. 3 warehouse pick, pack, and dispatch. dispatch details and shipment reference. 4 finance generate invoice. invoice amount and due date. 5 accounts record customer payment. payment status and accounting entry. what does the business model reveal? sales depends on inventory information; dispatch depends on a confirmed order and stock; finance depends on order and delivery information. the process crosses several departments, so coordination is essential. 8. benefits and limitations benefits gives a common understanding of how the organization operates. improves communication between departments. helps identify bottlenecks, duplicated tasks, and unnecessary steps. provides requirements for erp configuration and data design. supports process standardization and continuous improvement. clarifies responsibilities and information needs. limitations / challenges a model may become outdated when business processes change. incomplete input from employees can produce an inaccurate model. very complex diagrams may be difficult to understand. departments may disagree about the best process or ownership. a model alone does not improve operations; the organization must implement and monitor the changes. 9. business model vs data model basis business model data model main focus how the business works. what data is stored and how data items relate. describes functions, processes, people, resources, and dependencies. entities, attributes, relationships, tables, and constraints. example customer places order; warehouse dispatches product. customer, order, product, orderline, shipment records. purpose understand and improve business operations. organize information for storage, retrieval, and consistency. easy memory trick: business model = how work happens. data model = how information about that work is structured. 10. exam preparation pyq status: no direct ranchi supplied question-paper material. quick index meaning of integrated data model why erp needs an integrated data model how it works worked example: customer order main components characteristics of a good integrated data model benefits challenges and precautions integrated data model vs integrated database exam preparation learning resources 1. meaning of integrated data model an integrated data model is a unified representation of the data used throughout an organization. it describes the important business entities, their attributes, and the relationships among them, so that different departments can work with consistent and connected information. in simple words, it is a common blueprint that explains what information the company keeps and how different pieces of information are related. sales, inventory, purchasing, production, and finance may use the same business information instead of maintaining disconnected versions of it. one connected view of enterprise information sales inventory purchasing finance ↕ shared definitions and connected data ↕ integrated enterprise data model ↕ supports connected erp modules ↕ customer product order invoice important distinction: an integrated data model is the logical blueprint of enterprise data. it is not simply a drawing of one database, nor does the term always require every byte of data to be physically stored in one database. modern architectures can provide an integrated view across connected data stores as well. 2. why does erp need an integrated data model? before erp, departments may maintain separate files or databases. the same customer or product can be recorded more than once, sometimes with different spellings, codes, addresses, or balances. this creates inconsistency and makes organization-wide reporting difficult. without integration with an integrated data model each department may maintain its own copy of customer information. departments use a consistent customer definition and shared records. stock figures may differ between sales and warehouse systems. stock information is connected to the same product and inventory concepts. information must be re-entered between systems. data captured in one process can be reused by other authorized processes. reports may disagree because definitions differ. common definitions improve consistency in reporting. erp requires information integration and process automation. its data model should represent the organization as a whole rather than only one department. remember: the purpose is not merely to collect more data. it is to make enterprise data consistent, related, reusable, and available to authorized business functions. 3. how does an integrated data model work? identify business entities: determine the important things about which the organization stores information, such as customer, supplier, product, employee, order, and invoice. define attributes: specify the details recorded for each entity. for example, a customer may have customer_id, name, address, and contact_number. define relationships: explain how entities connect. for example, one customer can place many orders. use common definitions: departments agree on meanings, identifiers, formats, and rules. connect erp processes and modules: transactions entered through one process can be used by other connected modules, subject to access permissions. maintain data quality: validation, ownership, and controlled updates help keep information accurate. conceptual path from real business to erp data real-world business customers, products, orders → business model processes and relationships ↓ integrated data model entities, attributes, relationships → database structures tables, fields, keys ↓ erp programs and screens transactions and reports the business model describes how the organization works. the integrated data model describes the information needed to represent that business. the database implements the data structures, while erp programs allow users to perform tasks with that information. 4. worked example: customer places an order suppose a customer orders two laptops. different departments need different parts of the same transaction, but their information must remain connected. entity example attributes why it is needed customer customer_id, name, address identifies who placed the order. product product_id, description, unit_price identifies what is being sold. order order_id, customer_id, order_date, status records the customer's request. order_line order_id, product_id, quantity, agreed_price records each product and quantity in an order. inventory product_id, warehouse_id, available_qty tracks stock for the product. invoice invoice_id, order_id, amount, due_date records the amount billed. payment payment_id, invoice_id, amount, payment_date records settlement of the invoice. simplified entity relationship view customer customer_id (pk) 1 → many order order_id (pk) customer_id (fk) 1 → many order_line order_id (fk) product_id (fk) quantity many → 1 product product_id (pk) order 1 → 1 / many invoice 1 → many payment pk means primary key: a field (or set of fields) that uniquely identifies a record. fk means foreign key: a field that refers to a record in another table and helps establish a relationship. when sales creates the order, inventory can use its product and quantity details to check or reserve stock. the warehouse can use the order for dispatch, and finance can use the order and delivery information to prepare an invoice. this reduces repeated data entry and helps departments work from consistent records. note: the diagram is a simplified learning example. actual erp products have more entities, status rules, taxes, pricing conditions, warehouses, and accounting controls. 5. main components of an integrated data model component meaning example entity a business object or concept about which data is stored. customer, product, supplier. attribute a property or detail of an entity. customer_name, product_price. relationship a connection between entities. customer places order. identifier / key a field used to identify a record or link records. customer_id, order_id. constraint / business rule a condition that data must satisfy. order quantity must be positive. common definitions agreed meanings, formats, and naming rules. one standard meaning for product_id. three levels of data modeling conceptual data model: high-level view of the main business entities and their relationships; focuses on what the business needs to represent. logical data model: adds more detail such as attributes, keys, and relationship rules without tying the model to a particular database product. physical data model: describes how the design is implemented in a specific database, such as tables, columns, data types, indexes, and constraints. memory trick: conceptual = what things exist. logical = how they are structured and related. physical = how the database stores them. 6. characteristics of a good integrated data model enterprise-wide: represents data required across the organization, not just one isolated department. consistent: uses common definitions, formats, and identifiers. connected: shows meaningful relationships among business entities. minimizes unnecessary duplication: avoids maintaining conflicting copies of the same business facts where practical. supports business processes: provides information needed for transactions and process automation. accurate and governed: defines ownership, validation, and update responsibilities. secure: allows users to access information according to their roles and responsibilities. adaptable: can accommodate legitimate changes in business requirements. 7. benefits of an integrated data model reduced data redundancy: helps avoid unnecessary repeated storage of the same business information. improved data consistency: shared definitions reduce conflicting values across departments. better information sharing: authorized employees can access information relevant to their work. timely information: connected processes can use updated transaction information without waiting for manual consolidation. improved reporting: common data definitions make organization-wide reports more dependable. process automation: data captured in one step can support later steps in a business process. better coordination: departments can work with connected information rather than isolated records. supports decision-making: managers can obtain a more complete view of business operations. 8. challenges and precautions challenge explanation good practice poor data quality incorrect or incomplete legacy data can enter the new system. clean, validate, and deduplicate data before migration. different definitions departments may use the same word with different meanings. agree on a data dictionary and common standards. legacy system integration older systems may use different formats and identifiers. map fields and define controlled transformation rules. access and privacy not every employee should see every record. apply role-based access and audit controls. complexity and change business requirements and structures evolve. govern changes and maintain model documentation. important caution: an integrated model does not mean every employee can view or edit every item of data. integration and access control are separate concerns. information should be shared with authorized users according to business need. 9. integrated data model vs integrated database basis integrated data model integrated database meaning a logical description or blueprint of enterprise data and its relationships. a database implementation that stores and manages connected data. focus entities, attributes, relationships, definitions, and rules. actual storage, retrieval, transactions, and database operations. level design / representation. implementation / technology. example customer places many orders. customer and order tables linked by customer_id. many erp systems use a common database shared by integrated modules. however, the broader idea of an integrated enterprise data model is about a consistent view and structure of enterprise information; in modern environments, connected data may also be integrated across multiple systems or stores. 10. exam preparation pyq status: no direct ranchi university previous-year question on “integrated data model” was verified in the supplied question-paper
