bpr and erp practical example benefits and limitations bpr vs continuous improvement exam preparation 1. meaning and definition of bpr business process reengineering (bpr) is the fundamental rethinking and radical redesign of an organization's business processes to achieve major improvements in important performance measures such as cost, quality, service and speed. in simple words, bpr means asking: “if we were designing this work today, knowing what we know now, how should we perform it?” instead of making small changes to an inefficient process, an organization may redesign the complete process from beginning to end. remember: bpr is not merely computerizing an old process. it is redesigning the process itself; technology such as erp can then support the improved process. what is a business process? a business process is a connected set of activities that takes inputs and produces a defined result for a customer or another part of the organization. input customer order / data → activities verify, approve, fulfil → output delivered order 2. why is bpr needed? over time, organizations often add approvals, forms, hand-offs and separate systems to existing workflows. these additions may make work slow, costly and difficult to coordinate. bpr is considered when the existing process cannot meet business requirements. long processing time: work waits between departments or approval stages. high operating cost: repeated work, paper handling and unnecessary checks consume resources. duplicate data entry: the same information is entered into multiple systems, increasing errors. poor customer service: customers face delays and receive inconsistent updates. departmental silos: teams optimize their own tasks but the complete end-to-end process performs poorly. changing competition and technology: old procedures may not support new customer expectations or business models. 3. main features and principles of bpr feature / principle meaning fundamental rethinking question the assumptions behind the existing process instead of accepting them automatically. radical redesign rebuild the workflow when necessary rather than only making minor adjustments. process orientation focus on the complete process and its outcome, not only individual departments or tasks. customer focus design work around the value and service the customer needs. remove non-value-adding work eliminate unnecessary waiting, repeated approvals, duplicate entry and avoidable hand-offs. cross-functional teamwork involve employees and managers from all departments participating in the process. use information technology use shared data, automation and integrated systems to enable the redesigned workflow. measure results compare performance using time, cost, quality, error rate and customer satisfaction. 4. steps in the bpr process a practical bpr initiative normally follows these stages. organizations may repeat stages as they learn from implementation. 1. identify process choose a process that has significant performance problems or strategic importance. ↓ 2. study the current process (as-is) map activities, hand-offs, roles, systems, delays and costs. ↓ 3. set objectives define measurable targets such as reducing order time or errors. ↓ 4. redesign the process (to-be) remove unnecessary steps, combine work, clarify responsibilities and use technology appropriately. ↓ 5. implement the redesigned process configure systems, assign roles, train employees and communicate the change. ↓ 6. monitor and improve measure results against targets and correct problems. as-is and to-be as-is model to-be model shows how the process works today. shows how the redesigned process should work. helps locate delays, duplication and bottlenecks. shows the proposed improvements and new workflow. describes the current state. describes the desired future state. 5. relationship between bpr and erp bpr and erp are related but they are not the same thing. bpr focuses on redesigning business processes. erp is an integrated software system that supports business activities using shared information and connected modules. bpr examines how work should be performed across the organization. erp provides the integrated applications and data needed to support those workflows. bpr can help an organization identify inefficient legacy practices before configuring erp. erp implementation may also reveal opportunities for further process redesign. existing process as-is analysis → bpr redesign workflow → erp configuration support to-be process → monitor measure results important distinction: bpr does not automatically mean purchasing erp software. an organization may redesign a process without implementing a new erp system. similarly, installing erp without examining inefficient processes may simply automate existing problems. 6. practical example: processing a customer order before bpr — traditional process sales receives an order and records it in a spreadsheet. sales emails the warehouse to check stock. warehouse replies later, sometimes after manually checking records. finance separately verifies the customer's payment status. sales prepares another document for dispatch. customer receives an update only after several manual follow-ups. problems: repeated data entry, waiting between departments, delayed decisions and limited visibility. after bpr — redesigned process supported by erp sales enters the order once into the erp system. the system makes order information available to relevant departments. inventory availability and customer credit status can be checked using shared data and configured business rules. once required checks are satisfied, fulfilment and invoicing activities proceed through the redesigned workflow. authorized staff and the customer can receive timely status information. result sought: fewer hand-offs, less duplicate entry, faster processing and better visibility. actual results depend on process design, data quality, system configuration and employee adoption. 7. benefits and limitations of bpr benefits possible limitations / risks reduced process time and delays redesign can be expensive and time-consuming lower operating costs and less duplication employees may resist major changes improved quality and fewer errors poor planning can interrupt operations better customer service requires training and strong communication clearer responsibility across departments may require changes to roles and organizational structure better use of erp and information technology technology alone cannot guarantee successful redesign 8. bpr vs continuous process improvement basis bpr continuous improvement nature fundamental or radical redesign small, ongoing improvements scope may transform an end-to-end process often improves existing activities change can be substantial and disruptive usually gradual purpose achieve major performance improvement maintain and steadily improve performance 9. exam preparation very short answer — practice expand bpr. define a business process. what is meant by as-is process? what is meant by to-be process? short business example. suggested structure for a 15-mark answer introduction and definition of bpr. need and objectives of bpr. main features or principles. steps with a labelled process diagram. relationship between bpr and erp. benefits, limitations and conclusion. 10. quick self-check 1. is bpr only the installation of new software? no. bpr redesigns business processes. software may support the redesigned process. 2. what is the difference between as-is and to-be? as-is describes the current process; to-be describes the desired redesigned process. 3. why should bpr involve multiple departments? because an end-to-end process often crosses departmental boundaries. cross-functional involvement helps reveal hand-offs and design a coordinated workflow. 4. does every bpr project require erp? no. bpr can be performed independently. erp is one possible technology platform for supporting redesigned processes. 11. learning resources geeksforgeeks — introduction to business combination of people, procedures, data and technology that collects and processes data and supplies useful information to managers for planning, controlling, coordinating and decision-making. in simple language, an mis converts business data into meaningful reports so that managers can understand what is happening in an organization and decide what action should be taken. exam-ready definition: a management information system is an integrated system that collects, processes, stores and distributes relevant information to support the operations, management and decision-making functions of an organization. understand the three words management: planning work, organizing resources, directing employees and controlling performance. information: processed and organized data that is useful for a particular purpose or decision. system: interrelated components working together to achieve a common objective. thus, mis is not merely a computer or a software application. it includes the people who use information, the procedures followed, the data collected and the technology used to process and communicate it. 2. data, information and knowledge these terms are connected, but they do not mean the same thing. data raw facts → processing sorting, calculating, summarising → information meaningful result → knowledge understanding and experience term meaning example data raw, unprocessed facts. daily sales: ₹8,000, ₹10,000, ₹7,000. information data arranged and interpreted to give meaning. total sales for three days = ₹25,000. knowledge understanding gained by interpreting information and experience. sales are lower on one day; the manager investigates why. remember: data is the input; information is the useful output. mis mainly transforms organizational data into information that managers can use. 3. objectives and functions of mis the main objective of mis is to provide the right information to the right person, in the right form, at the right time, so that organizational work and decisions can be improved. main objectives support decision-making: supply facts and reports that help managers choose an appropriate course of action. improve planning: provide past and current information for setting targets, preparing budgets and allocating resources. support control: compare actual performance with plans and highlight deviations. improve coordination: share consistent information among departments such as finance, sales, production and hr. increase efficiency: reduce repetitive manual reporting and unnecessary duplication of data. provide timely reports: make relevant information available when managers need it. maintain information: store organizational records in an organized and retrievable form. monitor performance: help managers track sales, costs, inventory, productivity and other measures. functions of mis collect data from internal and, where required, external sources. validate, classify, calculate, summarize and store data. generate routine, periodic, exception and on-demand reports. distribute information to authorized users. provide feedback that helps managers monitor and improve operations. 4. components of mis a common way to explain an information system is through five connected components. all five are needed for a useful mis. people managers, employees, it staff procedures rules and steps data business records software applications hardware computers, servers, devices component role example in a retail company hardware physical devices used to input, process, store and display data. pos terminal, server, barcode scanner. software programs that process data and generate reports. billing and inventory application. data facts stored and processed by the system. products, prices, sales and stock records. people users and specialists who operate and manage the system. cashier, store manager, database administrator. procedures instructions and rules for using the system correctly. steps for recording a sale and approving a stock adjustment. important: communication networks are also a major part of modern information-system infrastructure because they connect users, devices, databases and locations. 5. how mis works mis generally follows an input–processing–storage–output–feedback cycle. input sales, purchases, stock, payroll data ↓ processing validate, classify, calculate and summarize ↓ database / storage organized business records ↓ output reports, summaries, alerts and dashboards ↓ managerial action plan, decide and control ↺ feedback and updated data step-by-step explanation input: data enters from business activities, forms, transactions, sensors or other systems. processing: the system checks, sorts, calculates and summarizes the data. storage: records are stored so they can be retrieved and used later. output: the system produces information such as a monthly sales report or low-stock report. decision and action: a manager studies the report and takes action. feedback: the result of the action and new business transactions become fresh data for the system. 6. mis and levels of management different managers need different types of information. operational managers focus on daily activities, middle managers focus on departmental performance and senior managers focus on long-term direction. top management strategic level • long-term goals and policy ↑ summarized trends and key indicators middle management tactical level • budgets, targets and departmental control ↑ periodic reports and performance summaries operational management operational level • daily transactions and activities ↑ detailed transaction records business operations sales, purchase, production, payroll, inventory level typical information example operational detailed, current and frequent information. today's orders, pending dispatches and stock balances. tactical / middle periodic summaries and comparisons. monthly sales by region and interactive computer-based information system that helps managers analyse data, compare alternatives and make decisions, especially when a problem is complex, changing or not fully structured. in simple language, dss helps a manager answer questions such as: what may happen if prices are reduced? which supplier is the best choice? how much stock should we maintain? which business option gives the best result? exam-ready definition: a decision support system is an interactive, computer-based system that uses data and analytical models to support managerial decision-making in semi-structured and unstructured situations. important: dss supports the decision-maker; it does not automatically replace the manager's judgement or take responsibility for the final decision. understand the words decision: selecting one course of action from two or more alternatives. support: providing relevant data, analysis, comparisons and possible outcomes. system: a coordinated combination of data, software, models, procedures and users. 2. why is dss needed? managers regularly face decisions where information is incomplete, many factors are involved, or the result of each option is uncertain. a routine report may show what happened, but a manager may also need to explore what could happen under different conditions. business environments change quickly. managers must compare several alternatives. some decisions are new and do not have a fixed procedure. large volumes of data are difficult to analyse manually. managers need to understand the likely impact of changing price, demand, cost, capacity or supply. business problem / decision to be made ↓ dss analyses data and applies models ↓ alternative options and likely outcomes ↓ manager evaluates options and chooses an action 3. types of managerial decisions a common way to understand dss is to classify decisions according to how clearly the problem and solution procedure are defined. decision type meaning example typical support structured routine and repetitive; clear rules or procedures exist. reordering stock when it reaches a fixed reorder level. tps and predefined rules; dss may assist with analysis. semi-structured some parts can be handled by rules, but human judgement is also needed. choosing a supplier using price, quality, delivery and reliability. dss is particularly useful. unstructured new or complex problem with no fixed procedure or single obvious answer. entering a new market or deciding a long-term business strategy. dss can organise evidence and compare scenarios; senior judgement remains important. remember: dss is especially associated with semi-structured and unstructured decisions, although it can also support structured decisions. 4. characteristics and capabilities of dss interactive: users can ask questions, change inputs and explore results. flexible: it can support different problems and changing assumptions. data-driven: it uses relevant internal and external data. model-driven: it applies mathematical, statistical, financial or simulation models. supports multiple alternatives: it compares possible courses of action. what-if analysis: it shows how results may change when assumptions change. timely support: it helps managers analyse information when a decision is required. user-oriented: results are presented through reports, tables, charts or dashboards. human judgement: the manager interprets results and makes the final decision. what-if analysis: a simple example a company currently sells 1,000 units at ₹500 each. a manager wants to test what may happen if the selling price is reduced to ₹475 and expected sales increase to 1,100 units. a dss can calculate and compare the revenue under both assumptions. scenario units price revenue current 1,000 ₹500 ₹5,00,000 proposed 1,100 ₹475 ₹5,22,500 the proposed scenario gives ₹22,500 more revenue in this simplified example. however, revenue is not profit: the manager must also consider costs, capacity, customer response and other factors. 5. components of dss traditional dss explanations commonly describe three core components. modern systems may include additional communication, knowledge and analytics capabilities. database / dbms stores and manages relevant internal and external data ↘ model base / mbms stores and manages analytical models ↙ dialogue / user interface allows the user to enter questions and view results ↓ manager / decision-maker interprets results and selects an action 1. database and database management system (dbms) stores data required for analysis. data may come from internal sources such as sales, inventory and finance, and external sources such as market or supplier information. dbms helps store, retrieve, organise and manage the data. 2. model base and model base management system (mbms) contains models used to analyse a decision problem. examples include forecasting, optimisation, statistical, financial and simulation models. mbms helps select, store and use the appropriate model. 3. dialogue generation and management system (dgms) / user interface provides the communication link between the user and dss. allows the manager to enter assumptions, select models and request analysis. displays results using reports, tables, charts and dashboards. exam tip: if asked for the traditional three components, write database + model base + dialogue/user interface. explain the function of each and draw the diagram. 6. how does dss work? identify the problem: the manager defines the decision that must be made. collect data: relevant internal and external data are gathered. select a model: a suitable analytical model is chosen. enter assumptions: the user provides values or constraints to test. analyse alternatives: dss calculates or simulates possible outcomes. compare results: options are evaluated using relevant criteria. make the decision: the manager selects an action. review the outcome: actual results can be compared with expectations to improve future decisions. 1. identify decision problem ↓ 2. collect and prepare data ↓ 3. select model and enter assumptions ↓ 4. analyse alternatives / run scenarios ↓ 5. present results to manager ↓ 6. manager decides and reviews outcome 7. types of dss one widely used classification groups dss according to the main resource or capability driving the support. these categories can overlap in real systems. type meaning example data-driven dss focuses on accessing and analysing large amounts of data. sales dashboard that filters sales by region, product and month. model-driven dss focuses on mathematical, statistical, financial or simulation models. model that finds a low-cost production schedule. knowledge-driven dss uses rules, facts or specialised knowledge to suggest actions. system that recommends a credit decision based on defined rules. document-driven dss searches and analyses documents and unstructured information. system that retrieves product specifications and policy documents. communication-driven dss supports collaboration and group decision-making. collaborative platform for a team comparing project proposals. 8. models and analytical techniques used in dss what-if analysis: changes input values to see how an outcome may change. sensitivity analysis: examines how strongly the result responds to changes in one or more variables. goal-seeking analysis: starts with a desired result and works backwards to find the input needed. optimisation: finds the best solution under stated objectives and constraints. simulation: imitates a real process to study possible outcomes under different conditions. forecasting: estimates future values using historical data and suitable methods. difference to remember: what-if asks “what happens if i change this input?” goal-seeking asks “what input is required to reach this target?” sensitivity analysis measures how much the output changes as assumptions vary. 9. dss vs mis basis mis dss budget. relationship: mis and dss are complementary. mis can supply reliable reports and data; dss can use those data with analytical models to explore alternatives and support decisions. 10. integrates and manages business processes and transaction data; dss primarily analyses information to support decisions. an erp product may include analytics or decision-support features, but the erp and eis are not the same. erp primarily integrates business processes and transaction data; eis presents selected high-level information for executive monitoring and strategic decision support. 10. practical business example imagine a retail company operating stores in several cities. the ceo wants to understand whether the business is meeting its annual growth target. eis display illustrative result executive interpretation total revenue ₹48 crore against ₹52 crore target revenue is below target region-wise sales east region is 15% below target investigate regional performance product category electronics sales declining review demand and product strategy customer retention retention has fallen by 4 percentage points investigate customer experience the ceo can drill down into the east region, examine product categories and compare monthly trends. the eis makes the important pattern visible; management still needs to investigate causes and decide the appropriate action. 11. benefits and limitations of eis benefits provides quick access to important organisational information. helps executives monitor strategic goals and kpis. combines information from different departments. highlights trends, exceptions and potential problems. reduces the effort required to prepare high-level summaries manually. supports more informed strategic discussions and planning. drill-down helps executives investigate areas of concern. limitations data quality: inaccurate source data can produce misleading dashboards. implementation cost: integration, software, infrastructure and maintenance can be expensive. information overload: too many indicators can distract executives from critical issues. dependence on systems: delayed or unavailable source systems can affect information freshness. security: sensitive strategic and financial information must be protected. human judgement: a dashboard cannot fully understand every business context or replace executive experience. 12. exam preparation pyq status: the following are syllabus-based practice questions. they are not presented as confirmed ranchi university previous-year questions. very move from a summary to detailed information? name two types of information that eis may combine. how can erp provide data to eis? does eis make the final strategic decision for the executive? answers meaning and definition of olap why olap is needed characteristics olap data cube olap operations types of olap olap architecture and working olap vs oltp relationship between olap, data warehouse and erp practical example benefits and limitations exam preparation self-check learning resources 1. meaning and definition of olap olap stands for online analytical processing . it is a technology used to analyse large amounts of business data from different perspectives. it helps users examine trends, compare performance and discover patterns for decision-making. in simple language, olap lets a manager ask analytical questions about business data, such as: which product generated the highest sales? which region performed best? how did sales change from one quarter to another? exam-ready definition: online analytical processing (olap) is a data-analysis approach that enables users to perform multidimensional analysis of large volumes of data quickly to support reporting, trend analysis and business decision-making. remember: olap is mainly for analysis. it is different from systems that record day-to-day transactions, such as order entry and billing systems. 2. why is olap needed? organisations generate large amounts of data through sales, finance, inventory, production and customer activities. managers need to analyse data across dimensions such as time, product, region and customer. ordinary transaction reports may not easily answer complex comparative questions. olap helps identify trends, exceptions and relationships in historical data. it supports planning, performance evaluation and informed business decisions. business data sales • finance • inventory • production ↓ data warehouse / analytical data store organised historical and integrated data ↓ olap analysis time • product • region • customer ↓ reports and insights trends • comparisons • patterns 3. characteristics of olap multidimensional view: data can be analysed across several dimensions, such as product, location and time. fast analytical queries: designed to retrieve summaries and comparisons efficiently. historical analysis: often works with accumulated data over months or years. interactive analysis: users can change dimensions and levels of detail to explore data. aggregation: combines detailed values into totals, averages and other summaries. complex calculations: supports comparisons, ratios, growth rates and other analytical measures. read-intensive use: typically performs many analytical reads rather than frequent transaction updates. 4. understanding the olap data cube an olap cube is a way of organising data for analysis across multiple dimensions. despite the name, a cube can contain more than three dimensions. for example, a retail company may analyse sales using three dimensions: time , product and region . the numerical value being analysed is called a measure , such as sales amount or quantity sold. dimensions time: month / quarter / year product: item / category region: city / state / country ↓ combined for analysis ↓ measure: sales amount (₹) question: what were the sales of laptops in ranchi during q1? term meaning example dimension a perspective or category used to analyse data time, product, region measure a numeric value being analysed sales amount, units sold hierarchy levels within a dimension year → quarter → month cell a value at the intersection of dimension members sales for a product in a region in a month 5. main olap operations olap operations allow users to view the same data in different ways and at different levels of detail. 5.1 roll-up roll-up summarises data by moving from a lower level of detail to a higher level in a hierarchy. example: daily sales are combined into monthly sales, then quarterly sales. daily sales → monthly sales → quarterly sales → yearly sales more detail ───────────────→ more summary 5.2 drill-down drill-down is the opposite of roll-up. it moves from summarised data to more detailed data. example: yearly sales → quarterly sales → monthly sales → daily sales. yearly sales → quarterly sales → monthly sales → daily sales summary ─────────────────→ more detail 5.3 slice slice selects one value of a dimension to create a smaller view. example: show sales only for the year 2026, while retaining product and region analysis. 5.4 dice dice selects a range or set of values from multiple dimensions. example: analyse laptops and phones, in jharkhand and bihar, during january to march. 5.5 pivot (rotate) pivot changes the orientation of a report to view the same data from another arrangement. example: swap rows and columns so that regions appear as columns and products as rows. operation what it does easy example roll-up summarises / moves upward month to year drill-down shows more detail year to month slice fixes one dimension value only year 2026 dice selects a sub-cube across dimensions selected products, regions and months pivot rotates the view swap rows and columns 6. types of olap 6.1 molap – multidimensional olap molap stores or organises data in multidimensional structures, often using precomputed summaries. it can provide fast query responses for supported analyses, but cube processing and storage can require additional resources. 6.2 rolap – relational olap rolap uses relational databases and tables to store data. analytical queries are translated into database queries, commonly sql. it can work with large volumes of relational data, though query performance depends on database design and optimisation. 6.3 holap – hybrid olap holap combines features of molap and rolap. it may keep summarised data in multidimensional structures and detailed data in relational tables, aiming to balance query speed and scalability. type data organisation general strength consideration molap multidimensional structures / cubes fast access to prepared summaries cube processing and storage overhead rolap relational tables works with large relational datasets query speed depends on sql and database optimisation holap combination of both balances summaries and detailed data architecture can be more complex 7. olap architecture and working operational data sources erp • crm • sales • finance databases ↓ etl process extract → transform → load ↓ data warehouse / data mart integrated historical data ↓ olap server / analytical engine cube processing • aggregation • query handling ↓ front-end analysis tools reports • dashboards • pivot tables ↓ business user / manager data collection: data is obtained from operational systems such as erp, sales and finance applications. etl: data is extracted, transformed into a consistent format and loaded into an analytical store. data organisation: data is organised into dimensions, measures and hierarchies. olap processing: the analytical engine handles queries, aggregations and requested views. presentation: results are shown through reports, charts, dashboards or pivot tables. analysis: users compare results, investigate patterns and use findings in decisions. important terms: a data warehouse stores integrated data for analysis. olap is a way to analyse that data. etl means extract, transform and load. 8. olap vs oltp oltp stands for online transaction processing. oltp systems handle routine business transactions, while olap systems analyse data to support business understanding and decisions. basis oltp olap main purpose record and process daily transactions analyse business data typical users clerks, operational staff, applications managers, analysts, decision-makers data current, detailed transaction data often historical, integrated and summarised data operations insert, update, delete and retrieve records complex queries, aggregation and comparison queries usually short and predefined often complex and exploratory design focus fast and reliable transaction processing fast analytical retrieval example record a customer's purchase compare five years of regional sales remember for exams: oltp runs the business; olap analyses the business. 9. relationship between olap, data warehouse and erp erp systems capture and integrate day-to-day business transactions across departments. a data warehouse can collect selected data from erp and other systems, preserve historical information and prepare it for analysis. olap tools then analyse this organised data across dimensions. erp and other operational systems record daily business transactions ↓ etl and data integration ↓ data warehouse stores integrated historical data ↓ olap multidimensional analysis and summaries ↓ managers and analysts reports • trends • business decisions do not confuse them: erp is primarily used to integrate and run business processes; a data warehouse organises data for analysis; olap provides analytical operations over that data. they can work together but are not interchangeable terms. 10. practical business example imagine a retail company that sells laptops and mobile phones in ranchi, patna and kolkata. management wants to compare sales by product, region and quarter. question olap operation / analysis what were total sales in 2026? roll-up across time show only sales in ranchi slice by region compare laptops and phones in two cities during q1 dice across product, region and time find which month caused a quarterly decline drill-down from quarter to month display regions as columns instead of rows pivot the report by exploring these views, managers can identify which products and locations are contributing to growth or decline. olap presents the analysis; managers interpret the findings and decide what to do. 11. benefits and limitations of olap benefits supports multidimensional analysis of business data. makes comparison across time, products and regions easier. helps identify trends, patterns and unusual results. provides interactive analysis through roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice and pivot. supports planning, budgeting and performance evaluation. can reduce repeated manual preparation of analytical reports. limitations implementation cost: data warehouse, olap tools and infrastructure may be expensive. data preparation: integration, cleansing and loading data require time and effort. data quality: incorrect or inconsistent source data can lead to misleading analysis. complexity: cube design, dimensions and measures require careful planning. maintenance: data and analytical structures must be refreshed and maintained. not transaction processing: olap is not intended to replace operational transaction systems. 12. exam preparation pyq status: these are syllabus-based practice questions. they are not presented as confirmed ranchi university previous-year questions. very short-answer practice (1 mark) what is the full form of olap? what is an olap cube? define a dimension in olap. what is roll-up? what is the full form of rolap? short-answer practice (5 marks) explain the meaning and characteristics of olap. describe the five major olap operations with examples. differentiate between molap, rolap and holap. explain the architecture and working of olap. differentiate between olap and oltp. long-answer practice (15 marks) define olap and explain its characteristics, data cube and major operations with suitable examples. explain the types of olap and describe its architecture and working with a neat diagram. compare olap and oltp. explain how erp, a data warehouse and olap work together. suggested structure for a 15-mark answer write the full form and definition of olap. explain why multidimensional analysis is required. describe dimensions, measures and the data cube. explain roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice and pivot with examples. discuss olap types and architecture, then conclude with benefits and limitations. 13. self-check which olap operation summarises data from month to year? which operation moves from a summary to more detailed data? which operation selects one value of a dimension? name the three common types of olap. what is the main difference between olap and oltp? answers roll-up. drill-down. slice. molap, rolap and holap. olap analyses data; oltp processes routine transactions. 14. learning resources geeksforgeeks — online analytical processing (olap) (concepts and olap operations). tutorialspoint — olap in data warehousing (olap concepts and types). microsoft learn — olap and multidimensional models (technical reference). youtube learning links these are channel-scoped youtube search links, not individually what is a supply chain? need and objectives of scm main activities and process three flows in a supply chain scm and erp relationship scm systems and technology benefits and challenges practical example scm vs logistics exam preparation self-check learning resources 1. meaning and definition of scm supply chain management (scm) is the coordination and management of all activities involved in sourcing raw materials, converting them into finished products, storing them, and delivering them to customers. it manages the movement of products, information and money among suppliers, manufacturers, warehouses, distributors, retailers and customers. simple meaning: scm makes sure that the right product reaches the right customer, in the right quantity, at the right place and time, while controlling the total cost. why the word “management” matters a supply chain is not just transportation. scm plans and coordinates the whole network so that one organisation's decisions do not create unnecessary cost or delay for another. 2. what is a supply chain? a supply chain is the connected network of organisations, people, activities, resources and technology involved in making and delivering a product or service. basic supply chain flow raw-material supplier → manufacturer → warehouse / distributor → retailer → customer materials generally move towards the customer; demand information and payments also travel through the network. participants in a supply chain participant role example supplier provides raw materials or components steel, fabric or chip supplier manufacturer converts inputs into finished goods car or phone factory warehouse stores goods until they are needed regional distribution centre distributor moves products in bulk to sales channels fmcg distributor retailer sells products to final customers shop or online store customer creates demand and receives the product end user important: a supply chain can be short or long. a service organisation also has a supply chain, even if its output is not a physical product. 3. need and objectives of scm reduce total cost: control purchasing, production, storage and transportation costs. improve customer service: deliver orders accurately and on time. maintain suitable inventory: avoid both stockouts and excessive stock. coordinate partners: share reliable plans and information across organisations. improve responsiveness: react faster to changes in demand or supply. improve quality: manage supplier quality and production consistency. increase visibility: understand where orders, materials and products are in the chain. exam point: the central objective is to satisfy customer demand efficiently while optimising the performance and total cost of the entire supply chain—not merely one department. 4. main activities and process of scm a commonly used way to understand scm is through five connected activities: plan, source, make, deliver and return. scm process cycle 1. plan forecast demand, capacity and inventory 2. source select suppliers and procure materials 3. make schedule and manufacture products 4. deliver store, process orders and transport goods 5. return handle returns, repairs and recycling explanation of each activity activity what happens? example plan estimate customer demand and decide resources, production and stock levels. forecasting festival-season demand. source identify suppliers, negotiate, purchase and receive materials. buying screens and batteries for phones. make convert materials into finished products and check quality. assembling and testing a phone. deliver manage orders, packaging, warehouses, transport and delivery. sending phones to retail stores. return manage defective products, customer returns, repairs and reverse movement. collecting a faulty phone for replacement. 5. three important flows in scm supply chains coordinate three major flows. these flows move in different directions and must be connected. material / product flow supplier → manufacturer → distributor → customer information flow customer demand, forecasts and order status move across partners financial flow invoices, payments and credit generally move back through the chain flow meaning example material flow movement of raw materials, components, work-in-progress and finished goods. components shipped to a factory. information flow sharing demand, orders, forecasts, inventory and delivery status. a retailer shares weekly sales data. financial flow movement of money and financial documents. buyer pays supplier after receiving goods. remember: poor information sharing can cause overproduction, excess inventory or shortages—even when transportation and factories work properly. 6. relationship between scm and erp erp (enterprise resource planning) integrates information and processes within an organisation. scm coordinates supply-chain activities across the organisation and its external partners. erp supporting internal operations and scm coordination erp system inside the organisation purchasing inventory production finance sales ↕ shared operational information scm network suppliers ↔ manufacturer ↔ warehouses ↔ distributors ↔ customers how erp supports scm purchasing data helps procurement teams manage supplier orders. inventory records show available stock and material requirements. production plans help estimate when materials are required. sales orders and forecasts provide information about customer demand. finance records support supplier invoices, payments and cost analysis. erp and scm are related but not identical. erp commonly provides integrated internal business data; scm extends coordination to the wider supply network. modern erp suites may include scm capabilities or connect to dedicated scm applications. 7. scm systems and technology technology / system use in scm demand forecasting estimates future customer demand using sales history and other information. inventory management tracks stock, reorder levels and replenishment. warehouse management system (wms) controls receiving, storage, picking, packing and dispatch. transportation management system (tms) supports route planning, carrier selection, shipment tracking and freight cost control. electronic data interchange (edi) exchanges standard business documents electronically between organisations. barcode and rfid identify and track products or assets. analytics and dashboards monitor performance, identify delays and support decisions. common scm performance measures order fulfilment time on-time delivery rate inventory turnover order accuracy supply-chain cost perfect order rate 8. benefits and challenges of scm benefits lower operating and inventory costs better customer satisfaction faster order fulfilment improved coordination better demand visibility reduced waste and delays improved supplier relationships challenges demand uncertainty supplier delays or failures transport disruption data quality and system integration cybersecurity and data sharing risks global regulations and complexity balancing cost with resilience what is the bullwhip effect? the bullwhip effect occurs when a small change in customer demand creates increasingly large fluctuations in orders as information moves upstream from retailer to distributor, manufacturer and supplier. illustration of increasing order variation customer small change → retailer larger order change → distributor greater change → factory / supplier largest variation ways to reduce it: share actual sales data, improve forecasting, shorten replenishment lead times, reduce unnecessary bulk ordering and coordinate plans with partners. 9. practical example: supply chain of a smartphone planning: the company forecasts how many phones customers may buy. sourcing: it purchases displays, batteries, chips and other components from suppliers. making: the factory assembles, tests and packages the phones. delivering: finished phones move to warehouses, distributors, stores or directly to customers. returning: defective or unwanted phones are collected for repair, replacement, refurbishment or recycling. erp can provide internal purchasing, inventory, production, sales and finance information. scm processes coordinate these activities with suppliers, logistics partners and sales channels. 10. scm vs logistics basis supply chain management logistics scope broad; coordinates the complete supply network. more focused on movement and storage of goods. activities planning, sourcing, making, delivering, returning and partner coordination. transportation, warehousing, handling, packaging and distribution. focus end-to-end supply-chain performance. efficient flow and storage of products. relationship includes logistics as an important part. one major function within scm. one-line answer: logistics is a part of scm; scm manages the broader network from suppliers to final customers. 11. exam preparation very short answer practice (1 mark) define supply chain management. name the five major activities of scm. what is a supply chain? name the three flows in scm. what is the bullwhip effect? expand wms and tms. short answer practice (5 marks) explain the meaning and objectives of scm. describe the five major activities of scm. explain material, information and financial flows. differentiate between scm and logistics. explain the relationship between erp and scm. write the benefits and challenges of scm. long answer practice (15 marks) define scm and explain its objectives, major activities and importance with a suitable diagram. explain the three flows in a supply chain and discuss how erp supports scm. discuss scm technologies, benefits, challenges and the bullwhip effect. pyq accuracy: the questions above are syllabus-based practice questions. they are not labelled as actual ranchi university previous-year questions because an exact scm question has not been verified from the supplied question papers. suggested structure for a 15-mark answer write the definition and introduction. draw the supply-chain flow diagram. explain objectives and five activities. describe the three flows. explain erp relationship and give an example. conclude with benefits and importance. 12. self-check questions which activity involves selecting suppliers and purchasing materials? which flow includes orders and demand forecasts? is logistics broader than scm or a part of scm? what can happen when small customer-demand changes become larger upstream order changes? name one way erp supports supply-chain coordination. show answers source. information flow. logistics is a part of scm. the bullwhip effect. for example, erp shares inventory, purchasing, production or sales information. 13. learning resources geeksforgeeks – supply chain management ibm – supply chain management tutorialspoint – supply chain management youtube learning searches these are channel-scoped search links, not claims of individually verified video lessons. gate smashers – scm 5 minutes engineering – scm vinay mishra – scm education 4u – scm er sahil ka gyan – scm end of erp practical example traditional system vs erp exam preparation self-check learning resources 1. meaning of erp enterprise resource planning (erp) is an integrated information system that helps an organisation manage and coordinate its major business activities using a common database and connected applications. erp connects functions such as purchasing, inventory, production, sales, finance and human resources. information entered in one business function can be made available to other authorised functions, reducing duplicate data entry and disconnected records. simple meaning: erp is a shared system that helps different departments work with consistent information and coordinated processes. important characteristics integration: connects different departments and business processes. common database: reduces separate, inconsistent data stores. real-time or timely information: updates can be available to other functions as transactions are processed. standardised processes: supports consistent ways of recording and managing work. modular structure: organisations can use connected modules for different functions. role-based access: users access information and actions according to their permissions. 2. manufacturing and erp manufacturing is the process of converting raw materials and components into finished products through activities such as planning, production, assembly, inspection and packaging. a manufacturing organisation must coordinate material availability, machines, employees, production schedules, product specifications, quality checks, finished-goods inventory and customer orders. manufacturing organisation: connected activities customer orders → production planning → material procurement → production → quality & dispatch erp connects the information required across these activities rather than treating each department as an isolated unit. why coordination is necessary suppose the sales department accepts an order for 500 units. production needs to know the due date and product specification. inventory must confirm whether components are available. purchasing may need to order missing materials. finance needs cost and purchase information. erp helps these teams coordinate using shared records. 3. why does manufacturing need erp? manufacturing problem how erp helps departments maintain separate records. provides integrated information and shared master data. raw materials are unavailable when production starts. connects inventory, production requirements and purchasing. production schedules are not aligned with customer orders. links sales orders with planning and production schedules. excess inventory increases storage cost. improves visibility of stock and material requirements. managers receive reports late. provides updated operational information and reports. product cost is difficult to calculate. connects material, labour and production-related cost records. quality issues are difficult to trace. can record inspection results, batches and product history. 4. major erp modules used in manufacturing module main responsibility manufacturing example production planning and control plans and monitors production activities. schedules 500 units for the coming week. material management / procurement manages purchasing and material availability. creates a purchase order for missing steel. inventory management tracks raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods. shows how many motors are available. sales and distribution manages customer orders, delivery and billing processes. records an order and planned delivery date. finance and controlling records financial transactions and supports cost analysis. tracks material and production costs. quality management supports inspection, testing and quality records. records inspection results for a production batch. plant maintenance supports maintenance of machines and equipment. schedules preventive maintenance for a machine. human resources manages employee and workforce information. maintains shift and employee records. remember: the exact modules and names vary by erp product. the key idea is that these functions exchange information through an integrated system. 5. how erp works in a manufacturing organisation consider a customer order for 500 tables. erp can connect the following activities: integrated manufacturing workflow 1. sales order order for 500 tables is entered. 2. check stock system checks finished goods and materials. 3. plan production quantity and schedule are prepared. 4. procure shortage of wood or fittings is identified. 5. produce work orders guide manufacturing. 6. inspect quality results are recorded. 7. dispatch finished tables are delivered and invoiced. what makes this integrated? the sales order provides demand information. inventory provides the available stock position. production planning uses demand and material information. purchasing responds to identified shortages. production consumes materials and records output. quality, warehouse and finance receive the relevant transaction information. not every erp automatically performs every decision. the system supports workflows and calculations, while authorised employees configure, review and approve activities. 6. erp, manufacturing planning and control manufacturing planning determines what to produce, how much to produce, when to produce it and what resources are required. erp provides connected information to support these decisions. planning area key question erp information used demand planning what quantity may customers require? sales orders, forecasts and historical demand. production planning what and when should we manufacture? demand, capacity, product and schedule information. material planning which materials and how many are needed? bill of materials, inventory and production plan. capacity planning are machines and labour available? work-centre capacity, shifts and workload. production control is work progressing as planned? work orders, operation status and production reports. connection to upcoming topics: material requirement planning (mrp), bill of material (bom), closed-loop mrp and mrp-ii provide more detailed methods for calculating and managing manufacturing requirements. they are covered separately in this unit. 7. common data used by manufacturing erp item or material master: identifies materials, components and finished products. bill of materials (bom): lists the components and quantities needed to make a product. routing: describes the sequence of manufacturing operations. work centre: identifies a machine, production line or group of resources where work is performed. inventory records: show stock quantities and locations. production order: authorises and tracks the manufacture of a specified quantity. supplier and customer records: store business-partner information. these records are often called master data or operational data depending on their purpose. accurate data is essential: an incorrect bom or stock balance can produce incorrect planning results. 8. benefits and limitations of erp in manufacturing benefits better coordination between departments improved material and inventory visibility more organised production planning reduced duplicate data entry improved order tracking better cost and performance reporting improved traceability when records are maintained properly limitations / risks high implementation and maintenance cost complex implementation and configuration employee training and change-management needs incorrect data can lead to poor plans customisation may increase complexity integration and downtime risks benefits depend on process discipline and user adoption 9. practical example: a bicycle manufacturing company a company receives an order for 1,000 bicycles. each bicycle requires a frame, two wheels, a seat, a handlebar, brakes and other components. sales enters the customer order and delivery date. production planning reviews the required quantity and available capacity. inventory checks component stock. purchasing arranges components that are short. production creates work orders and records completed bicycles. quality management records inspection results. finished goods are dispatched; sales and finance records are updated. without integration, departments might use separate spreadsheets and exchange updates manually. erp gives them a connected way to record and coordinate the order. 10. traditional departmental system vs erp basis traditional separate systems erp-based approach data each department may maintain its own data. connected modules use shared or integrated data. information sharing often depends on manual communication. information can be shared across authorised functions. duplicate entry more likely when systems are disconnected. can be reduced through integrated transactions. reporting combining reports may take time. cross-functional reporting is easier when data is consistent. coordination departments may work with different updates. supports coordinated workflows and planning. 11. exam preparation very short answer practice (1 mark) expand erp. what is an erp system? name any two erp modules used in manufacturing. what is a production order? what is meant by inventory management? short answer practice (5 marks) explain the meaning and characteristics of erp. why is erp required in a manufacturing organisation? describe any five erp modules used in manufacturing. explain how erp connects sales, inventory, purchasing and production. write the benefits and limitations of erp in manufacturing. long answer practice (15 marks) define erp and explain its role in a manufacturing revision quick index meaning of cad and cam computer-aided design (cad) computer-aided manufacturing (cam) cad vs cam integration of cad and cam cad/cam working process relationship between cad/cam and erp benefits and limitations practical example exam preparation self-check learning resources 1. meaning of cad and cam cad stands for computer-aided design . it refers to the use of computer software to create, modify, analyse and document the design of a product or component. cam stands for computer-aided manufacturing . it refers to the use of computer systems and software to plan, control or support manufacturing operations, often by generating instructions for automated machines. simple difference: cad helps create the product design; cam helps use that design information to manufacture the product. basic cad/cam connection cad design the product → design data geometry and dimensions → cam plan manufacturing → machine produce the part 2. computer-aided design (cad) cad software allows engineers and designers to prepare accurate digital representations of products before they are physically manufactured. main functions of cad 2d drafting: creates technical drawings using lines, dimensions and annotations. 3d modelling: creates three-dimensional representations of parts and assemblies. design modification: allows dimensions, shapes and features to be changed. assembly design: checks how different components fit together. visualisation: helps designers inspect the shape and appearance of a product. engineering documentation: prepares drawings and design specifications for production. design analysis support: some cad systems connect with simulation and engineering-analysis tools. types of cad representation type meaning example use 2d cad represents objects using two-dimensional drawings. floor plans and engineering drawings. 3d cad represents objects as three-dimensional models. machine parts and product assemblies. examples of cad software autocad – commonly used for 2d drafting and also supports 3d workflows. solidworks – 3d mechanical design and product modelling. autodesk inventor – mechanical design and 3d cad. catia – complex product and engineering design. 3. computer-aided manufacturing (cam) cam uses computer-based tools to prepare and manage manufacturing activities. in a common cnc workflow, cam software uses a digital part model to generate toolpaths and machine instructions. main functions of cam process planning: helps decide how a component will be manufactured. toolpath generation: calculates the path a cutting tool should follow. machine instruction generation: generates machine-readable instructions, often through post-processing into a suitable cnc format. machining simulation: helps preview operations and identify possible collisions or errors. manufacturing support: supports repeatable machining and production preparation. common cam-related equipment equipment use cnc milling machine removes material using rotating cutting tools. cnc lathe rotates a workpiece while a cutting tool shapes it. cnc router cuts or engraves materials such as wood, plastic or composites. industrial robot performs programmed tasks such as welding, painting or material handling. important: cam is not the same as the physical machine. cam software prepares manufacturing data or instructions; the machine controller executes compatible instructions. 4. difference between cad and cam basis cad cam full form computer-aided design computer-aided manufacturing main purpose designs and documents a product. plans or supports manufacturing the product. main users designers and design engineers. manufacturing engineers and production teams. typical output 2d drawings, 3d models and design specifications. toolpaths, process data and machine instructions. key question what should the product look like? how can the product be manufactured? example designing a gear in 3d. preparing cnc instructions to cut the gear. 5. integration of cad and cam cad and cam are more useful when design information can be transferred to manufacturing without repeatedly recreating the same geometry and dimensions. cad creates the digital product model. the model or a compatible exchange file is passed to cam. cam uses the geometry and manufacturing settings to prepare operations and toolpaths. a post-processor converts toolpath information into instructions suitable for a particular machine controller. the cnc machine executes the instructions to manufacture the part. integrated cad/cam workflow 1. design create 2d drawing or 3d model. 2. transfer share model data in a compatible format. 3. plan select tools, operations and cutting settings. 4. generate create toolpaths and post-process instructions. 5. simulate check the planned machining process. 6. manufacture run the program on the machine. common data exchange formats format general purpose step exchanges 3d product model data between engineering systems. iges older neutral format for exchanging cad geometry and related data. dxf commonly used to exchange 2d drawing information and some design data. g-code a widely used family of numerical-control programming instructions; exact dialect depends on the controller. 6. cad/cam in a manufacturing workflow consider a company producing a metal machine component. the design engineer creates a 3d model with dimensions and required features using cad. the design is reviewed and approved. the manufacturing engineer imports the model into cam software. the engineer selects the raw material, cutting tools, machining operations and settings. cam generates toolpaths and machine-specific instructions through a post-processor. the machining process is simulated and checked. the cnc machine produces the component. the finished component is inspected against the drawing and specifications. design revisions must be controlled. if the cad model changes, the related cam program may need to be regenerated and checked before production. 7. relationship between cad/cam and erp cad/cam and erp support different but connected parts of manufacturing. cad contains product design information such as geometry, dimensions and specifications. cam uses design information to prepare manufacturing operations and machine instructions. erp manages wider business information such as material purchasing, inventory, production orders, costing, sales and finance. how the systems complement one another cad product design → cam manufacturing preparation → production machine operations ↕ manufacturing plans, item data and production status may be integrated with erp erp purchasing • inventory • production orders • finance • sales • costing integration can help align engineering changes with purchasing and production, but it requires suitable interfaces, data standards and change-control processes. cad/cam does not replace erp, and erp does not replace detailed design or machining software. 8. benefits and limitations of cad/cam benefits improved design accuracy faster design modification better 3d visualisation reduced manual drafting and programming effort more repeatable machining operations support for complex shapes simulation can help detect manufacturing problems early improved link between design and production limitations / challenges software and hardware can be expensive training is required incorrect models or settings can cause errors data compatibility issues may occur machine-specific post-processors are needed software maintenance and upgrades are required automation still needs skilled review and quality control 9. practical example: designing and manufacturing a gear cad: an engineer creates a 3d gear model with the required dimensions and tooth geometry. design review: the model is checked against the engineering requirements. cam: the manufacturing engineer selects the stock material, machine, cutting tools and machining strategy. toolpath: cam calculates the tool movement needed to machine the gear. simulation: the process is reviewed for possible tool collisions or machining problems. cnc machining: the machine executes the approved program. inspection: the gear is measured to confirm that it meets the specifications. 10. exam preparation very short answer practice (1 mark) expand cad. expand cam. what is the main purpose of cad? what is a toolpath? what does cnc stand for? name one cad software package. short answer practice (5 marks) define cad and explain its main functions. define cam and explain its main functions. differentiate between cad and cam. explain how cad and cam are integrated. write the benefits and limitations of cad/cam. explain the relationship between cad/cam and erp. long answer practice (15 marks) explain cad and cam in detail, including their functions, differences and applications in manufacturing. describe the integrated cad/cam workflow with a neat diagram. discuss how cad/cam and erp complement one another in a manufacturing organisation. pyq accuracy: these are syllabus-based practice questions. they are not labelled as actual ranchi university functions separately. draw the integrated workflow diagram. compare cad and cam. explain benefits and limitations. give a manufacturing example and conclude. 11. self-check which system is primarily used to create a 3d product model? which system can generate toolpaths for cnc machining? what is the purpose of a post-processor? does erp replace cad software? name one neutral format used to exchange 3d cad data. show answers cad. cam. it converts manufacturing/toolpath data into instructions suitable for a specific machine controller. no. erp manages wider business processes; cad is used for product design. step (or iges). 12. learning resources autodesk – cad/cam overview autodesk – cad software overview solidworks – product design software geeksforgeeks – search cad/cam topics
