material requirement planning (mrp) complete exam-oriented notebook • concepts, inputs, calculations, process diagrams and erp integration core syllabus topic manufacturing planning exam revision quick index meaning and definition why mrp is needed objectives and functions main inputs of mrp mrp working process mrp calculations and example outputs of mrp important mrp terms types and development of mrp mrp and erp relationship advantages and limitations practical example mrp vs. traditional inventory control exam preparation self-check learning resources 1. meaning and definition of mrp material requirement planning (mrp) is a computer-based planning technique used by manufacturing organisations to calculate what materials are required, how much is required, and when they should be available for production. mrp starts with the production plan for finished products. it uses the bill of materials (bom), current inventory records and lead times to calculate the quantities and dates of components and raw materials that must be purchased or produced. simple meaning: mrp makes sure that the right materials are available in the right quantity at the right time, so production is not stopped because of missing components and excess stock is avoided. definition for examination material requirement planning is a systematic method of determining the time-phased requirements for dependent-demand items by using the master production schedule, bill of materials and inventory status records. 2. why is mrp needed? manufacturing a product may require hundreds or thousands of components. a company must know the quantity of each component and the date by which it is needed. manual estimation becomes difficult when demand, stock and production schedules change. complex products: a finished product may contain many subassemblies and components. dependent demand: the need for components depends on how many finished products are planned. time coordination: materials must arrive before the operation that uses them. inventory control: too little stock stops production; too much stock blocks money and storage space. changing schedules: mrp recalculates requirements when production plans or inventory records change. 3. objectives and functions of mrp objective / function explanation ensure material availability make sure required raw materials and components are available for planned production. maintain low inventory plan only the quantities needed, reducing unnecessary stock and carrying cost. plan purchase orders calculate when and how much material should be ordered from suppliers. plan production orders identify components and subassemblies that must be manufactured internally. schedule activities consider lead times so materials are available on their required dates. improve coordination connect purchasing, stores and production planning through a common material plan. 4. main inputs of mrp mrp mainly depends on three essential inputs. if these inputs are inaccurate, the material plan will also be inaccurate. three main inputs to mrp master production schedule mps + bill of materials bom + inventory records stock status ↓ mrp processing calculates net material quantities and time-phased order dates 4.1 master production schedule (mps) the master production schedule states which finished products are to be produced, in what quantities and in which time periods. it is the starting point for calculating material requirements. example: the mps may state that 100 bicycles must be completed in week 4. 4.2 bill of materials (bom) a bill of materials is a structured list of all raw materials, components and subassemblies needed to manufacture one unit of a finished product. it also specifies the quantity of each item. simple product structure / bom bicycle 1 unit ↓ frame × 1 wheel × 2 seat × 1 handle × 1 the bom tells mrp which components and quantities are needed for each bicycle. 4.3 inventory status records these records show the current material position. they commonly include: on-hand quantity: stock physically available. scheduled receipts: quantities already ordered and expected to arrive. allocated stock: stock already reserved for other orders. lead time: time required to purchase or manufacture an item. safety stock: extra stock kept as protection against uncertainty, where applicable. remember: mps answers “what finished products and when?”, bom answers “which components and how many?”, and inventory records answer “what do we already have or expect to receive?”. 5. working process of mrp read the mps: identify the finished products, quantities and due dates. explode the bom: break each finished product into its required components and subassemblies. check inventory: consider available stock and scheduled receipts. calculate net requirements: subtract usable inventory and expected receipts from gross requirements. apply lot-sizing rules: decide the order quantity, such as exact requirement or a fixed batch size. offset by lead time: work backwards from the date the material is needed to find when the order must be released. prepare planned orders: generate planned purchase orders or manufacturing orders. update the plan: recalculate when schedules, stock or supplier dates change. mrp flowchart master production schedule → bom explosion → inventory check ↓ net requirements calculation → lead-time offsetting → planned orders 6. mrp calculations and simple example 6.1 gross requirement gross requirement is the total quantity of an item needed before considering available stock or scheduled receipts. 6.2 net requirement net requirement = gross requirement − available supply for a basic calculation, available supply includes usable on-hand inventory and scheduled receipts. in a full mrp record, safety stock and allocation rules may also affect the calculation. example: calculate wheel requirements a company plans to manufacture 100 bicycles . each bicycle needs 2 wheels . the store has 30 usable wheels , and 20 wheels are already scheduled to arrive before they are needed. step calculation quantity 1. gross requirement 100 bicycles × 2 wheels 200 wheels 2. on-hand stock available in store 30 wheels 3. scheduled receipt already ordered and due on time 20 wheels 4. available supply 30 + 20 50 wheels 5. net requirement 200 − 50 150 wheels result: the company needs to arrange 150 additional wheels, assuming no safety stock, scrap allowance or other adjustments. 6.3 lead-time offsetting suppose the 150 wheels must be available at the start of week 4 and the supplier lead time is 2 weeks. the purchase order should be released in week 2, so the wheels can arrive in week 4. simple time-phased example week 2 release order → 2-week lead time → week 4 wheels available 7. outputs of mrp after processing the inputs, mrp generates information that helps purchasing and production teams act. output meaning planned purchase orders suggestions to buy materials from suppliers, including quantities and release dates. planned production orders suggestions to manufacture required components or subassemblies internally. order release information indicates when planned orders should be released. rescheduling notices indicates that an existing order may need to be moved earlier or later. exception reports highlights problems such as shortages, delays or unusual requirements. 8. important mrp terms term meaning dependent demand demand for a component that is calculated from the demand for another item, usually a finished product. independent demand demand that comes directly from customers or the market, such as demand for finished products. lead time time between placing/releasing an order and receiving the item or completing its manufacture. lot sizing rule used to decide how much to order or produce at one time. lot-for-lot ordering or producing exactly the net quantity required for a period. time-phased planning planning requirements and orders by specific time periods. bom explosion breaking a finished product into lower-level components using the bom. low-level coding assigning an item to the lowest level at which it appears in a product structure, helping ensure requirements are calculated correctly. 9. types and development of mrp 9.1 mrp i – material requirement planning mrp i focuses mainly on calculating the quantity and timing of materials and components needed for production. it uses mps, bom and inventory records. 9.2 mrp ii – manufacturing resource planning mrp ii extends material planning to broader manufacturing resources. it can include capacity planning, machines, labour, production scheduling and financial implications. it checks whether the production plan is feasible with available resources. 9.3 mrp i vs mrp ii basis mrp i mrp ii full form material requirement planning manufacturing resource planning main focus materials and components materials plus wider manufacturing resources resources considered primarily material availability materials, capacity, labour, machines and schedules scope narrower broader purpose ensure materials are available when needed coordinate and evaluate the overall manufacturing plan important syllabus connection: mrp ii is listed separately in unit iv. here it is introduced only to explain how mrp i developed into broader manufacturing resource planning. 10. relationship between mrp and erp mrp is a manufacturing planning method. erp is a wider integrated business system that connects manufacturing with purchasing, inventory, finance, sales, human resources and other functions. mrp working inside an erp environment sales demand / mps → erp system ↓ mrp calculation bom + inventory + lead times → material requirements and planned orders ↓ purchasing inventory / stores production finance sales information can provide demand for finished products. inventory records provide stock and scheduled receipt information. mrp calculates component requirements and planned orders. purchasing uses the plan to arrange external materials. production uses it to plan internally manufactured components. erp can connect these transactions with costs and financial records. 11. advantages and limitations of mrp advantages reduces unnecessary inventory. helps prevent material shortages. improves production scheduling. supports better purchasing decisions. shows future material requirements. improves coordination between stores, purchasing and production. limitations depends on accurate bom and inventory data. changes in schedules can require frequent recalculation. does not by itself guarantee sufficient machine or labour capacity. incorrect lead times can create late or early orders. implementation and maintenance require time, skills and cost. unexpected supplier disruptions can still affect production. 12. practical example: manufacturing a bicycle a bicycle manufacturer receives an order for 100 bicycles due in four weeks. the planner enters this requirement into the mps. the bom shows that each bicycle needs one frame, two wheels, one seat and one handle. mrp reads the plan for 100 bicycles. it explodes the bom to calculate 100 frames, 200 wheels, 100 seats and 100 handles. it checks available stock and scheduled receipts for each item. it calculates the net quantity still required. it uses supplier and manufacturing lead times to calculate order release dates. it creates planned purchase orders for bought-out parts and planned production orders for internally made parts. as a result, purchasing and production teams receive a time-based plan instead of guessing material quantities. 13. mrp vs traditional inventory control basis traditional inventory control mrp planning basis often based on stock levels, past usage or reorder rules. based on production schedule and dependent demand. time planning may focus on when stock reaches a reorder point. time-phases material requirements using lead times. product structure does not necessarily use a complete product bom. uses bom to calculate component requirements. coordination may be handled separately from production planning. connects material planning to production schedules. best suited for many independent-demand stock items. manufacturing items with dependent demand and known product structures. 14. exam preparation very short answer practice (1 mark) expand mrp. what is a bill of materials? name the three main inputs of mrp. what is lead time? what is dependent demand? short answer practice (5 marks) define mrp and explain its objectives. explain the three main inputs of mrp. describe the working process of mrp with a flowchart. what are the outputs of mrp? differentiate between mrp i and mrp ii. long answer practice (15 marks) define material requirement planning. explain its objectives, inputs, working process and outputs with a suitable diagram. explain how mrp calculates material requirements using mps, bom and inventory status records. give a numerical example. discuss the advantages and limitations of mrp and explain its relationship with erp. pyq accuracy: these are syllabus-based practice questions. they are not labelled as actual ranchi university previous-year questions because an exact mrp question has not been verified from the supplied papers. suggested structure for a 15-mark answer write the definition and simple meaning of mrp. explain why manufacturing organisations need mrp. draw and explain the three inputs: mps, bom and inventory records. explain the working steps in correct order. show a small net-requirement calculation. write outputs, advantages and limitations. conclude with the role of mrp within erp. 15. self-check which input tells mrp what finished products must be produced and when? which input lists the components needed to make one finished product? a product needs 4 bolts. the plan is to make 50 units. what is the gross bolt requirement? if gross requirement is 200 units and available supply is 65 units, what is the net requirement? if an item is needed in week 6 and its lead time is 2 weeks, when should its order normally be released? does mrp i fully check machine and labour capacity? show answers master production schedule (mps). bill of materials (bom). 50 × 4 = 200 bolts. 200 − 65 = 135 units. week 4, assuming the lead time is exactly two weeks and no other delay applies. no. mrp i mainly plans materials; broader capacity and resource planning is associated with mrp ii. 16. learning resources websites geeksforgeeks — search the site for “material requirement planning (mrp)” and “mrp vs mrp ii”. tutorialspoint — search for “material requirement planning” and “manufacturing resource planning”. ibm — enterprise resource planning — useful for understanding how material planning fits into a wider erp environment. youtube learning searches (preferred channels) these are channel-scoped search links, not claims that a particular individual video has been verified. gate smashers — mrp 5 minutes engineering — mrp vinay mishra — mrp education 4u — mrp er sahil ka gyan — mrp final revision line: mrp uses the master production schedule, bill of materials and inventory status records to calculate the net quantity and timing of materials required for production. it helps manufacturing organisations coordinate purchasing and production while controlling inventory. end of erp unit iv — topic 3: material requirement planning (mrp). mca • erp • unit iv • topic 4 bill of materials (bom) complete exam-oriented notebook • product structure, bom levels, types, examples and mrp integration core syllabus topic manufacturing data exam revision quick index meaning and definition need and objectives product structure and bom levels information in a bom types of bom bom creation process practical bom example role of bom in mrp and erp advantages and limitations bom vs routing exam preparation self-check learning resources 1. meaning and definition of bill of materials a bill of materials (bom) is a complete, structured list of all raw materials, parts, components and subassemblies required to manufacture, assemble or package one unit of a finished product. it also specifies the quantity of each item required. a bom describes what goes into a product . it does not primarily describe the sequence of manufacturing operations; that information is generally provided by a routing. simple meaning: a bom is like a recipe for making a product. just as a food recipe lists the ingredients and their quantities, a bom lists the parts and quantities needed to make a product. definition for examination a bill of materials is a hierarchical record of the materials, components and subassemblies required to produce a parent item, showing the quantity of each component needed for a specified quantity of the parent item. 2. need and objectives of bom identify components: shows every material and part required for a product. calculate quantities: specifies how many units of each component are needed. support material planning: provides the product structure used by mrp to calculate dependent demand. control production: helps production teams check that all required parts are available. support purchasing: helps purchasing identify which materials must be ordered. maintain product consistency: gives departments a common reference for the approved product structure. estimate product cost: material quantities and item costs can be used to calculate material cost. 3. product structure and bom levels a bom is usually arranged in a hierarchy. the finished product is at the top, subassemblies appear below it, and individual components or raw materials appear at lower levels. example: three-level product structure level 0 bicycle ↓ level 1 frame assembly level 1 wheel assembly level 1 seat assembly ↓ level 2 frame tube level 2 rim + spokes + tyre level 2 seat + support illustrative product structure. each parent item is made from the components shown directly beneath it. important terms term meaning parent item an item that is made from one or more lower-level components. child component a part or subassembly used to make a parent item. top-level item the final product at the highest level of the product structure. subassembly a group of components assembled together and then used as part of a larger product. level the position of an item in the product hierarchy. the finished product is commonly level 0. quantity per the number of units of a component needed to make one unit of its parent item. 4. information contained in a bom a bom record may contain several fields. the exact fields depend on the organisation and the erp system. field purpose example parent item number identifies the product or assembly being made. bike-100 component number uniquely identifies a material or component. tyre-20 description explains what the item is. front tyre quantity per shows the amount required for one parent item. 1 tyre unit of measure defines how quantity is measured. piece, metre, kg reference / position may identify where a component is fitted. front wheel position effective date indicates when a bom version becomes valid. valid from 1 january revision number identifies a particular approved version of the product structure. revision b important: a bom must be accurate and kept up to date. if the product design changes but the bom is not updated, mrp may calculate the wrong material requirements. 5. types of bill of materials different bom formats are used for different business purposes. common types include the following. 5.1 engineering bom (ebom) an engineering bom is prepared by the product design or engineering team. it represents the product as designed, often organised according to design drawings and engineering specifications. example: the engineering team defines the frame, brake assembly, wheels and other designed parts of a bicycle. 5.2 manufacturing bom (mbom) a manufacturing bom represents the components and subassemblies required to manufacture and assemble the product on the shop floor. it is organised to support production activities. example: the factory's mbom includes the parts, kits and subassemblies required at the relevant production stages. 5.3 sales bom a sales bom is used when a product is sold as a package or bundle. it connects the saleable product with the items included in that package. example: a computer package may include a desktop unit, keyboard, mouse and monitor. 5.4 service bom a service bom lists the parts and assemblies relevant to servicing, repairing or maintaining a product. it helps service teams identify replacement parts. 5.5 single-level and multi-level bom basis single-level bom multi-level bom structure shows only the immediate components of a parent item. shows components and lower-level subassemblies across multiple levels. detail simple and limited. more complete product structure. example bicycle → frame, wheels, seat. bicycle → wheel assembly → rim, spokes, tyre. use simple products or quick overview. complex products and detailed material planning. exam tip: do not confuse the format (single-level or multi-level) with the business purpose (engineering, manufacturing, sales or service). they describe different ways of classifying a bom. 6. process of creating and maintaining a bom identify the finished product: select the product or assembly for which the bom is required. collect design information: use approved drawings, specifications and engineering documents. identify all components: list raw materials, purchased parts and subassemblies. define quantities: specify the quantity of each component needed for one parent item. arrange the hierarchy: place components under the correct parent and create the required levels. review and validate: check quantities, units, part numbers and completeness. approve and release: make the approved bom available to planning and production. control revisions: update the bom when an approved product change occurs and maintain version history. bom preparation workflow product design → identify parts → set quantities and levels ↓ review and approve → release bom → maintain revisions 7. practical example: bom for one bicycle assume a simplified bicycle requires the following parts. the quantities shown are illustrative and are for one bicycle. level parent item component quantity required 0 bicycle frame assembly 1 0 bicycle wheel assembly 2 0 bicycle seat assembly 1 1 wheel assembly rim 1 per wheel 1 wheel assembly tyre 1 per wheel 1 wheel assembly spoke 36 per wheel 1 seat assembly seat 1 1 seat assembly seat support 1 calculate requirements for 50 bicycles to calculate the gross requirement, multiply the quantity per bicycle by the planned number of bicycles. component quantity per bicycle for 50 bicycles wheel assemblies 2 100 rims 2 × 1 = 2 100 tyres 2 × 1 = 2 100 spokes 2 × 36 = 72 3,600 seat assemblies 1 50 what the example teaches: the bom provides the quantity relationship. mrp then checks stock and scheduled receipts to determine how many additional items must be purchased or manufactured. 8. role of bom in mrp and erp the bom is one of the three main inputs of mrp. the master production schedule states how many finished products are planned, while the bom converts that finished-product quantity into component requirements. inventory records are then checked to calculate net requirements. how bom supports mrp mps finished-product plan bom product structure inventory records available stock ↓ mrp calculation explodes the bom, calculates gross and net component requirements, and uses lead times to plan orders. ↓ purchase orders production orders material availability in an erp system, the bom can be shared by production planning, purchasing, inventory management, costing and engineering. this reduces the need for each department to maintain separate product-part lists. 9. advantages and limitations of bom advantages provides a complete list of product components. supports accurate material planning. helps purchasing calculate material needs. improves coordination between engineering and production. supports product costing and inventory control. helps manage product changes through revisions. limitations / challenges creating a detailed bom can take time. incorrect quantities or part numbers cause planning errors. frequent product changes require careful revision control. different departments may use inconsistent item descriptions if standards are weak. a bom alone does not specify the complete sequence or timing of manufacturing operations. 10. bom vs routing bom and routing are related manufacturing records, but they answer different questions. basis bill of materials (bom) routing main question what materials and components are required? how and in what sequence is the product made? information parts, quantities, units and product structure. operations, work centres, sequence and processing times. purpose material planning and product structure definition. production scheduling and process planning. example one bicycle requires two wheels. fit wheels after preparing the frame. remember: bom = what is needed. routing = how and in what sequence it is made. 11. exam preparation very short answer practice (1 mark) expand bom. what is a bill of materials? what is a parent item? what is a subassembly? name any two types of bom. short answer practice (5 marks) define bom and explain its objectives. explain the information contained in a bom. differentiate between single-level and multi-level bom. explain engineering bom and manufacturing bom. differentiate between bom and routing. long answer practice (15 marks) define bill of materials. explain its structure, levels, types and importance in manufacturing with a suitable diagram. explain the role of bom in mrp. how does it help calculate the material requirements of a finished product? give an example. discuss the process of creating and maintaining a bom and explain its advantages and limitations. pyq accuracy: these are syllabus-based practice questions. they are not labelled as actual ranchi university previous-year questions because an exact bom question has not been verified from the supplied papers. suggested structure for a 15-mark answer write the definition and simple meaning of bom. explain its need and objectives. draw a multi-level product structure. describe the fields and types of bom. explain how bom supports mrp, using a short example. write advantages and limitations. conclude by explaining why accurate bom data is important to erp manufacturing. 12. self-check what does a bom describe: product components or the sequence of operations? what is the difference between a parent item and a child component? if one product needs 3 bolts, how many bolts are required for 40 products before stock is considered? which bom is primarily organised to support manufacturing and assembly? which record describes the sequence of operations: bom or routing? why must bom revisions be controlled? show answers it describes the components and quantities required to make the product. a parent item is made from lower-level items; a child component is one of the items used to make its parent. 3 × 40 = 120 bolts. manufacturing bom (mbom). routing. to ensure planning and production use the correct, approved product structure after design changes. 13. learning resources websites geeksforgeeks — search for “bill of materials (bom)” and “bom in manufacturing”. tutorialspoint — direct benefits question belongs to topic 3. ★ what to prepare from this topic ★ meaning and definition of product data management. types of product information managed by pdm. main functions of a pdm system. relationship between pdm and erp. 1.1 meaning of product data management during product development, a company creates many documents and files, such as product drawings, cad models, specifications, part details and bills of materials. these files are used by design, engineering and manufacturing teams. product data management (pdm) is a system used to store, organize, control and share all product-related information in a centralized manner. it helps employees access the correct and latest product data. definition: product data management is the process of managing product-related information, such as engineering drawings, cad files, specifications, bills of materials and revision records, through a centralized system. in simple words, pdm keeps all important product information organized in one controlled place instead of allowing different departments to maintain separate and possibly outdated copies. 1.2 need for pdm in a manufacturing company, product designs may be changed many times. if different departments use different versions of a drawing, mistakes can occur during purchasing or production. pdm is needed to: keep product information in one central location; make sure users work with the correct version of a design; control who can view or change product files; maintain the history of design changes; and share approved product information with other departments. 1.3 types of data managed by pdm data type examples design data cad drawings, 2d drawings and 3d product models. product specifications dimensions, materials, weight, tolerances and technical details. bill of materials (bom) parts, components and quantities required to make a product. documents design reports, manuals, test reports and instructions. revision and change records earlier versions of files and details of approved design changes. 1.4 main functions of pdm data storage: stores product files and documents in a central repository. document management: organizes drawings, specifications and other product documents for easy access. version control: maintains different versions of a design and helps users identify the latest approved version. access control: gives permission to authorized users to view, edit or approve product information. change management: records design changes, their reasons and approval status. search and retrieval: helps users find product information using details such as part number, name or project. workflow management: sends documents for checking, review and approval before release. 1.5 working of pdm a pdm system generally works in the following way: the engineer creates a drawing, cad model or product document. the file is stored in the pdm system with details such as part number and revision. authorized users review or update the file. the system records changes and sends the file for approval. after approval, the latest version is released for use by the concerned departments. example: a car company changes the design of a brake component. pdm stores the new drawing as a revised version and keeps the previous record. this helps the production team use the approved drawing rather than an outdated one. 1 create engineer makes a drawing or cad model 2 store saved with part number and revision 3 review / update authorised users edit the file 4 approve changes recorded and sent for approval 5 release latest version used by departments figure: how a pdm system handles a product file from creation to release. 1.6 relationship between pdm and erp pdm and erp are different systems, but they can work together. pdm mainly manages product design and engineering information, whereas erp manages business activities such as purchasing, inventory, production planning and finance. when both systems are integrated, approved product details and bills of materials from pdm can be shared with erp. erp can then use this information for material planning, purchasing and production. basis pdm erp main focus product design and engineering data. business resources and operations. information drawings, cad files, specifications and boms. inventory, purchase orders, production and financial records. purpose controls product information and design changes. integrates and manages business processes. remember: pdm manages product information, while erp uses relevant approved information to manage business operations. pdm does not replace erp. 1.7 important points for examination pdm stands for product data management . it stores product-related information in a centralized system. it manages cad files, drawings, specifications, boms and revision records. its important functions include storage, document management, version control, access control and change management. pdm can be integrated with erp to share approved product information. 1.8 previous-year question and practice questions verified ranchi essential concepts. no verified direct or related pyq for this topic was identified in the supplied question-paper analysis. it is still part of the official syllabus and should not be skipped. 2.1 introduction to data management every organisation uses data to perform its daily activities. a company stores details of customers, suppliers, employees, products, stock, purchases and sales. if this information is incorrect, duplicated or unavailable, business work may be delayed and decisions may be wrong. in an erp system, different departments use common business information. therefore, data must be collected, stored, organised, checked, protected and updated properly. this complete activity is called data management . 2.2 definition of data management explanatory definition: data management is the systematic process of collecting, organising, storing, maintaining, protecting and using an organisation's data throughout its life cycle. in an erp system, it ensures that departments work with accurate, consistent and up-to-date information for their business activities. exam-ready definition — what is data management? data management is the process of collecting, storing, organising, maintaining, protecting and controlling data so that it remains accurate, consistent, secure and available for authorised use. in erp, it ensures that reliable information is shared across different departments to support business operations and decision-making. in simple words: data management means taking proper care of business information—from the time it is entered into the system until it is updated, used, archived or removed. 2.3 need for data management in erp centralised information: erp connects departments through shared information, so users can work from common approved records. accuracy: correct customer, supplier, product and stock details reduce mistakes. avoiding duplication: it prevents the same customer or product being entered several times under different names. better decisions: managers need reliable information to plan purchases, production, sales and finance. security: business information must be protected from unauthorised access or changes. easy reporting: well-organised data helps prepare reports and check performance. 2.4 main types of data in an erp system erp data can be understood through these important categories. the first three are especially useful for understanding how an erp system works. type meaning examples 1. master data basic business information used repeatedly in many activities. it usually remains useful for a long period, although it can be updated. customer, supplier, employee, material and product details. 2. transaction data information created when a business activity or transaction takes place. sales order, purchase order, invoice, payment, goods receipt and stock movement. 3. organisational data information describing the structure and units of an organisation. company, plant, warehouse, sales organisation and department. 4. reference data standard values used to classify or describe other data. country codes, currency codes, units of measurement and payment terms. easy example: a customer record is master data . when that customer places an order, the order is transaction data . the plant handling the order is organisational data . a currency code such as inr is reference data . 2.5 master data and transaction data — difference basis master data transaction data meaning basic information about important business entities. records of business activities and events. purpose provides information needed to perform transactions. records what happened during a business activity. change frequency usually changes less often. created frequently during daily operations. examples customer, supplier, material and employee records. sales orders, invoices, payments and purchase orders. relationship can be used in many transactions. usually refers to one or more master-data records. 2.6 important activities of data management data collection: gathering information from departments, forms, existing systems and business activities. data entry and creation: entering new records into erp using approved formats and rules. data validation: checking whether information is complete and follows required rules. for example, the system may reject an invalid date or missing customer number. data storage and organisation: saving information in a structured way so authorised users and erp modules can find it. data updating: changing records when details change, such as a supplier's address or a product's description. data integration and sharing: making relevant information available to connected departments and erp modules. data security: using user permissions and other controls to prevent unauthorised viewing or modification. backup and recovery: keeping recoverable copies so important information can be restored after accidental loss or system failure. archiving and disposal: keeping old records for the required period and disposing of information safely when it is no longer needed and rules allow it. 2.7 data management process in erp collect: obtain business information, such as customer, supplier or product details. enter: add the information to erp using the correct fields and format. validate: check for missing values, incorrect formats and duplicate records. store: save approved information in the erp database. share and use: allow authorised departments to use the same information in purchasing, sales, inventory and accounting. maintain: update records when changes occur and monitor their accuracy. archive or remove: retain or dispose of old information according to company policy and legal requirements. 1 collect from forms, systems, departments 2 enter using approved fields and formats 3 validate check missing, wrong or duplicate data 4 store save approved data in the erp database 5 use / share authorised departments use the same data 6 maintain update, archive or dispose by policy figure: basic data-management process in an erp system. the process does not end after data is stored. information must be checked and maintained as the organisation changes. 2.8 data quality in erp data quality means how suitable and reliable information is for its intended use. good-quality data has these characteristics: accuracy: information correctly represents the real business detail. completeness: required information is present. consistency: the same information does not conflict across departments. timeliness: information is updated and available when needed. uniqueness: unnecessary duplicate records are avoided. validity: information follows the required format and business rules. example: if the same supplier is entered twice with slightly different names, purchasing may create duplicate orders or finance may maintain separate payment records. checking and correcting such records improves data quality. 2.9 data management during erp implementation when an organisation starts using a new erp system, it may need to transfer information from old software, spreadsheets or paper records. this activity is called data migration . identify which old records are needed in the new erp. collect and examine the existing data. remove duplicate, incorrect or unnecessary records. convert information into the format required by the new erp. map old data fields to the correct new erp fields. load the data into the new system. check records and accuracy before live business work begins. remember: data migration means moving data from an old system to a new system. data management is broader: it includes the ongoing care and control of data before, during and after migration. 2.10 advantages of proper data management improved accuracy: reduces errors caused by incomplete or incorrect records. better coordination: departments can use common and consistent information. faster work: employees spend less time searching for or correcting records. better decisions: managers can rely on reports created from dependable data. improved security: access rules help protect confidential business information. reliable reporting: consistent data supports financial, inventory and operational reports. smoother erp operation: connected modules exchange information with fewer data-related problems. 2.11 problems caused by poor data management duplicate customer, supplier or product records. incorrect stock balances and purchase requirements. errors in invoices, payments and financial reports. delays because employees cannot find correct information. unauthorised access or accidental loss of important data. wrong management decisions based on outdated or incomplete reports. 2.12 practical example consider a company that purchases raw materials from suppliers and manufactures products. its erp stores supplier details, material information, purchase orders, goods receipts and payments. the supplier's name, address and payment terms are master data . the material code, description and unit of measurement are also master data . a purchase order and goods receipt are transaction data . the erp checks required fields, stores records and makes approved information available to purchasing, inventory and finance. if the supplier's details are incorrect, the purchase order or payment may also be affected. proper data management helps prevent these problems. 2.13 important questions for examination verified pyqs: no verified direct or related pyq for data management was identified in the supplied question-paper analysis. practice questions — not confirmed pyqs: define data management in erp. explain the need and importance of data management in an erp system. explain the different types of data used in erp. differentiate between master data and transaction data. explain the major activities involved in data management. what is data migration? explain its steps in erp implementation. explain the characteristics of good-quality data. 2.14 quick revision data management: collecting, storing, organising, maintaining, protecting and controlling data. master data: basic information used repeatedly, such as customer and material details. transaction data: records of activities, such as orders, invoices and payments. organisational data: business structure, such as company, plant and department. reference data: standard values, such as currency and country codes. data migration: moving data from an old system to a new system. good data quality: accurate, complete, consistent, timely, unique and valid. 2.15 learning resources web resources checked geeksforgeeks — general computer and database concepts; a directly matching erp “write short notes on benefits of pdm and plant maintenance” (7.5 marks each). prepare this topic as a short-note answer. 3.1 meaning of benefits of pdm explanatory definition: benefits of product data management (pdm) are the improvements an organisation gains by storing, organising, controlling and sharing product-related information through a common system. pdm helps teams use correct and updated product data, coordinate their work, reduce mistakes and complete product development more efficiently. exam-ready definition — what are the benefits of pdm? the benefits of pdm are the advantages obtained by centrally managing product information, such as improved data accuracy, faster access to information, better teamwork, controlled document versions, fewer design errors, reduced costs and improved productivity. 3.2 major benefits of pdm centralised storage of product data: product information such as cad drawings, specifications, bills of materials (boms) and technical documents is stored in one organised location. this reduces scattered files and duplicate records. quick access to correct information: employees can search and retrieve the required product data easily. they spend less time searching emails, folders and different systems. version and revision control: pdm keeps track of different versions of drawings and documents. it helps users identify the latest approved version and prevents work based on outdated designs. improved collaboration: engineers, designers, production staff, purchase teams and quality teams can share the same information. this improves communication between departments and locations. reduction in errors and rework: using approved and updated information reduces mistakes caused by incorrect drawings, missing details or old specifications. less rework saves time and money. higher productivity and faster development: easy access, reuse of existing designs and automated workflows help employees complete tasks faster and reduce product development time. better document and change control: pdm supports approval workflows and records product changes. relevant departments can be informed when a design or specification is updated. improved data security: access permissions help ensure that only authorised users can view, edit or approve sensitive product information. this protects confidential designs and intellectual property. better product quality: correct specifications and controlled revisions help ensure that products are designed and manufactured according to approved requirements. improved decision-making and visibility: managers can access reliable product information and change history, helping them plan resources and make informed decisions. 3.3 how pdm benefits an organisation — example suppose a company manufactures electric fans. the design team updates the motor specification. with pdm, the revised drawing and specification are saved as an approved version and made available to production, purchasing and quality teams. production avoids using the old drawing, purchasing orders the correct motor, and quality inspectors check the product against the latest specification. this reduces confusion, errors and delay. 3.4 short exam answer (7.5 marks) q. write a short note on the benefits of product data management (pdm). product data management (pdm) provides a central system for managing product-related information such as drawings, specifications, cad files, bills of materials and technical documents. its major benefits are: it stores product information in a centralised location. it provides quick access to accurate and updated data. it controls document versions and revisions. it improves communication and collaboration between departments. it reduces design mistakes, duplication and rework. it increases productivity and reduces product development time. it improves document security through access control. it supports better product quality and decision-making. thus, pdm helps an organisation manage product information efficiently, reduce operational costs and improve coordination throughout product development. 3.5 quick revision central repository = product data in one place. version control = use the correct/latest approved file. collaboration = departments share common information. change control = product changes are recorded and communicated. main result = fewer errors, less rework, lower cost and higher productivity. 3.6 learning resources geeksforgeeks — sap functionality and erp features that as a confirmed pyq for this university. 4.1 meaning of finance module in erp explanatory definition: the finance module is the part of an erp system that manages an organisation’s financial transactions and accounting activities. it brings information about income, expenses, payments, receipts, assets and budgets together so that the organisation can monitor its financial position and prepare reliable reports. exam-ready definition — what is the finance module in erp? the finance module in erp is an integrated software component used to record, process, monitor and report an organisation’s financial transactions, including accounting, payments, receipts, budgeting, cash management and financial reporting. 4.2 objectives of the finance module maintain accurate and complete financial records. automate accounting, payment and billing activities. monitor income, expenses, assets and liabilities. provide timely financial reports to management. support budgeting, planning and financial control. help the organisation meet accounting and tax requirements. 4.3 main components / functions of the finance module general ledger (gl): it is the main book of accounts where financial transactions are summarised under categories such as assets, liabilities, income, expenses and capital. it is the base for preparing the trial balance and financial statements. accounts payable (ap): it manages money the organisation has to pay to suppliers and vendors. it records supplier invoices, payment due dates, approvals and payments. example: recording and paying a raw-material supplier’s bill. accounts receivable (ar): it manages money customers owe to the organisation. it handles customer invoices, receipts, outstanding balances and follow-up of overdue payments. example: recording payment received from a customer. cash and bank management: it monitors cash received and paid, bank balances, bank transactions and bank reconciliation. it helps the organisation understand available cash and plan payments. fixed asset accounting: it maintains records of long-term assets such as buildings, machinery, computers and vehicles. it records asset purchase, transfer, depreciation and disposal. budgeting and financial planning: it helps prepare budgets, allocate funds to departments and compare actual spending with planned amounts. this helps control unnecessary expenses. cost and profitability analysis: it helps identify the cost of activities, products, departments or projects and analyse where the organisation earns profit or incurs loss. tax and statutory reporting: it helps calculate and record applicable taxes and prepare financial information required for tax and regulatory reporting. exact tax features depend on the erp and local rules. financial reporting: it generates reports such as the trial balance, profit and loss statement, balance sheet and cash-flow statement to help management understand financial performance. 4.4 integration of finance with other erp modules the finance module is connected with other erp modules. when a business activity takes place, the related financial information can be transferred to accounting automatically or through configured workflows. purchase / materials management: supplier invoices and material purchases update payable and inventory-related accounts. sales and distribution: customer billing updates revenue and accounts receivable. inventory: stock receipts, issues and valuation affect inventory-related financial records. human resources / payroll: salary and employee expense information can be posted to finance. production: material, labour and overhead costs help calculate product and production costs. simple flow: business transaction → relevant erp module → financial posting → general ledger → financial reports. 1 business transaction purchase, sale, stock, payroll 2 erp module mm, sd, inventory, hr, production 3 financial posting automatic or by workflow 4 general ledger main book of accounts 5 financial reports p&l, balance sheet, cash flow figure: how transactions from other modules reach the general ledger and reports. 4.5 benefits of the finance module accuracy: reduces repeated manual entry and accounting mistakes. real-time information: gives updated information about payments, receipts and balances. time saving: automates routine accounting and reporting tasks. better financial control: helps monitor budgets, expenses and outstanding payments. improved cash management: provides visibility of cash inflows and outflows. better decisions: reports help managers plan investments and control costs. transparency and accountability: transaction records and approval controls make activities easier to trace. integrated operations: connects financial data with purchasing, sales, inventory, payroll and production. 4.6 practical example a manufacturing company purchases raw materials from a supplier for ₹50,000. the purchase information is recorded through the purchasing process. the finance module records the supplier liability in accounts payable and updates the relevant accounting records. when the company pays the supplier, the payment is recorded and the outstanding payable is reduced. the general ledger reflects the accounting impact, and management can view the updated financial position. 4.7 short exam answer q. explain the finance module of erp and its main functions. the finance module is an important part of an erp system. it manages and controls the financial activities of an organisation by recording transactions and providing financial information for decision-making. its main functions are: general ledger: maintains the main record of financial transactions. accounts payable: manages payments due to suppliers. accounts receivable: manages money to be collected from customers. cash and bank management: tracks cash, bank balances and payments. fixed asset accounting: records assets, depreciation and disposal. budgeting: helps prepare budgets and control expenses. financial reporting: prepares financial statements and reports. the finance module is integrated with other erp modules such as sales, purchase, inventory, production and payroll. therefore, it improves accuracy, saves time, strengthens financial control and supports better decision-making. 4.8 quick revision gl = main book of accounts. ap = money to be paid to suppliers. ar = money to be received from customers. cash management = cash, bank and liquidity. fixed assets = asset records and depreciation. budgeting = planned spending and control. reporting = financial statements for decisions. 4.9 learning resources geeksforgeeks — sap functionality and features (erp financial-management notes on benefits of pdm and plant maintenance.” plant maintenance is therefore important for the examination. prepare its meaning, objectives, types, functions/process and benefits. 5.1 introduction to plant maintenance every manufacturing organisation uses machines, tools, equipment and other physical assets to produce goods. these machines must be kept in good working condition. due to continuous use, machines may develop faults, wear out or stop working. regular inspection, servicing and repair are therefore necessary. plant maintenance is the activity of inspecting, servicing, repairing and maintaining machines, equipment and other physical assets of an organisation so that they remain safe, reliable and available for production. exam-ready definition — what is plant maintenance? plant maintenance is the process of inspecting, maintaining and repairing plant machinery, equipment and other technical assets to keep them in proper working condition, prevent unexpected breakdowns and ensure continuous and efficient production. in simple words: plant maintenance means taking proper care of factory machines and equipment through regular checking, servicing and repair so that production work is not interrupted. 5.2 objectives of plant maintenance prevent machine breakdown: identify possible problems and take action before machines stop working. increase equipment life: regular servicing and timely repair help machines remain useful for a longer period. reduce production downtime: keep machines available so that production can continue with fewer interruptions. maintain product quality: properly working machines help produce goods with consistent quality. improve safety: inspection and repair reduce risks to workers and equipment. control maintenance cost: planned maintenance can reduce expensive emergency repairs and production losses. use resources properly: plan the required technicians, spare parts, tools and maintenance time. 5.3 types of plant maintenance plant maintenance can be performed in different ways depending on the condition of the equipment and the maintenance plan. type meaning example 1. preventive maintenance maintenance performed at planned time intervals or according to usage, before a breakdown occurs. changing machine oil every three months and checking belts every month. 2. corrective maintenance maintenance carried out to correct a fault or defect that has been identified in equipment. replacing a damaged bearing after inspection detects a problem. 3. breakdown / reactive maintenance repair performed after equipment has stopped working or failed. repairing a motor after it suddenly stops during production. 4. predictive maintenance maintenance planned using condition-monitoring information to estimate when a failure may occur. using vibration or temperature readings to identify early signs of motor failure. remember the difference: preventive maintenance is done before failure according to a schedule. corrective maintenance fixes an identified defect. breakdown maintenance responds after a failure. predictive maintenance uses equipment-condition information to decide when maintenance is needed. 5.4 main activities / functions of plant maintenance inspection: checking machines and equipment to identify their actual condition, wear, damage or faults. preventive servicing: performing regular activities such as cleaning, lubrication, tightening and replacement of parts according to a schedule. repair: restoring faulty or damaged equipment to proper working condition. maintenance planning: deciding what work is required, when it will be done and how much time it will take. resource and spare-parts management: arranging technicians, tools, materials and spare parts required for maintenance work. work-order management: recording maintenance work, assigning responsibility and tracking the progress of the job. maintenance records: maintaining equipment details, repair history, service dates, work performed and maintenance costs. performance monitoring: reviewing breakdowns, downtime and maintenance expenses to improve future maintenance activities. 5.5 plant maintenance module in erp in an erp system, the plant maintenance module helps an organisation manage maintenance activities in a planned and organised way. it stores equipment information, records maintenance requests, creates maintenance plans and work orders, and tracks the completion and cost of maintenance work. it provides common information to maintenance staff and other departments. for example, when a machine needs a spare part, the maintenance process can be connected with the inventory and purchasing functions of erp. 5.6 working process of plant maintenance in erp a typical maintenance process in an erp system follows these steps: equipment registration: machine and equipment details are recorded in the system. inspection or maintenance request: a user reports a fault, or a planned maintenance date becomes due. notification: the problem or maintenance requirement is documented. planning and work order: the maintenance team decides the work to be performed, assigns technicians and identifies required tools and spare parts. scheduling: a suitable date and time are selected, considering machine availability and production requirements. execution: technicians inspect, service or repair the equipment. completion and recording: the work order is completed and details of labour, materials, time and cost are recorded. maintenance history: the records are saved for future inspection, analysis and planning. 1 equipment registration machine details recorded 2 maintenance request fault reported or plan falls due 3 notification problem is documented 4 planning & work order tasks, people, parts assigned 5 scheduling date fixed around production 6 execution inspect, service or repair 7 completion & recording labour, material, cost entered 8 maintenance history saved for analysis and planning figure: plant maintenance process in an erp system (steps 5.6 above). how to read the diagram: follow the steps left to right. a reported fault or a due preventive-maintenance date starts the process. the work order drives scheduling and execution, and the recorded history helps plan future maintenance. 5.7 integration of plant maintenance with other erp modules plant maintenance is connected with other erp modules because maintenance work requires materials, employees, production schedules and financial information. materials management: provides spare parts and other materials required for maintenance. if a required item is unavailable, purchasing may be initiated. production planning: coordinates machine maintenance with production schedules and planned shutdowns. human resource management: provides information about technicians, employee availability, skills and working hours. finance / controlling: records maintenance expenses, labour costs, spare-parts costs and the total cost of maintenance. quality management: equipment condition and maintenance records can support quality checks because machine performance affects product quality. 5.8 benefits of plant maintenance reduces machine breakdowns: regular inspection and preventive maintenance help identify problems early. increases machine life: proper servicing and timely repair reduce unnecessary wear and damage. reduces downtime: well-maintained equipment is less likely to stop unexpectedly, helping production continue. improves productivity: machines remain available and employees can complete production work more efficiently. reduces operating cost: planned work can reduce emergency repair expenses, material wastage and production losses. improves product quality: machines working in proper condition help maintain consistent product standards. improves workplace safety: inspection and repair help identify unsafe equipment conditions. better planning and control: erp records help managers plan maintenance schedules, spare parts, technicians and budgets. maintains maintenance history: records of previous faults and repairs help identify repeated problems and make better decisions. thus, plant maintenance helps an organisation keep its machines reliable, reduce interruptions, control costs and maintain efficient production. 5.9 practical example suppose a factory uses a machine to manufacture metal parts. the erp system contains the machine's details and its regular service schedule. when the scheduled service date arrives, the system helps the maintenance team plan the work. the team checks the machine, changes its oil and replaces a worn belt. the required spare part is issued from inventory, and the technician records the completed work and time spent. the maintenance history is updated. this reduces the chance of a sudden breakdown during production. 5.10 previous-year write short notes on the benefits of plant maintenance. 5.11 exam-ready answer — benefits of plant maintenance (7.5 marks) q. write a short note on the benefits of plant maintenance. answer: plant maintenance is the process of inspecting, servicing and repairing machines, equipment and other plant assets to keep them in proper working condition. it helps an organisation prevent unexpected breakdowns and maintain continuous production. the major benefits of plant maintenance are: reduces breakdowns: regular inspection helps detect faults before they become serious. increases equipment life: timely servicing and repair keep machines in good condition for a longer period. reduces downtime: proper maintenance reduces unexpected machine stoppages. improves productivity: available and reliable machines help production work run smoothly. controls cost: planned maintenance reduces emergency repair costs and production losses. improves quality: properly maintained machines help produce consistent-quality products. improves safety: inspection and repair reduce the risk of accidents caused by faulty equipment. supports planning: erp records help plan technicians, spare parts, schedules and maintenance budgets. therefore, plant maintenance improves equipment reliability, increases productivity, reduces costs and supports the smooth operation of an organisation. 5.12 quick revision plant maintenance: inspection, servicing and repair of machines and equipment. preventive: planned maintenance before failure. corrective: repairing an identified fault. breakdown: repair after equipment failure. predictive: using condition information to estimate maintenance needs. erp process: equipment record → notification → planning / work order → scheduling → execution → completion → history. main benefits: less breakdown, less downtime, longer equipment life, lower cost, better quality and safety. 5.13 learning resources sap help — plant maintenance (inspection, preventive maintenance, repair and integration). sap help — maintenance processing (notifications, work orders and maintenance history). oracle — equipment / plant maintenance process flow (equipment master, maintenance schedule, work orders and completion). youtube resources these are topic-specific youtube search links, not individually verified video recommendations. preferred channel · search
