identify a confirmed question from this topic. it is still part of the official unit v syllabus, so prepare the definition, objectives, functions, inspection process, integration and benefits. questions below are practice or predicted questions, not verified pyqs. 6.1 introduction to quality management every organisation wants to provide products and services that satisfy customer requirements. in manufacturing, a product may have defects because of poor-quality raw materials, machine problems, incorrect production methods or human errors. therefore, an organisation must plan quality standards, inspect materials and products, identify defects and take corrective action. quality management (qm) is the systematic process of planning, checking, controlling and improving the quality of materials, production processes and finished products so that they meet specified standards and customer requirements. exam-ready definition — what is quality management? quality management is the process of planning, monitoring, inspecting and controlling the quality of raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods to ensure that products meet predefined specifications, standards and customer expectations. in simple words: quality management means making sure that the right quality is maintained at every stage — from purchasing raw materials to manufacturing and delivering the final product. 6.2 objectives of quality management maintain product quality: ensure that products meet defined specifications and standards. customer satisfaction: deliver reliable products that fulfil customer needs. reduce defects: identify and prevent errors, rework and rejection. control production processes: monitor operations so that variations are identified early. improve continuously: use inspection results and defect information to improve processes. reduce cost: minimise wastage, scrap, rework, returns and warranty-related expenses. ensure compliance: maintain required quality records and follow applicable standards and procedures. improve supplier quality: check purchased materials and monitor supplier performance. 6.3 main functions of quality management an erp quality management module supports the following major functions: quality planning: defines quality requirements, inspection plans, inspection characteristics, sampling procedures and test methods before inspection is performed. quality inspection: checks raw materials, semi-finished goods, finished products and other relevant items against predefined specifications. quality control: compares actual inspection results with required limits and identifies whether the product or process is acceptable. results recording: stores measured values and inspection observations in the erp system for later review and analysis. defect recording: records non-conformities, defects and failures found during inspection. corrective action: helps the organisation investigate the cause of a problem, assign corrective tasks and monitor their completion. quality certificates: supports the preparation and management of certificates that provide information about the quality of a product or batch. quality reporting: provides information and reports to evaluate quality performance, defects and inspection results. 6.4 types of quality inspection incoming / goods receipt inspection: raw materials or purchased goods are inspected when they arrive from a supplier. example: checking the thickness and quality of steel sheets received by a factory. in-process inspection: materials are checked during manufacturing to find problems before the entire production process is completed. example: checking the dimensions of a component after machining. final inspection: the completed product is inspected before it is transferred to finished-goods stock or delivered to a customer. example: testing a finished electric motor before dispatch. outgoing / delivery inspection: products are checked before dispatch to ensure that the goods being delivered satisfy the required conditions. recurring inspection: stock or equipment is inspected at planned intervals to confirm that it continues to meet quality requirements. calibration / equipment inspection: measuring and test equipment is checked or calibrated to ensure that its readings are reliable. 6.5 quality management module in erp in an erp system, quality management is an integrated module that connects quality-related activities with purchasing, inventory, production, sales and other business functions. it keeps quality information in a common system instead of maintaining separate records in different departments. for example, when purchased raw material is received, the erp system can create an inspection lot. the quality department performs the inspection, records the results and makes a decision to accept or reject the material. the result can then guide the inventory or purchasing process. 6.6 important components of erp quality management quality master data: basic information such as inspection characteristics, inspection methods, sampling procedures, catalogs and material-related quality data. inspection planning: inspection plans and specifications that explain what to inspect, how to inspect it and which limits or methods to use. inspection lot: a system record/request used to carry out and document a quality inspection for a particular quantity of material, product or equipment. results recording: entry and evaluation of measured values or observations for the inspection characteristics. defects recording: documentation of faults or results that do not meet the required specifications. usage decision: the final decision about whether the inspected material or product is accepted, rejected, blocked, sent for rework or otherwise processed according to the organisation's rules. quality notifications: records used to report and manage quality problems, investigate causes, assign corrective tasks and track their status. quality information and certificates: reports, evaluations and certificates that help monitor quality performance and communicate product quality information. important exam terms: an inspection lot is the record for an inspection. results recording stores what was found. a usage decision records the final accept/reject decision after the required inspection results are evaluated. 6.7 working process of quality management in erp a typical erp quality inspection follows these steps: define quality requirements: the organisation sets specifications, inspection characteristics and acceptable limits. create an inspection plan: the system stores the inspection method, sampling procedure and characteristics to be checked. trigger inspection: a business event, such as goods receipt or completion of production, creates an inspection requirement. create inspection lot: the erp system or authorised user creates an inspection lot for the relevant material or product. perform inspection: the inspector checks the sample or product according to the inspection plan. record and evaluate results: measured values and defects are entered and compared with the defined specifications. make usage decision: the authorised user or configured system process decides whether the material is accepted or rejected. take follow-up action: depending on the decision, stock may be released, blocked, returned, reworked or scrapped. a quality notification or corrective action may also be initiated. store quality history: the system retains inspection and defect information for reporting and future improvement. 1 inspection plan characteristics, limits, sampling 2 trigger goods receipt or production complete 3 inspection lot record created for the quantity 4 perform inspection check samples per plan 5 record results & defects compare with limits 6 usage decision accept, reject or block 7 follow-up action release, return, rework or scrap 8 quality history kept for reports and traceability figure: typical erp quality inspection workflow, from inspection plan to quality history. 6.8 integration of quality management with other erp modules materials management (mm): qm checks purchased materials at goods receipt. inspection results help decide whether received stock can be released for use, kept blocked or returned to the supplier. production planning (pp): qm supports inspection during production and after production. defects found during manufacturing can be reported so that production processes can be corrected. sales and distribution (sd): qm supports quality checks before delivery and helps maintain quality-related information or certificates for customers. plant maintenance (pm): qm can support inspection and calibration of machines, measuring devices and technical equipment. finance / controlling: quality-related costs, such as scrap, rework, inspection and non-conformance costs, can support cost monitoring and analysis. 6.9 benefits of quality management in erp improved product quality: regular inspection helps ensure that products meet required specifications. higher customer satisfaction: better-quality products reduce complaints and increase customer confidence. early defect detection: problems can be identified during purchasing or production rather than after delivery. reduced wastage and cost: less scrap, rework, rejection and product return helps reduce operating costs. centralised information: quality plans, inspection results and defect records are available in one integrated system. better supplier control: inspection records help an organisation evaluate the quality of materials received from suppliers. faster decisions: recorded results and system-based workflows help authorised employees make acceptance or rejection decisions. traceability: inspection history makes it easier to review when, how and against which specifications a product or batch was checked. continuous improvement: reports and defect analysis help identify repeated problems and improve processes. 6.10 practical example suppose a company manufactures electric fans and purchases copper wire from a supplier. when the copper wire arrives, the erp system creates an inspection lot. the quality inspector checks the wire's thickness, conductivity and quantity according to the inspection plan. the inspector records the measured results in the system. if the results meet the required specifications, the quality department makes an accepted usage decision and the material can be released for production. if the results do not meet the specifications, the material may be rejected or blocked . a quality notification can be created and the purchasing department can coordinate with the supplier. this example shows how erp quality management connects inspection with inventory, purchasing and production. 6.11 difference between quality assurance and quality control quality assurance (qa) quality control (qc) focuses on preventing defects by improving processes. focuses on identifying defects in materials or products. process-oriented approach. product / inspection-oriented approach. includes procedures, standards, training and process planning. includes testing, measurement, inspection and result evaluation. example: preparing a standard manufacturing procedure. example: measuring a finished component to check its dimensions. 6.12 exam preparation — questions verified pyq status no direct or related quality management question was identified in the supplied question-paper analysis. therefore, no question below is labelled as an actual pyq. 1-mark / very short-answer practice define quality management. what is an inspection lot? what is a usage decision? name any two functions of the erp quality management module. what is a quality notification? 5-mark / short-answer practice explain the objectives of quality management. describe the different types of quality inspection. write a short note on the functions of erp quality management. explain the integration of quality management with materials management and production planning. 15-mark / long-answer predicted questions define quality management. explain its objectives, functions and benefits in an erp system. explain the complete quality inspection process in erp with a suitable diagram. discuss the major components of erp quality management and its integration with other erp modules. 6.13 exam-ready short note — quality management in erp quality management in erp quality management is the process of planning, inspecting, controlling and improving the quality of raw materials, work-in-progress and finished products so that they meet specified standards and customer requirements. the quality management module in erp supports quality planning, quality inspection and quality control. it maintains inspection plans, inspection characteristics, sampling procedures and quality records. when materials are received or production is completed, the system can create an inspection lot. the inspector performs the required tests and records the results. after evaluating the results, an authorised person makes a usage decision to accept or reject the material or product. defects can be recorded and quality notifications can be used to manage corrective actions. quality management is integrated with materials management, production planning, sales and distribution, plant maintenance and finance / controlling. this integration helps the organisation connect inspection decisions with purchasing, stock, production, delivery and cost records. benefits: it improves product quality and customer satisfaction, detects defects early, reduces wastage and rework, controls supplier quality, maintains inspection history, supports traceability and helps continuous improvement. thus, erp quality management helps an organisation maintain consistent quality throughout its business processes. 6.14 quick revision meaning: planning, inspecting, controlling and improving quality. objectives: customer satisfaction, fewer defects, lower cost and consistent quality. types: incoming, in-process, final, outgoing, recurring and equipment inspection. important records: inspection plan, inspection lot, results, defects and quality notification. final step: usage decision — accept, reject or take the configured follow-up action. integration: mm, pp, sd, pm and finance / controlling. benefits: better quality, traceability, less wastage and continuous improvement. 6.15 learning resources sap help — quality management (qm) (features, integration and qm components). sap help — inspection lot creation (inspection lot creation and process). sap help — processing of inspection results (recording and evaluating inspection results). sap help — usage decision for inspection lot (acceptance or rejection decision). youtube resources these are topic-specific youtube search links, not individually verified video recommendations. preferred channel · search link gate smashers quality management in erp s/4hana. main modules and their functions. important features, advantages and limitations. how sap integrates departments in an organisation. 1.1 introduction and meaning of sap sap stands for systems, applications and products in data processing . it is a german enterprise software company best known for developing integrated business software, including enterprise resource planning (erp) systems. sap erp helps an organisation manage important business activities—such as finance, purchasing, inventory, production, sales, human resources and maintenance—through connected applications and shared business data. exam definition: sap is an integrated enterprise software solution that connects different functional areas of an organisation and helps manage business processes and information through a common system. in simple words, sap connects departments so that information entered in one department can be used by other authorised departments. this reduces repeated data entry and helps managers work with consistent information. 1.2 history and development of sap sap was founded on 1 april 1972 by five former ibm employees: dietmar hopp, hasso plattner, claus wellenreuther, klaus tschira and hans-werner hector. the original company name was systemanalyse programmentwicklung , meaning system analysis and program development. its original idea was to develop standard business software that could integrate business processes and process data in real time. year / generation development importance 1972 sap was founded in germany. its founders aimed to create integrated, real-time business software. r/1 early real-time business applications. established the foundation for integrated financial and business processing. 1979 — r/2 mainframe-based business software. supported integrated business functions, including multi-company and international operations. 1992 — r/3 client-server erp software. helped sap expand globally and supported a three-tier client/server architecture. 2000s — sap erp / ecc expanded enterprise application suite. provided integrated modules for finance, logistics, human resources and other functions. 2011 — sap hana in-memory data platform. enabled high-speed transaction processing and analytics. 2015 — sap s/4hana next-generation erp suite built on sap hana. modernised the erp core and supports current cloud and on-premise deployment options. remember for exams: r/2 is associated with mainframe computing, r/3 with client-server architecture, and s/4hana with the sap hana in-memory platform. 1.3 sap erp architecture and integration traditional sap r/3 is commonly explained through a three-tier client-server architecture: presentation layer: the user interface through which employees enter data and view reports. application layer: executes business rules, validates transactions and processes application logic. database layer: stores business data such as customer records, material information, orders and financial transactions. 1 presentation layer user interface where employees enter data and view reports 2 application layer executes business rules, validates transactions and processes application logic 3 database layer stores customer records, materials, orders and financial transactions figure 1a: sap r/3 three-tier client-server architecture. sap erp one shared database fi financial accounting co controlling mm materials mgmt sd sales & distribution pp production planning qm quality mgmt pm plant maintenance hcm human capital mgmt figure 1b: sap erp modules share one database, so data entered in one module is available to the others. because the modules share data, a transaction in one department can affect another department. for example, when a sales order is created, the system can check inventory, trigger delivery activities and support billing and accounting. 1.4 main modules of sap erp module full form / area main work fi financial accounting records financial transactions, accounts payable, accounts receivable, general ledger and financial statements. co controlling supports internal cost tracking, cost centres, budgeting and management accounting. mm materials management manages purchasing, goods receipt, stock and material movements. sd sales and distribution handles customer orders, pricing, delivery, shipping and billing. pp production planning plans production, materials, capacity and manufacturing schedules. qm quality management supports quality inspection, recording of results and quality control. pm plant maintenance manages equipment maintenance, breakdowns, inspections and maintenance orders. hcm / hr human capital management / human resources manages employee, organisational, payroll and personnel information. ps project system supports project planning, scheduling, costs and monitoring. note: module names and product packaging vary across sap generations and editions. the table lists commonly taught sap erp functional areas. 1.5 important features of sap integration: connects business functions so information can flow between departments. centralised data: maintains common business records and reduces duplicate data. real-time processing: updates relevant information when transactions are posted. modular structure: organisations can implement functional modules according to their requirements. standard business processes: provides structured workflows for common business activities. reporting and analysis: helps users monitor operations and support decisions. scalability and international support: supports complex organisations, multiple locations and different currencies, depending on the product and configuration. security and authorisation: access can be controlled according to user roles and responsibilities. 1.6 advantages of sap improves coordination among departments. reduces duplicate data entry and inconsistent records. provides timely information for operational and management decisions. improves control over purchasing, inventory, production and finance. supports standardisation of business processes. helps monitor costs, resources and organisational performance. can support large, multi-location and international businesses. 1.7 limitations / challenges of sap high cost: licensing, implementation, infrastructure, support and training can require substantial investment. complex implementation: large projects need careful planning, configuration and testing. training requirement: employees need training to use the system correctly. change management: existing processes and employee responsibilities may need to change. dependence on data quality: incorrect master data can lead to incorrect planning and reports. customisation challenges: excessive customisation can increase cost and make future upgrades more difficult. 1.8 practical example of sap consider a company that manufactures refrigerators. a customer places an order through the sales department. sap sd records the sales order. the system checks stock information maintained through mm. if stock is insufficient, pp can help plan production. mm supports the purchase of required raw materials. when goods are delivered, sd supports delivery and billing, while fi records the financial impact. thus, several departments work on connected information rather than maintaining separate records. ★ exam-ready short note: sap (5–7.5 marks) sap stands for systems, applications and products in data processing. it is a german enterprise software company known for integrated erp solutions. sap was founded in 1972 by five former ibm employees. its erp software developed through generations such as r/1, r/2, r/3, sap erp and sap s/4hana. sap erp integrates the major functional areas of an organisation. important modules include fi (financial accounting), co (controlling), mm (materials management), sd (sales and distribution), pp (production planning), qm (quality management), pm (plant maintenance) and hcm/hr (human resources). the major features of sap are integration, centralised data, real-time processing, modular structure, reporting and security. it improves coordination, reduces duplicate data entry and supports better decision-making. however, implementation can be costly and complex and requires employee training and proper data management. conclusion: sap helps organisations manage different business functions through an integrated erp environment. 1.9 important questions for examination 1-mark questions what is the full form of sap? in which year was sap founded? what is sap r/3 known for in erp history? what is the full form of fi, mm and sd? 5-mark questions write a short note on sap. explain any five important modules of sap erp. differentiate between sap r/2 and sap r/3. explain the three-tier architecture of sap r/3. 10–15-mark predicted questions explain the applications and products in data processing. founded in 1972 by five former ibm employees. r/2 = mainframe; r/3 = client-server; s/4hana = built on sap hana. important modules: fi, co, mm, sd, pp, qm, pm and hcm/hr. main strengths: integration, centralised data and real-time business processing. main challenges: cost, complexity, training and data quality. 2 topic 2 of 4 baan erp red priority — main modules carefully. ★ what to prepare from this topic ★ meaning and background of baan erp. history and later ownership of the baan product line. main components: manufacturing, finance, project, distribution and tools. important manufacturing functions and dynamic enterprise modeler (dem). features, advantages, limitations and applications. verified short-note question. 2.1 introduction and meaning of baan baan refers to the erp software originally developed by the dutch software company baan corporation. it was designed to integrate business functions, with particular strength in manufacturing and complex industrial operations. exam definition: baan is an integrated erp software package originally developed by baan corporation of the netherlands. it supports major business functions such as manufacturing, finance, project management and distribution through connected applications and shared information. baan became known for supporting manufacturing organisations that needed to coordinate product structures, production planning, shop-floor activities, inventory, purchasing, finance and distribution. 2.2 history and development of baan baan corporation was founded in the netherlands in 1978 . the baan erp product family grew into a recognised enterprise software solution, particularly for discrete manufacturing and project-driven industries. period development importance 1978 baan corporation was founded in the netherlands. established the company that later developed baan erp software. 1990s baan grew in the erp market; baan iv became a well-known product generation. built a strong presence in manufacturing and industrial organisations. 2000 invensys acquired baan. the product became part of invensys's software business. 2003 ssa global acquired the baan business from invensys. the product line continued under ssa global. 2006 infor acquired ssa global. the former baan product line became part of infor's erp portfolio. today the product lineage continues as infor ln. infor describes ln as an erp solution developed originally by baan for complex, global, project-driven manufacturers. important clarification: baan is the historical erp product name. it is not a separate current independent vendor. its product lineage is now associated with infor ln. in an examination answer, explain baan in its historical erp context, as asked in the syllabus. 2.3 main components of baan erp study material commonly groups baan erp into five broad components: component main functions 1. manufacturing bill of materials, product configuration, priority — predicted / syllabus-based question evidence: the supplied ranchi priority sheet does not identify a direct question specifically asking for the advantages and disadvantages of in-house erp implementation. it is an official syllabus topic and is suitable for a 5- or 10–15-mark answer. 1.1 introduction erp implementation is the process of planning, configuring, testing and introducing an erp system in an organisation. in an in-house implementation , the organisation uses its own employees and internal project team to carry out most of the implementation activities instead of handing the complete responsibility to an outside implementation partner. internal employees may include it staff, department representatives, project managers, database administrators and selected end-users. the organisation may still purchase the erp software from an external vendor and may obtain limited specialist assistance when required. important clarification: in-house implementation does not necessarily mean that the company develops an erp package from zero. it usually means that the company takes primary responsibility for implementing and configuring a purchased erp system using its own people. 1.2 definition exam-ready definition: in-house erp implementation is an approach in which an organisation implements an erp system mainly through its own internal employees and resources, taking responsibility for project planning, process analysis, configuration, data preparation, testing, training and ongoing support. 1.3 how in-house implementation works form an internal project team: select a project manager, it staff and representatives from departments such as finance, hr, purchasing, sales and production. study business requirements: document existing processes, problems and the organisation's needs. plan the erp project: define scope, schedule, budget, responsibilities and risks. configure the erp package: set up modules, workflows, user roles, approval rules and reports using internal expertise. prepare and migrate data: clean existing records and transfer approved data into the new system. test the system: perform module, integration, security and user-acceptance testing. train employees and go live: train users, introduce the system and monitor early operations. provide support: resolve issues, maintain the system and improve processes. 1 top management approval and resources 2 internal project team project manager, it, departments 3 requirements & configuration study processes, set up modules 4 data migration & testing clean, load and verify 5 training & go-live train users, switch over 6 internal support maintain and improve figure 1: flow of an internally led erp implementation. the team may call in outside specialists where needed. 1.4 advantages of in-house implementation better knowledge of business processes: internal employees understand the organisation's actual work, rules, culture and operational problems. greater control: management can directly control project decisions, priorities, schedules and implementation methods. improved ownership and commitment: employees who help configure the system are more likely to understand and accept the new working environment. knowledge retention: erp knowledge remains within the organisation, helping with future maintenance, upgrades and improvements. potential reduction in consulting fees: the organisation may reduce the amount of paid external consulting support. better alignment with internal requirements: internal staff can explain organisation-specific needs during configuration and testing. direct communication: department representatives can communicate issues directly to the project team. 1.5 disadvantages of in-house implementation lack of specialised expertise: employees may not have sufficient experience with erp configuration, integration, data migration or project management. longer implementation time: internal employees must balance erp work with their normal duties, which can delay the project. high training requirement: staff may need extensive training before they can configure and manage the erp system effectively. risk of mistakes: incorrect configuration, weak testing or poor data migration can create serious operational problems. limited outside perspective: employees may continue old processes instead of identifying better practices available in the erp package. dependence on key employees: if trained staff leave the organisation, important system knowledge may be lost. hidden internal cost: employee time, training, infrastructure and project delays can make the approach expensive even when consultancy fees are lower. 1.6 in-house implementation vs external implementation partner basis in-house implementation external partner-led implementation people mainly the organisation's own employees. external consultants and implementation specialists work with the organisation. business knowledge usually strong knowledge of internal processes. must learn the organisation's processes and requirements. erp expertise depends on the skills of internal staff. can provide specialised product and implementation experience. cost pattern may reduce consulting fees, but internal staff time and training still cost money. consulting and partner fees can be substantial. control more direct internal control. some activities are shared with the partner. knowledge after go-live knowledge is developed internally. knowledge transfer must be planned to avoid long-term dependence. 1.7 example suppose a medium-sized manufacturing company purchases an erp package. it forms an internal team consisting of its it manager, accountant, purchase officer, store manager and production supervisor. these employees map the company's processes, configure the relevant modules with available expertise, test purchase and production transactions, train colleagues and coordinate go-live. if advanced database or integration work is needed, the company may hire a specialist for that limited task. this is an internally led or in-house implementation. 1.8 conditions for success strong support from top management. availability of trained internal employees. clear project scope, budget and schedule. participation of employees from all important departments. proper data cleaning, testing and user training. documentation and knowledge-sharing so that the project does not depend on one person. external specialist support when internal skills are insufficient. ★ exam-ready 5-mark answer in-house erp implementation is an approach in which an organisation uses its own employees and internal resources to implement an erp system. the internal team performs requirement analysis, project planning, configuration, data migration, testing, training and support. advantages: better understanding of business processes, greater control, employee ownership, knowledge retention and possible reduction in consulting fees. disadvantages: shortage of erp expertise, longer implementation time, training requirements, risk of configuration errors, limited outside perspective and dependence on key employees. it is suitable when an organisation has capable internal staff, management support and sufficient time. a hybrid approach can be used when specialist expertise is required. 1.9 important questions for examination 1-mark questions what is in-house erp implementation? name two internal members who may be part of an erp implementation team. what is meant by knowledge retention in erp implementation? 5-mark questions write a short note on in-house erp implementation. explain any five advantages and disadvantages of in-house erp implementation. differentiate between in-house and external partner-led implementation. 10–15-mark predicted questions explain in-house erp implementation in detail. discuss its advantages and disadvantages with a suitable example. compare in-house, external partner-led and hybrid erp implementation approaches. question status: these are syllabus-based practice and predicted questions. the supplied ranchi question analysis does not identify a direct in-house implementation pyq. 1.10 quick revision in-house implementation = implementation led mainly by the organisation's own employees. it does not necessarily mean developing erp software from scratch. advantages: business knowledge, control, ownership, internal knowledge and potential consulting-fee savings. disadvantages: skill gaps, longer time, training, risk of mistakes and dependence on key staff. a hybrid approach combines internal business knowledge with external specialist expertise. 2 topic 2 of 6 erp vendors red-related priority — external erp-paper evidence for vendor, consultant and end-user roles question evidence: the supplied priority sheet identifies an external erp-paper question asking about the roles of vendors, consultants and end-users. this supports preparing vendor roles, but it is not listed as a direct ranchi pyq on vendors alone. the direct ranchi 15-mark question in unit vii is on the erp implementation life cycle. 2.1 introduction an erp vendor is a company that develops, owns, licenses or supplies erp software to organisations. the vendor provides the erp product and may also provide product updates, technical documentation, maintenance, customer support, training resources and a network of certified implementation partners. organisations select an erp vendor according to their business size, industry, budget, required modules, technology environment and future plans. exam definition: an erp vendor is a software company that develops and supplies an erp package or cloud erp service and provides product-related updates, support and other services required to use the system. 2.2 major responsibilities of an erp vendor develop erp software: design and maintain modules for finance, hr, purchasing, inventory, production, sales and other business functions. provide licences or subscriptions: make the software available under suitable commercial terms, such as perpetual licences or cloud subscriptions. product updates and upgrades: release fixes, security updates, new features and supported product versions. technical documentation: provide installation guides, configuration information, user documentation and technical references. product support: help customers resolve product defects and technical issues under the support agreement. integration capabilities: provide apis, connectors and tools that allow the erp system to communicate with other applications. partner ecosystem: work with implementation partners, consultants and technology providers who help customers deploy and extend the erp system. product roadmap: communicate future product direction, supported technologies and changes that may affect customers. 2.3 examples of major erp vendors vendor example erp products / product families general area sap sap s/4hana; sap cloud erp broad enterprise erp for finance, procurement, manufacturing, supply chain and other functions. oracle oracle fusion cloud erp; oracle e-business suite cloud and enterprise applications for finance, procurement, projects, risk and related functions. microsoft dynamics 365 finance; dynamics 365 supply chain management; business central business applications for organisations of different sizes and operational needs. infor infor cloudsuite product families industry-focused enterprise applications, including manufacturing and distribution. sage sage x3 and other sage business-management products business management and erp solutions, including finance, distribution and manufacturing use cases. epicor epicor kinetic erp solutions with a strong focus on manufacturing and distribution organisations. product names and portfolios can change over time. the examples above are included to illustrate the erp vendor market; they are not a ranking of vendors. 2.4 types of erp vendors / solutions large enterprise erp vendors: supply broad, highly integrated erp suites for complex and often multinational organisations. mid-market erp vendors: focus on the needs of small and medium-sized organisations, often with more focused implementation scope. industry-specific erp vendors: offer solutions designed for sectors such as manufacturing, retail, construction, healthcare or distribution. cloud erp providers: deliver erp capabilities through cloud infrastructure, commonly using a subscription model. open-source erp providers: offer erp software whose source code is available under an open-source licence, subject to the licence terms. 2.5 vendor selection process choosing the right erp vendor is a major decision because the selected product may influence the organisation's processes, data, cost and technology for many years. identify requirements: list business processes, users, locations, reporting needs and required modules. prepare a shortlist: identify vendors whose products match the organisation's industry, size and requirements. evaluate functionality: compare finance, hr, purchasing, inventory, production, sales and other required features. check technology: review cloud or on-premise options, integration, security, scalability, usability and data-management capabilities. evaluate total cost: consider software subscription or licence, implementation, infrastructure, migration, training, support and future upgrades. check vendor capability: examine product stability, support arrangements, implementation ecosystem, references and product roadmap. demonstration and proof of concept: ask shortlisted vendors to demonstrate important business scenarios using realistic requirements. final selection and contract: select the best-fit solution, define responsibilities, service levels, deliverables, support and exit/data arrangements. 1 identify requirements processes, users, modules 2 shortlist vendors industry and size fit 3 evaluate functionality finance, hr, inventory, production 4 check technology cloud / on-premise, security, scale 5 evaluate total cost licence, implementation, support 6 check vendor capability references, partners, roadmap 7 demo / proof of concept realistic business scenarios 8 select and contract define slas and exit terms figure 2: the eight-step vendor selection process described in section 2.5. 2.6 factors to consider while selecting an erp vendor factor what the organisation should check functional fit does the erp cover the organisation's important business processes? industry experience does the vendor understand the organisation's industry and regulatory needs? cost and value what is the total cost over the expected life of the system? scalability can the solution support more users, locations, transactions and business growth? integration can it connect with existing systems, suppliers, customers and other applications? security and compliance are access controls, data protection, audit and compliance requirements addressed? support and updates are support channels, service levels, product updates and upgrade paths suitable? partner ecosystem are capable implementation partners and trained specialists available? vendor stability is the vendor likely to maintain and support the product over the long term? 2.7 difference between erp vendor and erp implementation consultant erp vendor erp implementation consultant develops, owns or supplies the erp product. advises and assists the customer in implementing the erp product. responsible for product development, updates and product-level support. helps with requirement analysis, process mapping, configuration, testing, training and deployment. provides the software platform and product roadmap. helps the organisation use the software to meet its business requirements. may provide implementation services directly or through partners. may work for an independent consulting firm, an implementation partner or the vendor. 2.8 advantages of selecting a suitable erp vendor access to a tested and maintained erp product. regular updates, fixes and product improvements. availability of documentation, support and training resources. integration tools and a partner ecosystem. industry knowledge and established implementation methods. better opportunity for long-term scalability and product continuity. 2.9 risks of selecting an unsuitable erp vendor mismatch between product features and business requirements. unexpected implementation, customisation or subscription costs. insufficient local support or lack of skilled implementation partners. difficulty integrating with existing systems. vendor lock-in or costly migration to another product. product discontinuation, weak updates or inadequate support. 2.10 practical example a manufacturing company needs finance, purchasing, inventory, production planning and quality-management functions. it prepares a list of requirements, shortlists suitable erp vendors, compares their manufacturing capabilities, checks integration with existing machines and systems, reviews the total cost and asks for a demonstration. after checking references and support arrangements, it selects a vendor and signs a contract. the vendor supplies the erp product; an implementation team then configures and deploys it with the company's employees. ★ exam-ready 5-mark answer an erp vendor is a company that develops and supplies erp software or cloud erp services to organisations. major responsibilities include software development, licensing or subscriptions, product updates, technical documentation, product support, integration facilities and maintaining a partner ecosystem. examples of erp vendors include sap, oracle, microsoft, infor, sage and epicor. before selecting a vendor, an organisation should examine functional suitability, industry experience, technology, security, scalability, total cost, support, implementation partners and future product development. a suitable vendor provides a reliable erp product that supports integrated business processes. an unsuitable vendor may cause high costs, poor business fit, integration problems and long-term dependency. 2.11 important questions for examination 1-mark questions what is an erp vendor? name any two erp vendors. give one responsibility of an erp vendor. what is meant by vendor lock-in? 5-mark questions write a short note on erp vendors. explain the major responsibilities of an erp vendor. list the important factors considered while selecting an erp vendor. differentiate between an erp vendor and an implementation consultant. 10–15-mark predicted questions explain the role and responsibilities of erp vendors in an erp project. discuss the major factors involved in selecting an erp vendor. explain the types of erp vendors and give suitable examples. question status: vendor-related roles have external erp-paper support as part of the combined question on vendors, consultants and end-users. the supplied ranchi question analysis does not list a direct standalone question on erp vendors. these standalone questions are practice / predicted questions. 2.12 quick revision erp vendor = company that develops or supplies erp software / cloud service. main duties: product development, licences/subscriptions, updates, documentation, support and integration facilities. examples: sap, oracle, microsoft, infor, sage and epicor. vendor selection should consider functionality, cost, industry fit, technology, security, scalability, support and partner ecosystem. vendor supplies the product; an implementation consultant helps configure and deploy it for the customer. 3 topic 3 of 6 erp consultants yellow priority — syllabus-based; related external-paper evidence question evidence: the supplied ranchi question-priority sheet identifies an external erp-paper question on the combined roles of vendors, consultants and end-users. it does not identify a direct standalone ranchi pyq on erp consultants. prepare this topic as a likely 5-mark short note and as part of a longer answer on the roles of vendors, consultants and end-users. 3.1 introduction an erp consultant is a professional or specialist who advises an organisation and helps it plan, configure, customise where necessary, test and implement an enterprise resource planning system. a consultant understands both business processes and erp technology and helps connect the organisation's requirements with the capabilities of the selected erp package. consultants may work independently, for a consulting firm, or as part of an erp vendor's implementation partner network. they may support the project from software selection through go-live and post-implementation support. 3.2 definition exam-ready definition: an erp consultant is a specialist who analyses an organisation's business requirements and provides professional guidance and services for selecting, planning, configuring, integrating, testing and implementing an erp system. 3.3 diagram: roles of an erp consultant erp consultant links business needs to the software requirement analysis study processes and needs fit-gap & design map needs to erp functions configuration modules, workflows, roles data migration extract, clean, map, load integration & testing connect systems, run uat user training material and sessions go-live & support cutover, stabilise, hand over figure 1: the main roles of an erp consultant across an implementation. 3.4 types of erp consultants functional consultant: specialises in a business area or erp module such as finance, human resources, sales, purchasing, inventory or production. studies business requirements, maps processes to standard erp functions, configures the relevant module and supports functional testing and user training. technical consultant: works on technical aspects such as system installation, database and infrastructure, programming, reports, interfaces, extensions, data migration and troubleshooting. techno-functional consultant: has knowledge of both business processes and technical features. helps translate functional needs into technical solutions and coordinates between functional and technical teams. erp project-management consultant: helps plan and coordinate project scope, schedule, budget, resources, communication, risks, milestones and deliverables. erp selection consultant: helps an organisation define requirements, compare erp products and vendors, assess costs and prepare a selection recommendation before purchase. 3.5 major roles and responsibilities understand business requirements: meet managers and employees, study existing workflows and collect the organisation's functional and technical requirements. analyse existing processes: identify process problems, duplication, delays and opportunities for improvement. process mapping and fit-gap analysis: compare the organisation's requirements with standard erp capabilities and identify gaps that may need process changes, configuration or approved extensions. recommend a suitable solution: advise on erp modules, deployment approach, configuration options and implementation priorities. plan the implementation: help prepare the project plan, milestones, resources, responsibilities, risk controls and communication arrangements. configure the erp system: set up business rules, master data structures, workflows, roles, approvals and module parameters according to the approved design. support data migration: help extract, clean, map, validate and load data from old systems into the new erp system. coordinate integration and testing: help connect erp with other applications and support functional, integration and user-acceptance testing. train users: prepare training material, demonstrate processes and train key users and end-users. support go-live: assist with the transition to the live system, resolve implementation issues and monitor early operations. provide post-implementation support: help investigate problems, stabilise the system, transfer knowledge and recommend improvements. 3.6 functional consultant vs technical consultant basis functional consultant technical consultant main focus business processes and erp functions technology and system development typical work requirements, process mapping, module configuration and functional testing installation, programming, reports, interfaces, database and technical migration works closely with department heads, process owners and end-users it staff, developers, database and infrastructure teams example configures purchase approval workflow in the purchasing module builds an interface that transfers supplier data from another system 3.7 skills required by an erp consultant business knowledge: understanding of finance, purchasing, sales, inventory, production or hr processes. erp product knowledge: knowledge of erp modules, configuration and integration. analytical skills: ability to study processes, identify gaps and solve problems. communication: ability to discuss requirements with managers, technical teams and users. project-management skills: planning, coordination, documentation, time and risk management. training and interpersonal skills: ability to explain system changes and help employees adapt. technical skills: depending on the role, knowledge of databases, data migration, reporting, interfaces, programming or infrastructure. 3.8 advantages of using erp consultants provides specialist knowledge and implementation experience. helps translate business requirements into a workable erp design. can reduce avoidable configuration and implementation errors. supports data migration, testing, integration and training. brings structured project methods, documentation and risk management. can transfer knowledge to the organisation's internal team. 3.9 limitations and risks consulting services can increase the total project cost. the organisation may become too dependent on external specialists. a consultant may not fully understand the organisation's culture or every operational detail. miscommunication between consultants and employees can lead to an unsuitable solution. excessive customisation recommended without proper analysis can increase complexity and maintenance cost. knowledge may leave with the consultant if documentation and knowledge transfer are weak. 3.10 erp consultant's role during implementation project stage consultant's contribution before implementation requirement analysis, erp evaluation, vendor comparison and project planning design business process mapping, fit-gap analysis and solution blueprint configuration module setup, approved customisation, reports and integrations preparation data migration, testing, documentation and user training go-live cutover assistance, issue resolution and operational support after go-live stabilisation, knowledge transfer, maintenance and improvement 3.11 difference between erp vendor and erp consultant basis erp vendor erp consultant meaning company that develops or supplies erp software specialist who advises and helps implement erp main responsibility provides the erp product, licences or cloud service, updates and product support analyses requirements, designs the solution, configures and supports implementation relationship owns or supplies the product may work for the vendor, a partner firm or independently example sap, oracle, microsoft functional, technical or implementation consultant important: a vendor and a consultant are not always separate organisations. some erp vendors provide consulting services directly, while independent consulting firms and implementation partners may work with products from several vendors. 3.12 practical example a college decides to implement an erp system for admissions, student records, fees, examinations, payroll and finance. a functional consultant meets staff from each department and documents the existing processes. the consultant maps these requirements to erp modules, identifies gaps, recommends configuration, supports data migration and testing, and trains college employees. a technical consultant may separately handle database setup, integrations and reports. after go-live, the consultants help resolve initial issues and transfer system knowledge to the college's it team. ★ exam-ready 5-mark answer: erp consultants an erp consultant is a specialist who helps an organisation plan and implement an erp system. the consultant analyses business requirements, studies existing processes, maps requirements to erp modules, recommends solutions, configures the system, supports data migration and testing, trains users and assists during go-live. the main types are functional, technical, techno-functional, project-management and selection consultants. functional consultants focus on business modules, while technical consultants handle installation, programming, databases and integration. erp consultants provide expert knowledge and structured implementation support, but their services may increase cost and create dependency if knowledge is not transferred to internal employees. ★ predicted 10–15-mark answer outline question: explain the roles and responsibilities of erp consultants in erp implementation. introduction and definition of erp consultant. types: functional, technical, techno-functional, project-management and selection consultants. responsibilities: requirements, process analysis, fit-gap, solution design, configuration, migration, integration, testing, training and go-live. skills required and consultant contribution at each implementation stage. advantages and limitations. conclusion: consultants provide specialist support, while the organisation must retain ownership and internal knowledge. 3.13 important questions for examination 1-mark questions who is an erp consultant? name two types of erp consultants. what is a functional consultant? what is fit-gap analysis? 5-mark questions write a short note on erp consultants. explain the responsibilities of an erp consultant. differentiate between functional and technical consultants. differentiate between an erp vendor and an erp consultant. 10–15-mark predicted questions explain the different types, roles and responsibilities of erp consultants. discuss the importance, advantages and limitations of consultants in erp implementation. explain the role of vendors, consultants and end-users in erp implementation. question status: these standalone questions are practice / predicted. the supplied priority sheet identifies external-paper evidence for the combined roles of vendors, consultants and end-users, but not a direct standalone ranchi pyq on consultants. 3.14 quick revision erp consultant = specialist who connects business requirements with erp software. types: functional, technical, techno-functional, project-management and selection consultants. main work: analyse, map, design, configure, migrate, integrate, test, train and support. functional consultants focus on business processes; technical consultants focus on technology. consultants provide expertise but can increase cost and create dependency if knowledge transfer is weak. 4 topic 4 of 6 erp end-users red-related priority — external erp-paper evidence · 5–10 marks verified question evidence: the supplied ranchi university priority sheet records an external erp-paper question: “explain the roles of vendors, consultants and end users in erp implementation.” it is marked red for 5–10 marks. this is related external-paper evidence, not a direct standalone ranchi question on end-users. 4.1 introduction an erp end-user is an employee or authorised person who uses the erp system to perform regular business activities. end-users enter, update, retrieve and verify information through erp modules according to their job responsibilities. examples include accountants, purchase officers, storekeepers, sales executives, production supervisors, hr officers and managers. end-users are important because erp software is useful only when people use it correctly and consistently. they work with the live system and provide practical feedback about whether the configured processes meet actual business needs. 4.2 definition exam-ready definition: erp end-users are the authorised employees or business participants who interact directly with an erp system to perform their daily tasks, record transactions, access organisational information and support integrated business operations. 4.3 diagram: types of erp end-users erp end-users authorised people who use the system operational users daily transactions and entries managerial users reports, dashboards, approvals key / super users module experts who help colleagues occasional users self-service: leave, payslips administrators accounts, roles and permissions figure 1: types of erp end-users and what each typically does. 4.4 types of erp end-users operational end-users: perform daily transactions such as creating sales orders, recording purchases, issuing materials, entering attendance, preparing invoices and updating stock. managerial end-users: use reports, dashboards and summaries to monitor performance, approve transactions, allocate resources and make departmental decisions. key users / super users: have deeper knowledge of selected erp modules. they help colleagues, answer routine questions, support testing and communicate issues to the erp project team. occasional or self-service users: use the erp direct ranchi university pyq · 15 marks verified question from the supplied ranchi 2022–24 priority sheet: “what do you understand by erp implementation life cycle? with a neat diagram, discuss its different phases.” marks: 15 · prepare this topic thoroughly, including the phases, explanation, diagram, example and conclusion. 5.1 introduction erp implementation is a major organisational project in which an enterprise resource planning package is selected, planned, configured, tested and introduced into business operations. the erp implementation life cycle is the structured sequence of stages followed to move from the initial decision to implement erp to stable operation and continuous improvement. it provides a roadmap for coordinating people, processes, data, software, infrastructure, time, cost and organisational change. the exact names and number of phases differ among erp books, vendors and implementation methodologies. for the examination answer below, a widely taught classic academic sequence is explained; a modern sap methodology is also noted separately. 5.2 definition exam-ready definition: erp implementation life cycle is a systematic sequence of activities and phases through which an organisation evaluates and selects an erp package, plans the project, analyses and redesigns business processes, configures and tests the system, trains users, goes live and provides post-implementation support. 5.3 diagram: erp implementation life cycle (11 phases) 1 pre-evaluation screening need, objectives, readiness 2 package evaluation compare and select erp 3 project planning scope, team, budget, schedule 4 gap analysis requirements vs erp functions 5 bpr / process redesign simplify and standardise 6 configuration & customisation set up modules and rules 7 team training project team and key users 8 testing unit, integration, data, uat 9 go-live cutover to production 10 end-user training role-based adoption 11 post-implementation support stabilise and improve plan design build and test deploy and run figure 2: erp implementation life cycle. draw these 11 phases in order in the exam. 5.4 phases of the classic erp implementation life cycle phase 1 — pre-evaluation screening the organisation first examines whether it needs an erp system and whether erp is suitable for its size, industry, business problems and long-term goals. it studies the market, identifies broad requirements and prepares an initial business case. identify business problems such as disconnected databases, duplicate data, delayed reports or poor coordination. define broad objectives and expected benefits. estimate project size, budget, risks and readiness. decide whether erp adoption is justified. output: initial business case, broad requirements and approval to investigate erp solutions. phase 2 — package evaluation suitable erp packages and vendors are identified and compared. the organisation checks whether the software supports its business processes and industry requirements. prepare functional and technical requirements. compare erp products, modules, deployment options and technology. evaluate vendor reputation, industry experience, support and implementation partners. conduct product demonstrations and reference checks. compare licence or subscription costs, implementation expenses and total cost of ownership. output: selected erp package and vendor, with a documented selection decision. phase 3 — project planning after selecting the package, the organisation creates a detailed implementation plan. this phase establishes project governance and coordinates people, time, money and resources. appoint project sponsor, project manager and cross-functional team. define scope, objectives, milestones, budget and schedule. assign responsibilities to departments, vendor and consultants. prepare communication, risk, quality and change-management plans. identify infrastructure, integration and data requirements. output: approved project plan, team structure, schedule, budget and governance arrangements. phase 4 — gap analysis gap analysis compares the organisation's existing business processes and requirements with the standard functions available in the selected erp package. it identifies the difference between what the organisation needs and what the package can provide without changes. study current business processes (as-is). study the standard erp processes and proposed future processes (to-be). identify missing functions, process differences, reporting needs and integration gaps. decide whether to adopt standard erp processes, change the business process or approve a necessary extension. output: gap list, fit-gap analysis and approved solution requirements. phase 5 — business process reengineering (bpr) / process redesign business process reengineering means fundamentally rethinking and redesigning business processes to achieve major improvements in performance, cost, quality and service. during erp implementation, organisations may need to change old working methods to align with integrated erp processes. remove unnecessary or duplicate activities. simplify workflows and approval procedures. define responsibilities and controls clearly. standardise processes across departments or branches where appropriate. document the redesigned process before system configuration. output: redesigned business processes and an agreed process blueprint. bpr should be planned carefully; changing every process without justification can increase risk and resistance. phase 6 — configuration and customisation the selected erp package is configured to support the approved business processes. configuration means setting available options, rules and parameters. customisation means changing or extending the standard product through additional code or extensions when a genuine requirement cannot be met by configuration or process change. set up company codes, business units, plants, warehouses and organisational structures. configure finance, hr, purchasing, inventory, production, sales and other required modules. set approval rules, user roles, workflows, taxes, numbering and reports. develop approved extensions, interfaces or reports where necessary. prepare master data structures and migration mappings. output: configured erp system and documented solution design. excessive customisation should be avoided because it can increase cost and complicate upgrades. phase 7 — implementation team training the core implementation team, key users and super users receive detailed training on the erp product, configuration and business processes. they become the internal experts who can help other employees. train functional and technical project-team members. train key users in their modules and responsibilities. explain configuration, process flows, security and support procedures. prepare training material and user guides for the wider workforce. output: trained project team and key users ready to support testing, training and deployment. phase 8 — testing the configured erp system is tested to confirm that it works correctly and supports complete business processes. testing should cover individual functions as well as transactions that cross departments. unit / configuration testing: check individual configured functions. integration testing: verify that connected modules exchange information correctly. data migration testing: confirm migrated records are complete, accurate and reconciled. performance and security testing: check response, access controls and system behaviour under expected conditions. user acceptance testing (uat): business users execute realistic scenarios and confirm that requirements are met. record defects, correct them and repeat tests where necessary. output: approved test results, resolved critical defects and business acceptance to proceed. phase 9 — going live / deployment go-live is the point at which the organisation starts using the new erp system for real business transactions. the project team moves the approved solution and final data into the production environment. prepare a cutover plan and communicate the go-live date. complete final data migration and reconciliation. confirm users, roles, infrastructure, integrations and support coverage. switch from the old system or agreed legacy process to the new erp system. monitor transactions closely and resolve urgent issues. output: erp system operating in the production environment. phase 10 — end-user training and adoption all employees who will use the erp system receive role-based training. training explains the tasks each user must perform and the procedures they must follow in the live system. train users according to their roles and erp modules. demonstrate real transactions and common error-handling steps. provide user manuals, quick guides and help-desk support. explain security, passwords, approvals and data-quality responsibilities. collect feedback and provide additional support to users who need it. output: users prepared to perform their duties using the erp system. in practice, training often starts before go-live and continues after deployment; this separate phase highlights the importance of user adoption. phase 11 — post-implementation support and maintenance after go-live, the organisation stabilises the system, resolves remaining problems and checks whether expected benefits are being achieved. erp implementation does not end on the first day of live operation. provide help-desk and technical support. monitor system performance, security, data quality and transaction errors. resolve defects and improve reports or workflows. maintain documentation and train new employees. review project objectives, costs, benefits and user feedback. plan upgrades, patches and continuous improvement. output: stable erp operations, support arrangements and a continuous-improvement plan. 5.5 summary table of all phases no. phase main purpose / output 1 pre-evaluation screening identify need, objectives, readiness and initial business case. 2 package evaluation compare products and select erp package/vendor. 3 project planning approve scope, team, budget, schedule and governance. 4 gap analysis identify differences between requirements and standard erp functions. 5 bpr / process redesign redesign and standardise business processes. 6 configuration and customisation set up modules, rules, workflows and approved extensions. 7 implementation team training prepare project members and key users. 8 testing verify functions, integration, data, security and user acceptance. 9 go-live / deployment move to production and begin live transactions. 10 end-user training and adoption prepare employees to use erp correctly in their roles. 11 post-implementation support stabilise, maintain, measure benefits and improve continuously. 5.6 modern example: sap activate methodology modern erp vendors may use a different phase structure from the classic academic sequence. for example, sap activate describes six phases: discover: understand solution options, business value and project scope. prepare: finalise planning, onboard the project team and prepare the environment. explore: conduct fit-to-standard workshops and confirm the solution design. realize: configure, build, test and validate the solution through iterations. deploy: complete cutover, final testing and transition to production. run: operate, support and continuously optimise the erp solution. exam tip: use the classic phases in section 5.4 for the long-answer response, unless the question specifically asks about a vendor methodology such as sap activate. the number and names of phases vary by methodology. 5.7 implementation strategies used during the life cycle strategy meaning key point big bang all selected modules or locations go live at approximately the same time. faster transition, but higher cutover risk and need for strong readiness. phased implementation modules, departments or locations are introduced in planned stages. risk is spread over time, but temporary interfaces with old systems may be needed. pilot implementation erp is first introduced in one selected department, branch or location. lessons from the pilot are applied before wider rollout. parallel running old and new systems operate together for a defined period. provides a comparison and fallback, but increases workload and cost. 5.8 critical success factors of erp implementation top management support: leaders must provide direction, resources and timely decisions. clear objectives and scope: project goals must be realistic and measurable. effective project management: activities, milestones, costs, responsibilities and risks must be controlled. business process alignment: erp configuration should support approved and efficient processes. end-user participation: employees must contribute to requirements, testing, training and adoption. good data quality: incorrect or duplicate data should be cleaned before migration. suitable training and change management: users should understand the system and the reasons for new processes. testing and risk control: business scenarios, integrations and security should be tested before go-live. vendor and consultant support: the project needs suitable product expertise and implementation assistance. post-go-live support: issues must be resolved and benefits monitored after deployment. 5.9 common problems during the implementation life cycle unclear objectives and frequent scope changes. selection of an erp package that does not fit business requirements. weak project planning or insufficient management support. resistance to process change and low employee participation. excessive customisation and complex integrations. poor data quality and incomplete migration. insufficient testing or inadequate user training. unplanned downtime, cutover problems or weak post-go-live support. 5.10 practical example consider a manufacturing company that wants to integrate purchasing, inventory, production, sales and finance. first, it identifies problems caused by separate spreadsheets and delayed stock information. it evaluates erp products and selects a suitable package. a project team then plans the work, compares current processes with erp functions and redesigns purchase and production workflows. the team configures the modules, migrates item and supplier data, trains key users and tests the complete procure-to-pay and order-to-cash processes. after final checks, the company goes live. employees receive role-based training and the support team monitors errors, performance and user feedback. this complete journey represents the erp implementation life cycle. ★ complete exam-ready 15-mark answer question: what do you understand by erp implementation background and problem: before its global standardisation programme, different nestlé businesses and countries used different information systems, data structures and business processes. this made it difficult to obtain consistent information and coordinate operations across the group. erp solution: nestlé launched the globe (global business excellence) programme around 2000, using sap as the foundation for a common global business platform. the aim was to standardise key processes and data across functions such as finance, supply chain, factories, human resources, sales and marketing. implementation approach: the programme used a common global template based on standard business practices. local changes were intended to be limited to legal, fiscal or specific business requirements. business employees and leaders were involved in defining and adopting the common processes. challenges and learning: the historical rollout showed that a global erp programme can face employee resistance, process-reengineering difficulties, training gaps and coordination problems. a widely discussed account of nestlé usa's earlier sap implementation described how insufficient involvement of affected business groups and inadequate preparation contributed to resistance and disruption. this is an important reminder that software configuration alone cannot ensure success. outcome and later original globe rollout. lessons learned: global organisations benefit from common processes and standardised data. top-management support and business participation are essential. employees affected standardisation; lesson — change management and employee involvement. waycool: sap s/4hana; reported 22-day go-live across 44 plants; lesson — integration, dedicated team and training. raychem rpg: oracle fusion cloud erp, scm and cx; reported 25% improvement in competitive bidding response times. common success factors: management support, clear goals, user participation, clean data, training, testing and support. do not confuse reported customer metrics with general guarantees for every erp project. sources and learning references institute of chartered accountants of india — erp overview
